title: Can a Hausa-First Approach Expand Digital Inclusion for Northern Nigerian Women?

content:
By Saratu Abubakar

Through a Hausa-first approach, Her Tech Hub is exploring how language can shape women’s access to technology, digital skills and economic opportunities in Northern Nigeria.

Technology is becoming increasingly woven into education, work and economic activity. But as access to technology becomes more important, so does the language used to explain it. Technical concepts can be difficult to navigate when the language of instruction is unfamiliar to the learner. This raises an important question about digital access in places where some learners and potential users are not first-language English speakers: could learning about technology through a familiar language make its concepts more accessible to marginalised groups, such as women?

Convened by Her Tech Hub under the theme Bridging the Digital, Gender and Language Divide for Northern Women, FasaHer Conference brought attention to the relationship between language, technology and women’s participation in the digital economy. Its Hausa-first approach places language at the centre of conversations about technology education, digital access and the possibility of creating lasting economic opportunities for Northern Nigerian women.

When language becomes a barrier to technology

English is widely used in technology education and shapes how people develop digital skills. However, for those whose first language or cultural context differs from the dominant language of instruction, relying primarily on English can create barriers to access and learning.

Encountering technical concepts for the first time in a language one is not proficient in can make learning more difficult. The same challenge extends to entrepreneurs trying to understand digital tools, communicate their products to customers or use technology to improve their businesses. It can also affect the customers these business owners are trying to reach.

In response to these language barriers, FasaHer’s Hausa-first approach promotes the teaching of technology concepts through a more familiar language. For Hausa-speaking women who are more comfortable communicating in their mother tongue, using Hausa alongside English can help them engage with technical ideas more easily at different stages of learning.

Safiyya Daba, Founder  of Her Tech Hub, explained that the Hausa-first approach uses contextual mapping and native analogies to break down complex technical principles into more intuitive concepts. Rather than relying on rigid, literal translations, the framework uses familiar language and contexts to make technology education more accessible to Hausa-speaking women and young learners.

Learning in a familiar language can make concepts easier to understand, build confidence and create room for curiosity. For entrepreneurs, it can make digital tools easier to understand and encourage them to explore how these tools might support their businesses. Accessible language therefore provides a starting point from which learners can develop the practical skills needed to apply what they learn. Ultimately, learning in a familiar language can help more people use and build with technology.

Hausa Tech Ƙamus

At the FasaHer conference, Her Tech Hub unveiled the Hausa Tech Ƙamus, a dictionary designed to translate tech  terminologies into conversational Hausa.The Ƙamus is expected to serve as a tool for making technical vocabulary more accessible to Hausa speakers and expanding the availability of Hausa-language resources for technology education.

According to Daba, the dictionary contains 200 vetted foundational terms covering generative artificial intelligence, cloud architecture, data protection and everyday digital productivity. Its approach to translating technical terminology is based on contextual mapping rather than rigid, literal translations, with the aim of making these concepts more accessible to Hausa speakers.

For learners who are more comfortable engaging in Hausa, repeatedly encountering unfamiliar terms without clear explanations can create a barrier to learning. They may have to work through both the meaning of a concept and the language used to describe it. The Ƙamus could therefore serve as a useful reference that learners can return to whenever they encounter unfamiliar technical terminology.

While it is a welcome initiative, the yardstick for the success of the Ƙamus will be how effectively it is incorporated into the technology learning ecosystem to support learning and practical application.

Why Culturally Relevant Learning Matters

Culturally relevant learning can make education more accessible by taking learners’ circumstances into account. In technology education, this means considering participants’ educational backgrounds, business activities and levels of technical experience. A Hausa-first approach offers one way to do this by connecting technical concepts to familiar experiences and everyday needs.

Making technology education relevant also means recognising that learners have different interests and goals. A woman running a small business, for example, may want to use digital tools to reach customers, manage orders or improve record-keeping. Another learner may be interested in artificial intelligence, programming or pursuing a career in technology. Both need access to relevant knowledge, but the training and support that help them achieve their goals may differ.

A key consideration is whether a Hausa-first approach to learning equips learners with knowledge they can apply to their individual circumstances. Understanding a digital tool is one thing; knowing how to use it to address a particular need is another. The relevance of training lies partly in how well it connects what is being taught to what learners hope to achieve.

By making technical knowledge easier to engage with, a Hausa-first approach can provide an important entry point into technology education. Combined with practical training and continued opportunities to develop their skills, it can contribute to more meaningful participation in the digital economy.

Economic Opportunity

A Hausa-first approach extends beyond helping women understand technical concepts. It also seeks to improve access to knowledge that could help entrepreneurs use digital tools more effectively and pursue economic opportunities. This is particularly relevant for women looking to apply digital skills to their businesses.

However, language is not the only factor shaping women’s participation in the digital economy. Daba highlights other barriers, including limited access to devices, high data costs and inadequate access to digital skills training. In response to some of these challenges, Her Tech Hub is introducing subsidised digital literacy cohorts, low-bandwidth micro-learning modules and an automated WhatsApp lookup tool to support continuous learning.

Technology provides useful tools for improving business operations, but access to these tools is only one part of building a business. Making effective use of them also requires knowledge, access to markets and financial resources.

Access to finance remains an important constraint for women-led enterprises in Northern Nigeria. A March 2025 report by CrossBoundary, examining financing for women-led enterprises in the region, found that more than 70% of participants relied on personal savings, family and friends to finance their businesses. The report also identified limited access to collateral and gaps in awareness of financing options as barriers to business growth. These constraints can affect how much entrepreneurs are able to invest in their businesses.

For women who are more comfortable communicating in Hausa, language may also influence how easily they access and understand business and financial information. Where information about funding opportunities, business requirements and financing options is primarily communicated in English, a Hausa-first approach could help make some of this knowledge more accessible. It could support women’s understanding of formal business processes and available financing options. However, understanding these opportunities does not necessarily guarantee access to funding, which may also depend on financial resources, eligibility requirements and other institutional factors.

Building a More Inclusive Digital Future

The economic value of digital education lies in how learners apply the skills they acquire. In its 2025 account of the Gina Mata, Gina Al-Umma programme, the World Bank reported that a midline assessment found 27% of participants in its virtual-economy training had increased their income by incorporating social media marketing into their businesses. This illustrates how practical digital skills can help women strengthen existing businesses and explore new income opportunities, highlighting the importance of connecting technology education to tangible economic outcomes.

FasaHer’s Hausa-first approach offers an opportunity to examine how familiar-language instruction and resources such as the Hausa Tech Ƙamus can make technology education more accessible to women. These skills could help women apply technology to their businesses and work towards making them investment-ready.The economic opportunities available through digital education are also shaped by access to knowledge, tools and resources. Language is one part of that equation, alongside digital skills and access to finance.

Recognising the different ways women can engage with technology and contribute to its development is important to building an inclusive digital ecosystem. This means creating opportunities for women to participate not only as users of technology, but also as entrepreneurs, innovators and creators of digital solutions. As Northern Nigeria’s technology ecosystem continues to grow, ensuring women’s participation at these different levels is an important part of building an inclusive and sustainable digital future for the region.

title: FasaHer Wants More Northern Nigerian Women in Tech
excerpt: HER Tech Hub is set to host FasaHer on October 10 at Baba-Ahmed University, Kano, bringing together female entrepreneurs, tech professionals and aspiring tech builders from across Northern Nigeria. The...
content:
HER Tech Hub is set to host FasaHer on October 10 at Baba-Ahmed University, Kano, bringing together female entrepreneurs, tech professionals and aspiring tech builders from across Northern Nigeria.

The organisers describe FasaHer as a “Hausa-first” initiative designed to make technology and entrepreneurship opportunities more accessible to women across Northern Nigeria.The conference will be addressing some of the barriers facing women in the region’s technology ecosystem.

According to the organisers, less than 18 per cent of Northern Nigeria’s technology workforce is made up of women, highlighting the need for more targeted opportunities and support for women looking to build careers and businesses in the sector.

The conference is expected to bring together  tech leaders and enthusiasts  for practical masterclasses and sessions focused on entrepreneurship, technology and digital skills.

A key feature of the conference is its focus on accessibility, with sessions delivered in both Hausa and English.

title: How iDICE Is Building Pathways for Emerging Founders in Northern Nigeria
excerpt: “Mentorship is more important than funding sometimes. If you get funding but don’t know how to manage it, you just run around in circles....
content:
By Tahir Ahmad & Saratu Abubakar

“Mentorship is more important than funding sometimes. If you get funding but don’t know how to manage it, you just run around in circles. We focused on solving real problems first, and the opportunities followed,” Muhammad Auwal Ahmad, founder of Flowdiary, told The Zango in an exclusive interview last year.

His observation captures one of the less discussed challenges facing emerging founders in Northern Nigeria. While access to funding remains a major concern for startups, money alone does not necessarily give a founder the knowledge to build a sustainable company. Without access to skill-building programmes, mentorship, infrastructure and capital, promising ideas can struggle to move beyond potential.

In Nigeria, the Investment in Digital and Creative Enterprise (iDICE) initiative is using its position as a government-backed programme to help build an ecosystem that supports emerging startups. The bigger question is whether the structures being put in place can provide the support needed to move promising ideas from potential to sustainable ventures.

Launched in March 2023, iDICE is a $618 million programme designed to strengthen Nigeria’s digital and creative economy through skills development, access to finance, and institutional and ecosystem support. Implemented by the Bank of Industry, the initiative brings together a range of programmes including startup development and innovation infrastructure.

Startup Bridge

For many innovators entering the technology ecosystem, particularly those moving from an idea into a business, knowing what to build is only the beginning. They also need people who can help them understand customers, refine their business models, manage finances, measure traction, prepare for investment and navigate the mistakes that often accompany entrepreneurship.

At first glance, Startup Bridge looks like another entrepreneurship programme: founders receive training, mentorship and, for those who meet specified milestones, access to funding. However, it takes a broader position. Through Startup Bridge, the iDICE initiative supports Nigerian founders from early-stage ideas to scalable ventures through targeted training, mentorship and access to capital. It operates under two distinct programmes: Founders Lab and Growth Lab. The Founders Lab provides performance-based grants of up to ₦10,000,000, while the Growth Lab offers equity investment of $100,000.

For a newcomer entering the tech ecosystem, the journey from an idea to a functioning and sustainable venture can be difficult. Many founders may have technical skills or a solution to a problem but lack other skills needed to build and grow a company.

When government backs startups at the early stages of development, it can help bridge the gap between a promising idea and a venture that is ready for private investment. At this stage, private investors often require more than a bright idea. They need evidence that a product works, that there is a market for it and that the founder can execute. Government-backed programmes such as Startup Bridge can provide some of the funding, training and support needed to help founders reach that stage, creating better conditions for private investment to follow.

The need is particularly relevant to Northern Nigeria, where a growing generation of young people are building technology solutions around different needs. But turning promising ideas into durable ventures requires more than technical ability. It requires an ecosystem that helps founders develop the commercial, managerial and strategic capabilities needed to survive beyond the early excitement surrounding a new product.

The Ecosystem

Behind every thriving startup ecosystem is a network of organisations and people helping founders navigate the journey from an idea to a viable venture. Local ecosystem actors such as regional hubs often begin that journey with founders, providing the connections, knowledge and support they need at different stages of building their ventures.

In Northern Nigeria, these organisations have played an important role in strengthening the region’s emerging technology ecosystem, creating spaces for founders to develop their ideas, access mentorship, connect with funding and build networks that matter. Often through private investment, these ecosystem actors set up varying degrees of infrastructure that allow founders to kick-start their journey.

That role is reflected in the experience of Said Ismail Aliyu, CEO of Northdemy, who works closely with founders through an innovation hub. He argues that Northern Nigeria is not short of talent or ambition. Rather, what is often missing are structured pathways that can take founders from learning a skill, to building a product, creating a business and eventually accessing capital and markets.

The Startup Bridge hub model builds on this existing role by working with local institutions to support founder mobilisation, screening, localised engagement and community building. It also shows why local hubs matter: they can connect founders to opportunities and networks beyond their immediate environment while providing support closer to where they are building.

The experience of its first cohort also demonstrates why mentorship should not be treated as an optional addition to funding. One lead mentor involved in the programme reflected on 15 weeks of structured venture support, describing work with founders around business-model refinement, financial modelling, pitch-deck preparation and market-expansion strategies. The mentor said the process helped founders improve their metrics, validate market traction and strengthen investor readiness.

That approach addresses a common weakness in the startup conversation: focusing on how much money a founder can raise before asking whether the founder has the systems and knowledge to deploy it effectively.

A Founder’s Experience

Shariff Muhammad, founder of PayTuition, the value of the iDICE Startup Bridge programme extends beyond the funding attached to it. PayTuition is a platform that helps parents and students pay school fees online while allowing primary, secondary and tertiary institutions to manage fee collection.

Muhammad said the programme gave him access to knowledge, industry experience and connections that would have been difficult to obtain independently. For him, the opportunity to interact directly with experienced entrepreneurs was particularly significant as a founder building from Northern Nigeria.

“You might not leave with the grant, but the knowledge, the experience, the connections that comes with it is very, very immense,” he said.

Muhammad said iDICE’s decision to bring industry experts into the programme created opportunities for founders to learn directly from people who had built and scaled businesses. He described the one-on-one interactions as particularly valuable, especially for entrepreneurs operating outside Nigeria’s major technology centres.

“Imagine someone building from Gagarawa in Jigawa State having to connect with an entrepreneur who built a billion-dollar company from Lagos, having a one-on-one session with that person,” he said.

Muhammad also said that such access addresses one of the gaps facing founders in Northern Nigeria, which is limited access to experienced mentors and wider business networks.

“The mentorship has not been there, especially we builders from Northern Nigeria here,” he said.

The programme’s milestone-based structure was another aspect he highlighted. Rather than simply providing funding upfront, Muhammad said founders were expected to meet specific milestones before progressing to the next stage. This, he argued, gave participants an opportunity to develop the knowledge and systems needed to build their ventures before putting the funding to work.

For PayTuition, the eventual grant therefore became an extension of the learning process rather than its sole benefit. Muhammad said the funding would allow founders to put into practice what they had learned during the programme, turning training and mentorship into further product and business development.

The North

Nigeria’s technology story has often been told through a relatively small number of major urban centres. But an innovation economy that depends on talent from only a few locations leaves potential outside those centres less connected to the capital, expertise and networks needed to develop it.

Startup Bridge’s first cohort included ventures from every state and the FCT. This broadens the reach of the country’s ecosystem and creates more points of entry for founders outside the established technology centres. Rather than making a founder’s location a barrier to accessing early-stage support, the model brings that support closer to where founders are building.

For Northern Nigeria’s emerging ecosystem, that proposition is particularly significant. Structured mentorship can help reduce the isolation that sometimes comes with building a startup outside Nigeria’s most established technology hubs. Irrespective of location, the programme allows a founder to benefit from access to experienced entrepreneurs, investors, technical experts and fellow founders without having to rely solely on informal networks within their immediate environment.

Mentorship programmes can help reduce some of those gaps by connecting emerging founders to people and institutions beyond their immediate environment. They can also create communities where founders learn from one another rather than building in isolation.

The impact can extend beyond the individual entrepreneur. When a founder learns how to manage finances, validate a product, build a team or approach investors, those skills can eventually be transferred to employees, peers and future founders. Successful entrepreneurs can subsequently become mentors themselves, creating a cycle in which experience remains within the ecosystem.

The Future

Recent developments under iDICE illustrate the scale of this potential. The first Founders Lab cohort selected 185 founders from all 36 states and the Federal Capital Territory, while the programme has since expanded to a second cohort of 200 innovators. The first cohort also reached a stage where 50 selected high-performing idea-stage founders were set to receive about ₦330 million in non-dilutive funding for continued venture development.

However, the value of iDICE extends beyond the number of grants awarded. Its longer-term significance will be measured by what happens after the funding is allocated and the mentorship ends. What matters is whether supported founders can turn early-stage capital and support into sustainable companies, continue solving real market problems, create jobs and attract further investment. If those ventures can survive beyond the programme and grow without continued public support, the Nigerian government could contribute to shaping a more self-sustaining technology ecosystem in the years ahead.

What matters is building a system in which a young person with an idea can find not only funding, but also someone who can ask the right questions, provide honest feedback and help turn an idea into a viable enterprise.

Ahmad’s experience with Flowdiary captures the principle simply: opportunities can follow when founders first concentrate on solving real problems.

For the Northern tech ecosystem, the next step may therefore be to build more pathways that help founders do exactly that, with mentorship, structured programmes, community, market access and appropriate capital working together. If sustained, such an ecosystem could help move Northern Nigeria’s technology community from producing promising ideas to developing a deeper pipeline of capable founders and scalable ventures.

title: NITDA Opens National AI Innovation Challenge, Invites Nigerians To Build With N-ATLAS
excerpt: The National Information Technology Development Agency (NITDA) has opened applications for the 2026 National AI Innovation Challenge, inviting Nigerian developers, startups, universities, researchers and innovators to build practical artificial intelligence...
content:
The National Information Technology Development Agency (NITDA) has opened applications for the 2026 National AI Innovation Challenge, inviting Nigerian developers, startups, universities, researchers and innovators to build practical artificial intelligence solutions using N-ATLAS.

The challenge, implemented through the National Centre for Artificial Intelligence and Robotics (NCAIR) and the Office for Nigerian Digital Innovation (ONDI), is designed to deepen the development and adoption of Nigeria’s artificial intelligence capabilities through locally relevant applications.

Applications opened on September 22 and will close on October 12, 2026, at 11:59 p.m. WAT, according to the official challenge portal.

N-ATLAS, which stands for Nigerian Atlas for Languages and AI at Scale, is an open-source multilingual large language model developed to understand and generate Nigerian languages and forms of expression.

The Federal Ministry of Communications, Innovation and Digital Economy launched N-ATLAS in September 2025 as an open-source AI resource intended to support the development of AI applications that reflect Nigeria’s linguistic diversity. The model was developed with Awarri and in partnership with NITDA and NCAIR.

NCAIR describes N-ATLAS as an open-source multilingual model that initially supports Yoruba, Hausa, Igbo and Nigerian-accented English. The model also includes automatic speech recognition capabilities for voice-based applications.

The 2026 National AI Innovation Challenge is intended to move N-ATLAS beyond model availability towards practical infrastructure, applications and specialised tools that developers, businesses and citizens can use.

Participants are required to build working solutions integrated with N-ATLAS and can choose from three challenge areas: developer infrastructure, voice-first access and sector-specific AI.

Under developer infrastructure, participants are expected to create tools that make N-ATLAS easier to integrate, test, adapt and deploy. Examples include software development kits, browser-based testing environments, fine-tuning tools and developer documentation.

The voice-first category focuses on applications that allow Nigerians to access services without relying primarily on text. Proposed applications could use channels such as WhatsApp voice notes, interactive voice response systems, USSD-based voice services and low-bandwidth mobile applications.

Possible applications include agricultural advisory services, education support, primary healthcare information, civic information and financial literacy.

The third category focuses on adapting N-ATLAS for specific sectors, including education, primary healthcare, agriculture, legal and civic services, and financial literacy.

Participants in this category will be expected to fine-tune N-ATLAS for a defined domain and demonstrate measurable improvements over the base model. They must also deploy their work through a documented application programming interface that other developers can integrate.

The challenge is open to two broad groups: academia and research teams, and innovation and enterprise teams.

Academic teams can include university-based researchers, postgraduate researchers and faculty, while the innovation and enterprise track covers startups, technology companies, social enterprises, independent developers and innovation hubs. Team requirements vary by track, but submissions must include a functioning technical solution integrated with N-ATLAS.

NITDA said the challenge is intended to deepen technical development of N-ATLAS through developer tools, fine-tuned models, datasets and ecosystem contributions, while also encouraging real-world applications and collaboration between universities, the private sector and government.

The challenge organisers have also ruled out concept-only submissions. According to the official guidelines, research papers, proposals or frameworks without a functioning build will not be evaluated, while solutions built around other general-purpose foundation models rather than N-ATLAS will not qualify.

The challenge forms part of broader efforts by NCAIR to promote research, development and practical applications of artificial intelligence and other emerging technologies in Nigeria. NCAIR is a NITDA special-purpose vehicle focused on AI, robotics, drones, Internet of Things and other emerging technologies.

The Federal Government launched N-ATLAS in 2025 against the backdrop of Nigeria’s linguistic diversity. The Ministry of Communications, Innovation and Digital Economy said the project was designed to advance natural language processing for under-represented languages while creating opportunities for applications in education, health, commerce and governance.

The 2026 challenge will therefore focus on how developers and researchers can turn that underlying model into practical products and infrastructure for Nigerian users.

Following the October 12 application deadline, the organisers have scheduled N-ATLAS integration checks for October 15 to 17, shortlisting between October 16 and 20, and a mentorship phase from October 25 to November 4. Finalists are scheduled to showcase their solutions at the Digital Nigeria Showcase from November 8 to 10.

Nigerian developers, startups, researchers, universities and other eligible innovators can apply through the National AI Innovation Challenge platform before the October 12 deadline.

title: Applications Open for the 2026 Innovative Pitch Contest
excerpt: The Innovative Pitch Contest (IPC) has opened applications for its 2026 edition, inviting Senior Secondary Schools across Nigeria to participate in the competition designed to promote innovation, creativity and problem-solving...
content:
The Innovative Pitch Contest (IPC) has opened applications for its 2026 edition, inviting Senior Secondary Schools across Nigeria to participate in the competition designed to promote innovation, creativity and problem-solving among young people.

Now in its third edition, the competition, organised by Thescathcompanies, aims to identify innovative ideas and nurture entrepreneurial skills among secondary school students by challenging them to tackle real-world problems and transform their ideas into viable solutions.

The 2026 edition is open to schools across all 36 states of Nigeria, with the organisers announcing an expanded prize package comprising cash prizes, scholarships and access to incubation programmes for successful participants.

According to the organisers, IPC provides students with a platform to develop, refine and present innovative ideas capable of addressing real-world challenges while encouraging them to think creatively and develop practical solutions.

Interested Senior Secondary Schools across Nigeria can apply for the 2026 Innovative Pitch Contest through the official application portal. Applications will close on October 30, 2026.

title: NITDA Opens Startup Applications For Builders Festival, Targets ₦3bn Investment Pipeline
excerpt: The National Information Technology Development Agency (NITDA), in partnership with Tech Revolution Africa, has opened applications for startups to participate in the 2026 Builders Festival, an initiative designed to connect...
content:
The National Information Technology Development Agency (NITDA), in partnership with Tech Revolution Africa, has opened applications for startups to participate in the 2026 Builders Festival, an initiative designed to connect technology companies with real-world challenges facing Nigerian institutions.

The programme will form part of the Digital Nigeria International Conference, Exhibition and Awards (DNICE) 2026, scheduled to hold from November 10 to 12 at the Bola Ahmed Tinubu International Conference Centre in Abuja.

According to the organisers, the Builders Festival will match startups with institutions seeking technology-driven solutions to operational and structural challenges, with selected founders given opportunities to pitch their products, enter a deal room and pursue investment and deployment opportunities.

The initiative is targeting more than ₦3 billion in investments and is expected to bring startups, investors, government agencies, businesses and other ecosystem stakeholders together.

The official Digital Nigeria platform describes the Builders Festival as an initiative where “Nigeria’s toughest challenges meet its smartest builders”, with a focus on connecting institutions with deployment-ready startups through structured matching and pilot-ready collaboration.

The programme will cover startups developing solutions across sectors including healthcare, education technology, logistics, supply chain, artificial intelligence, cloud computing, data, agricultural technology, connectivity, financial technology and e-governance.

Under the programme, participating institutions identify operational challenges, after which qualified startups with relevant solutions are matched with the organisations. The matched teams will then meet in a live deal room at DNICE 2026 to discuss pilot commitments and potential partnerships.

The process represents a shift from the conventional hackathon model, according to information released by NITDA and Tech Revolution Africa.

In June, the organisations announced the Builders Festival as a “demand discovery” programme that allows government agencies, non-governmental organisations and private-sector institutions to present specific problems requiring technology-based solutions.

The challenges initially identified include areas such as financial inclusion, regulatory compliance, healthcare distribution, data infrastructure and supply chain logistics. Growth-stage technology startups are then expected to propose solutions to the selected challenges.

Dr Aristotle Onumo, NITDA’s Director of Stakeholder Management and Partnerships, said the programme was intended to connect local technology innovation with institutional needs.

“Our objective at NITDA is to foster an environment where local innovation directly services institutional needs,” Onumo said.

He added that the framework would help mobilise Nigerian technology talent to address administrative and commercial infrastructure challenges.

Glory Olamigoke, Co-founder of Tech Revolution Africa, said the initiative was designed to address what she described as a coordination gap between institutions with complex problems and technology builders capable of solving them.

“Africa does not suffer from a shortage of technical talent; it suffers from a coordination gap between complex, systemic problems and the builders who can solve them,” Olamigoke said.

Beyond investment opportunities, the Builders Festival is expected to provide participating startups with access to potential customers and institutions that could deploy their products.

The organisers’ broader targets include more than 100 business deals, 150 participating institutions and over 500 investors, ecosystem leaders, executives and partners. Tech Revolution Africa and NITDA have described the programme as a platform for moving startups from product development towards commercial deployment.

Successful startups will be invited to showcase their solutions during the live Builders Festival at DNICE 2026, where they will have the opportunity to engage institutions and investors.

The official Digital Nigeria website currently lists the conference for November 10 to 12 in Abuja and identifies NITDA as the initiative behind the conference. It also lists the Builders Festival as one of its major components.

Startups interested in participating can submit their applications through the Digital Nigeria and Builders Festival platforms as the organisers prepare for the November conference.

The initiative is expected to provide another pathway for Nigerian technology companies to demonstrate how locally developed products can address institutional challenges while creating opportunities for commercial deployment, partnerships and investment.

title: Global Tech Africa 2026 Set To Bring Tech, Investment Conversations To Kano
excerpt: Global Tech Africa 2026 Set To Bring Tech, Investment Conversations To Kano Kano is set to host the 2026 edition of the Global Tech Africa (GTA) Conference from November 3...
content:
Global Tech Africa 2026 Set To Bring Tech, Investment Conversations To Kano

Kano is set to host the 2026 edition of the Global Tech Africa (GTA) Conference from November 3 to 5, bringing technology entrepreneurs, investors, policymakers and industry leaders together to explore technology-driven industrialisation and market access across Africa.

The conference, organised by the FutureMap Foundation in partnership with the National Information Technology Development Agency (NITDA), will be held at Amani Events Center, GRA, Kano, under the theme, “Connecting Africa, Accelerating Growth,” with a sub-theme focused on “Industrialization, Market Access & the Sahel Gateway.”

The organisers said the decision to bring the conference to Kano for the first time is linked to the city’s position as a major commercial centre and gateway to the Sahel.

According to the GTA organisers, Kano serves a market corridor covering more than 350 million people across the region and facilitates an estimated $2 billion to $5 billion in annual cross-border trade, with further growth expected as implementation of the African Continental Free Trade Area (AfCFTA) deepens.

The conference will focus on the use of technology to strengthen manufacturing, logistics, digital trade, payments, traceability, artificial intelligence and other areas capable of expanding regional markets.

The organisers have also outlined specific targets for the 2026 edition, including 1,000 business-to-business meetings, 15 industrial partnerships, 10 trade corridor agreements and more than 500 jobs created or committed through its jobs pipeline.

The programme is also expected to produce at least three regional trade or sister-city memoranda of understanding and a proposed Kano Digital Industrialisation Accord.

For startups and founders, the conference is expected to provide opportunities to meet investors, participate in curated business meetings and explore pathways for scaling products across African markets.

Its programme includes a closed-door deal room for matched founders and investors, investment roundtables, policy labs, workshops on scaling businesses across Africa and sessions examining the relationship between artificial intelligence and commercial opportunities.

Developers and technology professionals will also have access to technical and practical sessions, while creatives and other participants in the digital economy are expected to engage with discussions around talent, innovation and Africa’s emerging enterprise and content ecosystems.

The organisers said the conference is designed to move beyond conversations about technology consumption towards the creation, deployment and export of African technology and intellectual property.

The 2026 edition builds on previous Global Tech Africa conferences. According to the FutureMap Foundation, the 2024 edition brought together more than 2,000 participants, including policymakers from 10 African countries, more than 150 global investors and venture capitalists, and generated 30 strategic partnership agreements and $120 million in handshake investment commitments.

The conference has also previously brought together investors, regulators, entrepreneurs, academics and other technology stakeholders through plenary sessions, breakout sessions, pitch competitions, exhibitions and networking activities.

For the Kano edition, the organisers have positioned the city as a link between Nigeria and markets across the Sahel, with the conference expected to examine how technology can support trade and industrial activity along regional corridors.

The event is being backed institutionally by NITDA, with FutureMap Foundation serving as the convener. Qorebox has also been announced as a private-sector partner for the 2026 edition.

Registration details and further information about participation are being released ahead of the November conference.

GTA 2026 is expected to bring together government, industry, investors, technology entrepreneurs and development institutions in Kano for discussions centred on industrialisation, investment, market access and the use of technology to support intra-African trade.

title: Arewa Tech Fest Says Lagos Exchange Is Not Moving Festival From North
excerpt: Arewa Tech Fest (ATF) has clarified that its planned Lagos Exchange does not represent a relocation of the Northern Nigeria-focused technology festival to Lagos. The clarification follows what the organisers...
content:
Arewa Tech Fest (ATF) has clarified that its planned Lagos Exchange does not represent a relocation of the Northern Nigeria-focused technology festival to Lagos.

The clarification follows what the organisers described as misconceptions about the purpose of the Lagos Exchange, which they said is an investment roadshow designed to connect Northern Nigeria’s growing innovation ecosystem with investors, corporate partners and global stakeholders.

Arewa Tech Fest said the festival remains firmly rooted in Northern Nigeria, with previous editions held as Spotlight on Kano in 2024 and Spotlight on Katsina in 2025.

The next edition, Spotlight on Zamfara, is currently in development and will continue the festival’s focus on promoting innovation, entrepreneurship and ecosystem development across the region.

According to the organisers, the Lagos Exchange is a separate strategic engagement created to take Northern Nigeria’s innovation story to a wider investment audience.

“Contrary to common assumptions, the Lagos Exchange is not a festival and does not represent a relocation of Arewa Tech Fest to Lagos,” the organisers said in a statement.

They said the roadshow would provide a platform for Northern startups and emerging sectors to engage with capital providers, corporate organisations and international stakeholders.

The Lagos Exchange is expected to feature keynote addresses, executive roundtables, a capital room for private deal-making sessions and a demo day where startups from Northern Nigeria will pitch their businesses to investors.

The organisers said the initiative is intended to address the investment and visibility gap faced by businesses and innovators in the region by creating direct connections with capital and strategic partners outside Northern Nigeria.

“Arewa Tech Fest is built in the North, for the North. The Lagos Exchange is a deliberate extension taking Northern innovation to world,” the statement said.

The organisers added that the Lagos engagement represents the beginning of a broader strategy to take Northern Nigeria’s innovation ecosystem beyond regional boundaries.

They said similar investment-focused roadshows could be expanded to other cities across Africa and globally as ATF seeks to create more opportunities for Northern founders and enterprises.

Arewa Tech Fest said it remains committed to empowering Northern Nigeria’s innovation ecosystem while building connections that can help local talent, ideas and businesses gain greater visibility, investment and partnerships needed to scale.

The clarification positions the Lagos Exchange as an extension of ATF’s Northern-focused mission rather than a change in the location or identity of the festival.

title: From AI Consumer to Builder: Nigeria Charts Digital Sovereignty Path at GITEX 2026
excerpt: Nigeria has outlined an ambitious push to move from consuming foreign technologies to building and controlling its own artificial intelligence, data and digital infrastructure, as government and technology leaders gathered...
content:
Nigeria has outlined an ambitious push to move from consuming foreign technologies to building and controlling its own artificial intelligence, data and digital infrastructure, as government and technology leaders gathered in Abuja for the GITEX Nigeria 2026 Government Leadership & AI Summit.

The summit, themed “Beyond Connectivity: The Bridge to Sovereign AI and Innovation,” brought together government officials, technology leaders and industry stakeholders to examine Nigeria’s readiness to develop and control critical technologies as artificial intelligence assumes a growing role in economic development, national security and public administration.

At the centre of the discussions was a call for Nigeria to build the infrastructure, skills, policies and technological capabilities required to exercise greater control over its digital future.

Secretary to the Government of the Federation (SGF), George Akume, said Nigeria must move beyond being a consumer of technology and position itself as a builder, producer and exporter of digital solutions and artificial intelligence.

Akume, who was represented by the Permanent Secretary of the Political and Economic Affairs Office, Mrs Bekearedebo Warrens, said the Federal Government was implementing reforms designed to establish the foundations of a competitive digital economy.

He identified digital identity, connectivity, talent development, cloud infrastructure and data centres as key areas of the digital transformation agenda of the administration of President Bola Ahmed Tinubu.

“These reforms capture the very essence of where Nigeria is headed, not merely as a consumer of technology, but as a builder, producer and exporter of digital solutions and artificial intelligence,” he said.

According to the SGF, the government’s digital identity reforms are aimed at strengthening Nigeria’s data sovereignty and providing a more robust foundation for digital public infrastructure.

He also highlighted Project Bridge, through which the Federal Government plans to deploy about 90,000 kilometres of fibre-optic infrastructure to connect states, local government areas and wards across the country.

The connectivity programme, he said, is expected to be complemented by telecommunications infrastructure designed to extend broadband access to millions of Nigerians, particularly those in underserved communities.

Beyond infrastructure, Akume pointed to the 3 Million Technical Talent programme as a major part of Nigeria’s strategy to develop the human capital required for the digital economy.

He said the programme had recorded about 1.87 million registrations across the country’s 774 local government areas, with more than 125,000 Nigerians trained in fields including cloud computing, artificial intelligence, cybersecurity and software engineering.

The objective, he said, is to build a workforce capable of developing digital products and technologies rather than relying entirely on innovations created elsewhere.

On cloud infrastructure, Akume said the recently unveiled National Digital Cloud Policy was targeting $750 million in private investment in Nigeria’s cloud and data infrastructure over the next 24 months.

He said the policy, alongside Project Bridge and the 3MTT programme, was intended to bring together infrastructure, skills, government demand and private-sector investment to create a stronger domestic technology ecosystem.

The Director-General of the National Information Technology Development Agency (NITDA), Kashifu Inuwa Abdullahi, said artificial intelligence should be viewed as strategic infrastructure and not merely another technology.

Inuwa said the emergence of AI had made technological sovereignty increasingly important because the technology could help governments build intelligence around their economies, citizens and national security.

He argued that AI sovereignty should extend beyond geopolitics to include Nigeria’s ability to exercise digital self-determination across the entire technology stack.

According to him, developing indigenous AI capabilities requires more than building AI models.

Nigeria must also invest in connectivity, computing power, data centres, cloud infrastructure, data governance and the broader digital systems that support the development and deployment of artificial intelligence.

“As a nation, we have capacity to build and develop the technology that can help us to build the intelligence about our nation,” Inuwa said.

“We need to start thinking about the connectivity, the compute power, the data centres, the cloud capability.”

The NITDA Director-General said Nigeria must also strengthen ownership and control of AI technologies, algorithms and data to ensure that digital systems increasingly reflect the country’s needs and operate within its legal and governance frameworks.

He highlighted the importance of data sovereignty and effective governance in developing AI models capable of addressing Nigeria’s specific economic, social and security challenges.

Inuwa also stressed the need for operational sovereignty, particularly over AI systems deployed in critical sectors such as finance, healthcare and education.

The key question, he suggested, is not only whether Nigeria can access AI systems, but who controls them, where the underlying data is stored and processed, and whether they operate under Nigerian laws.

He warned that dependence on external control over critical AI infrastructure could expose the country to manipulation and outside influence.

The NITDA chief said the agency’s efforts were aligned with the Federal Government’s Nigeria First Policy and focused on strengthening Nigeria’s digital, data, cloud and AI sovereignty.

He pointed to the recent signing of regulatory instruments relating to cloud and data sovereignty as important steps towards encouraging investment in data centres and strengthening the country’s digital infrastructure.

For Nigeria, the discussions at GITEX 2026 signal a broader shift in thinking about the next phase of its technology development: from simply expanding access to digital tools to building the capacity to own, govern and develop the technologies shaping the future.

With AI increasingly becoming part of economic systems, public services and national security, stakeholders at the summit argued that the country must build the foundations to ensure it is not merely a market for technologies developed elsewhere.

Akume called on government institutions, investors, developers, innovators and the private sector to use GITEX Nigeria as a platform for practical partnerships that can translate policy ambitions into technology, infrastructure and locally developed solutions.

He said Nigeria already possesses significant elements of the expertise, infrastructure and partnerships needed to build a more sovereign digital economy, but would require stronger collaboration and wider adoption to realise that potential.

As GITEX Nigeria 2026 continues, the challenge for the country’s technology ecosystem will be turning the ambition of AI sovereignty into tangible investments in computing infrastructure, cloud capacity, local data centres, technical talent and homegrown innovation.

For Nigeria’s growing technology ecosystem, the message from Abuja was clear: the race for AI leadership will not be won by countries that only consume the technology, but by those capable of building and controlling the infrastructure and intelligence behind it.

title: What Africa’s Changing Tech Ecosystem Means for Northern Nigeria
excerpt: African startups raised $1.44 billion in the first half of 2026, but that remains just one part of the story. Beneath it is a changing investment landscape in which climate...
content:
African startups raised $1.44 billion in the first half of 2026, but that remains just one part of the story. Beneath it is a changing investment landscape in which climate technology has overtaken fintech, investors are becoming more selective, and sustainable business models are gaining greater attention. For Northern Nigeria, these shifts could redefine where the region finds its next opportunities for growth.

Despite years of ecosystem building and significant untapped potential, Northern Nigeria’s technology ecosystem continues to navigate a critical question: how to turn its innovation capacity into sustained investor interest and scalable companies. Emerging trends across Africa’s investment landscape offer important clues about what this next phase may require, revealing the shifting investor priorities and business models likely to shape the region’s path forward.

The State of Tech in Africa H1 2026 report by TechCabal highlighted some of these trends. According to the report, climate technology has overtaken fintech as the continent’s leading investment sector, mergers and acquisitions are accelerating, and investors are placing greater emphasis on sustainable business models, disciplined execution, and long-term value creation.

Nigeria accounted for 11.5% of all startup funding raised across Africa during H1, with two Northern Nigerian startups represented among the continent’s top-funded companies: Kaduna-based Tomato Jos, which raised $2 million, and Abuja-based Agriarche, which secured $1.8 million in funding. These milestones reinforce the region’s place within Africa’s startup ecosystem and highlight the importance of understanding the forces shaping capital flows and what founders must build to compete for investment.

The report highlights that investors are looking beyond rapid growth, prioritising companies that are well managed, built on sustainable business models, and capable of delivering long-term value.

Beyond Raising Capital

From 2019 to date, Nigeria has attracted more than $5.23 billion in investment across 968 deals, reinforcing its position as one of Africa’s leading startup ecosystems. However, much of this capital continues to flow towards established innovation hubs.

As an emerging ecosystem, Northern Nigeria’s challenge extends beyond building strong companies. Founders must also find ways to increase visibility among investors and demonstrate why businesses from the region are positioned to compete for capital.

While total funding remained stable in Africa, the first half of 2026 recorded a 42% decline in completed deals, signalling a more selective investment environment. One of the report’s most important observations is that funding remains available, with fund managers securing $1.73 billion in fresh capital awaiting deployment. The changing funding environment, marked by fewer completed deals, raises the bar for attracting investment, making it increasingly important for companies emerging from Northern Nigeria to stand out in a more competitive market.

According to Deji Garuba, Executive Director of Africa Innovation Foundry, this shift towards evidence-based funding is likely to shape the next phase of Northern Nigeria’s startup ecosystem.

One area where changing investor priorities are becoming particularly evident is climate technology, which overtook fintech as Africa’s largest-funded sector for the first time. This shift points to growing investor interest in companies developing practical solutions to some of the continent’s most pressing challenges. Within Northern Nigeria, many of the region’s local challenges also present opportunities to tap into this innovation, with the potential to develop solutions that are not only locally relevant but also scalable across similar markets on the continent.

According to Salisu Abdullahi, founder of Trash2Cash, Northern Nigeria risks being left behind if it does not move quickly to position itself within the growing climate-tech economy. The region has significant renewable energy potential that could not only help address environmental challenges, but also unlock investment, economic growth and green jobs.

“Of course, while Africa does not contribute as much carbon emissions to cause rising effects of climate change globally, it is affected heavily and more than the rest of the world in disproportionate ways by the negative effects of the climate change, and therefore, the just rise in climate tech to tackle these challenges heads-on,” he added.

Emerging Pathways

The report highlighted a record 63 mergers and acquisitions in the first six months of 2026, and a significant rise in partnerships and regional expansion. These developments suggest that collaboration is becoming a key driver of growth. Startups are exploring the benefits of partnerships and acquisitions to access new markets and strengthen operations.

The Northern Nigerian ecosystem is also beginning to see this trend. Although still an emerging market, mergers and acquisitions are becoming increasingly relevant in the region, through emerging pathways such as startup-to-startup consolidation and informal acquisitions, Garuba said.

“For M&A to become a mature growth strategy in Northern Nigeria, startups must evolve from building just ‘apps’ to building ‘assets’ like proprietary data systems, distribution networks, licensed financial rails and embedded MSME ecosystems. Without these, there is nothing meaningful to acquire,” he added.

For Northern Nigeria, building evidence-backed businesses that can scale beyond a certain level, strengthening collaboration between founders, and building visibility at the national level will be essential to creating stronger pathways for companies to access markets, capital, and opportunities for growth.

The first half of 2026 suggests that the qualities attracting investment are evolving. Building globally competitive companies will require more than individual ambition. It will depend on an ecosystem that supports founders, encourages collaboration, and creates the conditions for innovation to scale. Although still an emerging market, Northern Nigeria’s startup ecosystem has an opportunity to thrive in this changing investment landscape.

The organisers said the event would bring together policymakers, corporate executives, investors, entrepreneurs and other ecosystem players for discussions and partnerships around the growth of Nigeria’s digital economy.

Key discussions will focus on digital infrastructure, the future of Nigeria’s technology ecosystem, investment and capital flows, public-private partnerships, and the role of technology in expanding economic opportunities and inclusion.

For Northern startups and innovators, the Lagos Exchange could provide an avenue to gain exposure to investors and corporate organisations concentrated in Lagos, while giving Southern-based stakeholders greater access to opportunities emerging from the North.

The event will feature keynote addresses, fireside conversations, executive roundtables and curated networking sessions aimed at facilitating partnerships and potential business deals.

Arewa Tech Fest said the Lagos edition reflects its broader ambition to strengthen connections between regional ecosystems and position Northern Nigeria as a stronger participant in the country’s digital economy.

The organisers also said the growing participation of government institutions, businesses and technology ecosystem stakeholders demonstrates increasing interest in building stronger regional collaboration around innovation and economic development.

title: NASENI Selects 60 Young Innovators for FutureMakers Hackathon
excerpt: The National Agency for Science and Engineering Infrastructure (NASENI) will on Monday begin its FutureMakers Virtual Hackathon, bringing together 60 young innovators from Nigeria’s six geopolitical zones to develop technology...
content:
The National Agency for Science and Engineering Infrastructure (NASENI) will on Monday begin its FutureMakers Virtual Hackathon, bringing together 60 young innovators from Nigeria’s six geopolitical zones to develop technology solutions to challenges affecting their communities.

The five-day virtual programme, organised by the NASENI Innovation Hub, will run from August 17 to 21, 2026, followed by virtual pitch sessions from August 24 to 26.

The initiative adopts a zone-specific approach, with innovators required to develop solutions around challenge statements identified for their respective geopolitical zones.

NASENI said in a statement on Sunday that the 60 participants were selected from thousands of entries received during the competition.

During the hackathon, the selected innovators will work with technical facilitators and mentors to refine their ideas, build practical solutions and develop their projects into potentially viable ventures.

Participants who progress to the next stage will pitch their solutions before judges and industry leaders during the virtual sessions, which will be streamed live on YouTube and Facebook.

For each geopolitical zone, the first-place winner will receive ₦1.5 million, while second and third-place winners will receive ₦1 million and ₦500,000 respectively.

The top-performing innovators will also have the opportunity to pitch their solutions at the NASENI Invention Fest, where they could compete for a ₦5 million prize, a fully funded international study tour and scholarships to two leading Nigerian universities.

NASENI’s Executive Vice Chairman and Chief Executive Officer, Khalil Suleiman Halilu, said the FutureMakers Week represents the culmination of months of talent identification and selection.

“FutureMakers Week is the culminating moment of the programme cycle, where months of outreach and selection turn into built solutions and backed ventures,” Halilu said.

He said the programme was designed to combine nationwide participation with local problem-solving.

“Sixty innovators, six zones, six challenges: the programme is deliberately national in reach and local in problem definition,” he said.

For Northern innovators, the zone-based model could provide an avenue to develop technologies tailored to problems that are often shaped by the region’s distinct economic and social realities, rather than adapting solutions developed for other parts of the country.

The Hub Manager of the NASENI Innovation Hub, Busola Beckley Perez-Folayan, said the programme was designed as a long-term talent development pipeline rather than a one-off competition.

She said successful participants would gain access to SparkLab, mentorship, training and scholarship opportunities alongside financial support.

According to her, the decision to hold the hackathon virtually was also intended to reduce geographical barriers for innovators outside Nigeria’s established technology centres.

“The virtual format widens access to innovators beyond Abuja and Lagos. This is a working demonstration of government-backed innovation infrastructure delivering for young Nigerians,” Perez-Folayan said.

The programme is being implemented in collaboration with academic and innovation ecosystem partners, including MIVA Open University and the African University of Science and Technology (AUST), Abuja.

NASENI said FutureMakers forms part of its broader effort to support Nigeria’s transition from a predominantly consumer economy to a producer-driven one through science, engineering, technology and innovation.

The significance of the initiative extends beyond the prize money. By connecting young innovators to mentors, training, funding and potential academic opportunities, the programme could help strengthen the region’s emerging technology ecosystem and encourage more locally developed solutions to local problems.

title: 1,517 Applications Reveal Strong Appetite for Tech Skills in Northern Nigeria — Da Hausa Initiative
excerpt: The Hausa Tech Scholarship 2026 received 1,517 applications from young people seeking to develop technology skills, transition into digital careers and explore new opportunities in the technology sector, according to...
content:
The Hausa Tech Scholarship 2026 received 1,517 applications from young people seeking to develop technology skills, transition into digital careers and explore new opportunities in the technology sector, according to an analysis by Da Hausa Initiative.

The organisation’s analysis of the application data shows that 67.6 per cent of applicants with valid age data were between 20 and 29 years, with a median age of 26. The applicants included students, educators, creatives, entrepreneurs, engineers and technology professionals.

The findings point to a growing appetite for technology education among young people in Northern Nigeria, particularly in areas such as artificial intelligence, data, software development and machine learning.

Four technology tracks accounted for 70.5 per cent of valid course selections.

Full Stack Web Development was the most sought-after course, attracting 20.3 per cent of selections, followed by Comprehensive Data Analysis at 17.7 per cent, AI Literacy at 17.6 per cent and Machine Learning Mastery at 14.9 per cent.

AI Literacy alone attracted 227 applicants, while half of the 50 scholarships eventually awarded went to applicants in the AI Literacy track.

Da Hausa Initiative said the figures indicate that applicants are increasingly interested in technology fields that are shaping the future of work rather than only basic digital skills.

The scholarship was designed with Northern Nigeria in mind, and 96.2 per cent of the named application records analysed were classified within the region.

The North-West recorded the highest concentration, with Kano accounting for 409 applicants and Kaduna 218. Together, the two states represented approximately 43 per cent of all named application records.

Applications also came from states across the North-East and North-Central, while the initiative identified applications linked to Niger Republic, Benin Republic, Ghana, the United States, Indonesia, Libya and Saudi Arabia.

The geographical spread, according to the analysis, suggests that demand for technology education extends beyond the immediate communities targeted by the programme.

Despite 91.8 per cent of respondents with valid data reporting regular internet access, 52 per cent said they primarily relied on a phone for learning.

Da Hausa Initiative said the distinction is significant for programmes focused on web development, data analysis, machine learning and artificial intelligence because internet availability does not necessarily translate into equal capacity to practise and build digital skills.

The organisation argued that digital inclusion must therefore consider not only connectivity but also the devices and resources available to learners.

Skill and knowledge development was the most frequently cited motivation among applicants, at 66.4 per cent, followed by career or employment opportunities at 52.1 per cent.

Technology interest accounted for 47.2 per cent of responses, while 44.9 per cent cited community or social impact among their motivations. Applicants could identify multiple motivations.

The figures suggest that applicants view technology education not only as a route to individual career advancement but also as a means of contributing to businesses, communities and local economies.

The data also revealed a significant gender disparity at the application stage.

Women accounted for just 9.4 per cent of valid gender responses, compared with 90.5 per cent for men. However, the final scholarship cohort achieved an equal gender split, with 25 women and 25 men selected from the 50 scholars.

Da Hausa Initiative said the outcome demonstrates the potential impact of deliberate selection but acknowledged that the low proportion of female applicants remains a challenge for future cohorts.

The organisation said the more important question is how to encourage more women to participate at the application stage.

Following the application and data-cleaning process, 1,397 records were retained, with 1,347 applicants represented in the final pool used for selection analysis.

Only 50 applicants were selected, translating to an approximate selection rate of 3.7 per cent, or roughly one scholarship for every 27 retained applicants.

The initiative said the gap between the number of qualified applicants and available places demonstrates the scale of demand for technology education.

Of the 1,347 applicants in the final pool, 1,297 qualified applicants were not placed in the first cohort and remain potential candidates for future opportunities.

Da Hausa Initiative said the application data shows that Northern Nigeria has a significant pool of young people interested in technology, digital careers and emerging technologies.

It said the findings also highlight several layers of access, ranging from internet connectivity to the devices learners use, while showing that applicants are motivated by employment, income, community impact and long-term career development.

The initiative is calling on partners, sponsors and donors to support future cohorts, fund specific learning tracks and help address device and connectivity barriers.

It said 52 per cent of applicants learning primarily through phones highlights the need for support beyond tuition, including access to appropriate devices and reliable connectivity.

The figures offer a snapshot of an emerging digital talent pool in Northern Nigeria, which states that the demand for technology skills is already evident, while the challenge is expanding access sufficiently to match it.

title: Tomato Jos, Agriarche Emerge Among Nigeria's Top-Funded Startups in H1 2026

Tomato Jos and Agriarche LLC, have been named among Nigeria’s 16 most-funded startups in the first half of 2026, highlighting growing investor interest in agritech solutions emerging from the region.

Tomato Jos, an agricultural technology company focused on improving local tomato production and strengthening value chains, ranked among the country’s top-funded startups after closing a $2 million investment round.

Agriarche LLC also featured on the list after raising $1.8 million, reflecting continued investment in technology-driven agricultural solutions designed to improve productivity and food security.

Beyond agritech, the ranking included startups operating across fintech, energy, mobility and education technology, including Starsight, Nairagram, Sycamore, OneDosh, BFREE, Cybervergent, Stabyl, Tuteria, Bboxx, Cardtonic and Beacon Power Services.

The full State of Tech in Africa H1 2026 report, which will provide deeper insights into funding trends across the continent, is expected to be published by TechCabal Insights in partnership with FIDO.

title: Turning Northern Nigeria's Climate Challenge into a Startup Opportunity
excerpt: Every year, floods, drought, and desertification disrupt livelihoods across Northern Nigeria. While these challenges continue to intensify, they also present one of the region's biggest untapped opportunities for founders building...
content:
Every year, floods, drought, and desertification disrupt livelihoods across Northern Nigeria. While these challenges continue to intensify, they also present one of the region’s biggest untapped opportunities for founders building climate-focused solutions.

In recent years, Northern Nigeria has witnessed an increasingly unpredictable climate. Some communities experience prolonged dry spells that delay planting and reduce yields. Others face intense downpours that overwhelm drainage systems, wash away farmland, destroy homes and displace families. Rising temperatures, shrinking water sources, advancing desertification and more frequent extreme weather events have combined to reshape life across the region.

For decades, climate conversations in Northern Nigeria have centred on the region’s vulnerability and the growing impact of environmental challenges. While these issues remain urgent, they also present an opportunity to build technology-driven solutions, from digital platforms that help farmers make better decisions to affordable solar technologies, precision agriculture tools, and AI-powered weather forecasting systems. Climate tech could become one of the region’s next frontiers for innovation. 

Collectively, these efforts point towards an important possibility: Northern Nigeria’s greatest climate challenge could also become its greatest innovation opportunity.

From Underestimated Consumers to Creators of Climate Solutions

Despite facing significant challenges, Northern Nigeria possesses a rapidly maturing technology ecosystem driven by one of the country’s youngest populations and a steady stream of graduates in engineering, science, and agriculture. Supported by a growing network of innovation hubs, startup communities, and digital skills programs, young entrepreneurs across key cities like Kano, Kaduna, and Jos are actively building impactful solutions in fintech, healthcare, education, and e-commerce as an entrepreneurial potential that is increasingly recognized and backed by government agencies, private organizations, and development partners. Yet climate innovation remains a relatively underdeveloped frontier.

Around the world, climate technology has become one of the fastest-growing areas of innovation. Startups are developing artificial intelligence systems that predict floods before they occur. Others use satellite imagery to monitor crop health, detect drought stress or optimise irrigation. Renewable energy companies are making electricity more affordable for rural communities, while digital platforms connect farmers with weather information, insurance and financial services.

Many of these technologies were born from local challenges. For example, Kenya’s mobile money revolution emerged because traditional banking failed to reach millions of people. The Netherlands transformed flood management into a globally recognised area of expertise because geography left little alternative.

Northern Nigeria could follow a similar trajectory. Its climate challenges are significant, but they also provide a clear direction for innovation. Every flood, drought, failed harvest and water shortage highlights a problem waiting for a solution. 

For entrepreneurs, these problems represent opportunities to build products that serve local communities before expanding into national and continental markets. Rather than importing every climate solution, Northern Nigeria can begin designing technologies that respond to its own realities.

Climate Change Has Changed the Rules

Northern Nigeria sits within one of Africa’s most climate-sensitive regions. The Sahel, a semi-arid belt stretching across the continent, has long experienced natural climate variability. But scientific research over the past several decades has shown that rising global temperatures are intensifying many of these challenges. Higher temperatures increase evaporation, reduce soil moisture, place greater stress on crops and livestock and alter rainfall patterns. Instead of predictable rainy seasons, many communities now contend with delayed rainfall, short but intense storms and longer dry periods between precipitation. For farmers, these changes have profound consequences.

Agriculture remains the economic backbone of much of Northern Nigeria. Millions of households depend on cultivating crops such as maize, millet, sorghum, rice, beans and groundnuts, while livestock production supports livelihoods across vast rural communities. When rainfall becomes less predictable, the risks multiply.

Communities grapple with damaged infrastructure, declining groundwater levels, increased competition over grazing land and heightened pressure on already fragile public services. Urban areas are not immune either. Rapid expansion, inadequate drainage and rising temperatures make cities increasingly vulnerable to flooding and heat-related health risks.

Climate change has therefore become more than an environmental issue. It is increasingly shaping food security, economic development, public health, migration, education and national security.

An irrigation system designed for the drylands of Katsina could prove valuable across the wider Sahel. A flood warning platform developed for communities in Jigawa may benefit flood-prone settlements elsewhere in Nigeria. Affordable solar-powered cold storage created for tomato farmers in Kano could reduce post-harvest losses across West Africa. Innovation becomes most powerful when it grows from local knowledge.

Climate change will continue to reshape Northern Nigeria regardless of whether innovators respond. The question is whether the region will remain primarily a consumer of imported technologies or become a producer of solutions uniquely suited to African realities.

Additionally, the global transition towards cleaner technologies is creating new markets for renewable energy, climate-smart agriculture, environmental monitoring, circular economy solutions and digital resilience tools. Countries that invest early in these sectors stand to benefit economically while improving their capacity to adapt to climate risks.

Fueling Africa’s Next Climate Innovation Engine 

Northern Nigeria possesses many of the ingredients needed to participate in that future: abundant solar resources with a high daily sunlight levels capable of powering massive clean energy infrastructure, a growing pool of digital talent, expanding innovation ecosystems, and an entrepreneurial population accustomed to solving complex problems with limited resources. The challenge now is connecting those strengths with the region’s most urgent climate needs.

That requires more than technology alone. It demands collaboration between governments, universities, investors, development partners, researchers and entrepreneurs willing to see climate change not only as a crisis to manage but also as an opportunity to build.

The first rains have arrived. They signal the beginning of another farming season, and another reminder of the uncertainty that climate change has introduced into everyday life. They also pose a different question, one that could define Northern Nigeria’s next decade of economic development.

Can the region transform its greatest environmental challenge into Africa’s next engine of climate innovation?
