title: YARE: The Platform Making Digital Content Accessible in African Languages
excerpt: Every year, thousands of educational courses, public awareness campaigns, videos, websites, and digital products are created across Africa. Yet many never reach the people they are intended for, not because...
content:
Every year, thousands of educational courses, public awareness campaigns, videos, websites, and digital products are created across Africa. Yet many never reach the people they are intended for, not because the content lacks value, but because it is produced in languages many potential users do not speak or fully understand. In this edition of The Zango Spotlight, the focus turns to YARE, a platform built to bridge that gap by connecting creators, educators, translators, and voice artists through a single ecosystem designed for African languages.

Developed by Northino Tech Ltd., YARE is an AI-powered translation, localization, and voice-over platform that combines technology with human expertise to make digital content accessible in native African languages. Its broader goal is simple: remove language as a barrier to learning, communication, and opportunity.

At its core, YARE functions as a digital marketplace where content creators, organisations, educators, and businesses can upload materials and connect with verified translators and voice artists. Rather than relying solely on machine translation, the platform adopts a hybrid approach. An initial translation can be generated through AI-powered tools before being reviewed, refined, and culturally adapted by native-speaking language experts. This process helps ensure that content is not only translated accurately but also reflects the context and realities of the communities it is intended to serve. 

The platform extends beyond text translation into localization and voice-over services. Educational content, websites, training manuals, business documents, scripts, and multimedia projects can be adapted into different languages, while professional voice artists provide localized audio that makes content more engaging and accessible to diverse audiences. 

YARE’s workflow is designed to simplify what is often a fragmented process. Users upload content, select their target languages and service requirements, and are matched with translators whose expertise aligns with the project. Once completed, the work undergoes quality review before delivery. The platform also supports project tracking, secure payments, and collaboration between clients and language professionals within the same environment. 

A key feature of the system is its talent marketplace. Translators and voice artists are not treated as external contractors operating outside the platform. Instead, they have dedicated dashboards, digital wallets, project management tools, and payment systems that allow them to find opportunities, collaborate with clients, and receive compensation securely. This creates an ecosystem where both content creators and language professionals can work together more efficiently.

The problem YARE seeks to address is one that extends far beyond translation. Across Africa, important educational resources, health campaigns, government information, and digital learning materials are often produced in English or other dominant languages. As a result, significant portions of the population remain excluded from information designed to serve them. By creating a platform focused on African languages, YARE aims to ensure that knowledge travels further and reaches communities in the languages they use every day. 

The platform forms part of Northino’s broader effort to build a localized digital ecosystem for Africa. Alongside YARE, the company operates Northino Learning, which delivers digital skills training in native languages, and Northino Studio, a content creation hub focused on educational content production. Together, these initiatives reflect a wider vision of making digital knowledge more accessible to African communities.

Behind this vision is Abubakar Umar Muhammad, a software engineer and entrepreneur from Kano State who founded Northino to tackle one of the most persistent barriers to digital inclusion: language. His belief that African youth should be able to access learning opportunities and participate in the global digital economy without abandoning their native languages has shaped the direction of both Northino and YARE. Under his leadership, the company has gained recognition within Nigeria’s innovation ecosystem, including emerging as the winner of the third cohort of the iHatch Startup Incubation Programme organised by the National Information Technology Development Agency (NITDA) and the Japan International Cooperation Agency (JICA), securing the programme’s top prize. 

What also distinguishes YARE is the ecosystem it is building around African language professionals. Beyond offering translation services, the platform actively spotlights the people whose expertise keeps indigenous languages alive in digital spaces. Through its “Talent Spotlight” series on LinkedIn, YARE recently recognised Muddassir S. Abdullahi as its Translator of the Month. A translator, biographer and science communicator, Muddassir has translated major literary and scientific works into Hausa, contributed to healthcare translation projects, and founded 1001 Translation, an initiative dedicated to bringing world literature to Hausa readers. His profile reflects YARE’s broader philosophy that technology alone is not enough; preserving meaning and cultural context requires native speakers who understand the communities they serve.

The platform is also investing in a less visible but increasingly important area: language infrastructure for the age of artificial intelligence. According to updates shared by YARE, the company has spent months building what it describes as a living Fulfulde language corpus also known as Fulani Language, which is an effort aimed at addressing the near absence of African languages in global AI datasets. While Fulfulde is spoken by an estimated 40 million people, YARE notes that the language has “almost zero AI training data.” To bridge that gap, the platform says it has developed a growing repository comprising more than 11,000 words, over 11,000 dictionary entries, and a network of 208 verified native translators.

For YARE, this work goes beyond improving machine translation. It is about creating the foundations for more inclusive digital systems. Healthcare workers in Adamawa providing information to Fulfulde-speaking patients, humanitarian organisations supporting displaced Fulani communities, and government agencies communicating with citizens in Northern Nigeria all require language tools built on accuracy rather than approximation. By investing in these datasets, YARE is positioning itself not only as a translation marketplace, but as part of the infrastructure needed to ensure African languages have a place in the future of digital technologies.

Today, YARE supports translation, localization, and voice-over services across multiple languages and serves customers worldwide. More importantly, it reflects a growing movement within Africa’s technology ecosystem, one that views language not as a limitation to overcome, but as infrastructure that can be built upon.

As digital content continues to shape education, commerce, and communication, platforms like YARE highlight an important reality: access is not only about connectivity or devices. It is also about ensuring that people can learn, create, and participate in the language that feels most natural to them.

title: Nigerian Founder Wins Prestigious Oxford Skoll Scholarship
excerpt: Al Amin Idris, founder and CEO of Interface Africa, has been awarded the prestigious Skoll Scholarship at the University of Oxford, joining a select group of social entrepreneurs from around...
content:
Al Amin Idris, founder and CEO of Interface Africa, has been awarded the prestigious Skoll Scholarship at the University of Oxford, joining a select group of social entrepreneurs from around the world recognized for their commitment to addressing critical social and environmental challenges.

The scholarship, awarded through the Skoll Centre for Social Entrepreneurship at Oxford’s Saïd Business School, is regarded as one of the most competitive and prestigious awards available to social entrepreneurs globally. Recipients are selected through a rigorous process from an already highly competitive pool of Oxford MBA candidates.

Idris is the founder of Interface Africa, a technology company building market access infrastructure for underserved communities. The company combines data intelligence, community-based distribution networks, and payment infrastructure to help people access clean energy, financial services, and other essential products.

Over the years, Interface Africa has facilitated access to clean energy and financial services for tens of thousands of homes and businesses while unlocking millions of dollars in financing for underserved communities.

Speaking on the award, Idris described the scholarship as a recognition of the growing contribution of African entrepreneurs to solving global challenges.

“This is a significant milestone, not just for me, but for the growing community of entrepreneurs across Africa building solutions to real-world problems. It demonstrates that innovation emerging from our markets can compete and be recognized at the highest levels globally.”

The Skoll Scholarship is designed for entrepreneurs who have demonstrated impact through ventures addressing issues such as poverty, climate change, healthcare, education, and financial inclusion. Beyond financial support, scholars gain access to Oxford’s global network of academics, investors, policymakers, and social impact leaders.

Observers say the recognition reflects the increasing prominence of African-led innovation on the global stage, particularly in sectors such as financial inclusion, energy access, and climate resilience.

As part of the programme, Idris will pursue an MBA at Oxford University, where he intends to deepen his understanding of leadership, scaling innovation, and building institutions capable of driving long-term economic transformation.

For Nigeria’s startup ecosystem, the achievement represents another example of local entrepreneurs earning international recognition for building scalable solutions to some of the continent’s most pressing challenges.

Idris said his long-term ambition remains unchanged.

“Our mission is to build the infrastructure that enables millions of underserved people to access opportunity. The scholarship provides an opportunity to learn, grow, and bring those lessons back to accelerate impact across Africa.”

His selection places him among a small group of global social entrepreneurs chosen annually for the programme, reinforcing the growing influence of African founders in shaping solutions to the world’s most pressing development challenges.

title: ABU Students Bring Home Global Honours, Win Big at Huawei ICT Competition in China
excerpt: Ahmadu Bello University (ABU) students have emerged among the world's brightest young tech talents, clinching top honours at the Huawei ICT Skills Competition Global Finals in China after outperforming teams...
content:
Ahmadu Bello University (ABU) students have emerged among the world’s brightest young tech talents, clinching top honours at the Huawei ICT Skills Competition Global Finals in China after outperforming teams from 40 countries.

The competition, which ran from June 2 to June 5, 2026, brought together 177 teams from 40 countries to compete across network, cloud, computing, and AI innovation tracks.

In a statement issued by the university’s Director of Public Affairs, Mallam Awwalu Umar, the ABU contingent emerged among the top performers at the global finals, securing first place in the cloud category and second place in computing.

The university also celebrated another milestone as three members of TeamABU2026 received the prestigious Women in Tech Award alongside the Nigeria Network Team, in recognition of their outstanding contributions and excellence in the field of information and communication technology.

According to Umar, the journey to Shenzhen began in October 2025 when more than 220,000 students from around the world entered the competition. After progressing through the national finals held in December 2025 and the Southern Africa regional finals in March 2026, the ABU team earned a place at the global stage.

The network, cloud and computing finals featured an intensive eight-hour laboratory simulation on June 2, challenging contestants to solve real-world ICT problems under pressure.

A day later, participants competed in the AI innovation finals, where they were tasked with developing practical solutions using Huawei technologies.

One of the highlights of the competition was ABU’s AI project, ParaVision, which earned a grand prize in the innovation category.

Built on Orange Pi AIPro and powered by Huawei’s Ascend 310B4 chip, ParaVision is an artificial intelligence-driven system capable of conducting dual or simultaneous diagnostic testing and producing printed laboratory reports in less than three minutes. The system also features a multilingual interface supporting French, Arabic, Chinese and Swahili.

The winning team comprised Kumba-Banna Tekanyi of Computer Engineering; Yakubu Musa Yakubu of Computer Science; Adekunle Abdulroqeeb Oladimeji of Electrical Engineering; Wakili Sefiu Bolaji of Computer Engineering; Yunus Muhammad and Ruqayyah Hassan Labo of Electronics and Telecommunications Engineering; as well as Khadija Khalid and Grace Temitayo Olorunfemi, both of Computer Engineering.

They were mentored by Dr Bashir Halliru Sani of the Institute of Agricultural Research and Information Technology and Innovation (IAIICT), alongside Dr Zaharaddeen Haruna of the Department of Computer Engineering.

The Vice-Chancellor of ABU, Prof. Adamu Ahmed, attended the event in Shenzhen alongside the Deputy Vice-Chancellor (Academic), Prof. Raymond B. Bako.

Other university officials present included the Director of the Distance Learning Centre, Prof. Muhammad Bashir Mu’azu, and the Director of IAIICT, Prof. Emmanuel Adewale Adedokun.

The achievement adds to the growing profile of Nigerian students excelling in global technology competitions and highlights the potential of homegrown talent to compete and innovate on the world stage.

title: NITDA Opens Applications for Digital Export Acceleration Programme Pilot Cohort
excerpt: The National Information Technology Development Agency (NITDA), through the Office of Nigerian Digital Innovation (ONDI) and the Digital Trade Desk under the Federal Ministry of Communications, Innovation and Digital Economy,...
content:
The National Information Technology Development Agency (NITDA), through the Office of Nigerian Digital Innovation (ONDI) and the Digital Trade Desk under the Federal Ministry of Communications, Innovation and Digital Economy, has opened applications for the pilot cohort of the Digital Export Acceleration Programme (DEAP).

The announcement, shared on ONDI’s official X account, described DEAP as a six-month acceleration programme designed to help Nigerian startups, SMEs, and digital businesses scale beyond local markets and become export-ready enterprises.

According to the agency, the initiative is targeted at growth-focused businesses seeking regional and international expansion through structured support, ecosystem connections, market access opportunities, and strategic advisory services.

Selected startups and SMEs will receive export readiness support, market access advisory, investor readiness guidance, cross-border trade support, mentorship opportunities, and strategic partnerships aimed at positioning them for international growth.

NITDA said the programme is open to high-potential Nigerian businesses operating in sectors including technology, agribusiness, fashion, healthtech, fintech, manufacturing, creative industries, logistics, edtech, renewable energy, and other export-capable industries.

“If your business is ready for regional and global expansion under AfCFTA, this is your opportunity,” the agency stated in the announcement.

The programme will also provide participants with compliance and export support, as well as access to regional and global growth pathways.

“Big ideas deserve bigger markets,” ONDI noted, adding that the initiative is designed to help businesses transition “from local to regional to global.”

NITDA said only a limited number of businesses will be selected for the pilot cohort, with eligibility restricted to companies registered in Nigeria that have operated for at least two years and demonstrated market traction.

The agency further stated that applicants must show evidence that their products or services possess export or regional scalability potential.

According to the eligibility criteria released by the organisers, the programme is specifically targeted at startups with proven traction, SMEs preparing for regional expansion, digital or export-capable businesses, and companies seeking compliance and scale support.

Applications for the pilot cohort will close on May 30, 2026, while only shortlisted applicants will be contacted.

title: Sabou Capital Invests $2m In Tomato Jos As Nigeria Moves To Cut Tomato Paste Imports
excerpt: Sabou Capital has announced a $2 million impact-linked debt investment in Tomato Jos Farming and Processing Limited, in a move aimed at strengthening local tomato production and reducing Nigeria’s dependence...
content:
Sabou Capital has announced a $2 million impact-linked debt investment in Tomato Jos Farming and Processing Limited, in a move aimed at strengthening local tomato production and reducing Nigeria’s dependence on imported tomato paste.

The Naira-denominated facility will support Tomato Jos’ expansion plans, including increasing its processing capacity and growing its network of smallholder farmers across Northern Nigeria.

Speaking on the investment, Managing Partner of Sabou Capital, Surayyah Ahmad, said the deal aligns with the firm’s mission of backing businesses that create economic impact while reducing import dependency.

“Tomato Jos is exactly the kind of business we back, one that turns an import dependency into local jobs, farmer income, and a stronger domestic economy. We structured this deal so that our financial return grows with the impact they create,” Ahmad said.

Nigeria consumes more than 2.3 million tonnes of fresh tomatoes annually, but for years, up to 90 per cent of processed tomato demand was met through imports. With the Federal Government’s recent restriction on tomato paste imports, industry players say local manufacturers now have a significant opportunity to expand production and fill the supply gap.

Founded in 2014 by Mira Mehta, Tomato Jos operates a vertically integrated tomato processing business headquartered in Kaduna State. The company says it runs Nigeria’s most technologically advanced tomato processing facility and works with over 3,000 smallholder farmers, 60 per cent of whom are women.

According to the company, the investment comes at a critical period as domestic processors compete against larger international players in the food manufacturing sector.

“As Tomato Jos continues to grow, partners like Sabou Capital are crucial to our journey. The opportunity in front of us is real, but so is the competition; we’re up against international organisations with deep pockets,” Mehta said.

She added that support for the company goes beyond financial returns, noting that Tomato Jos’ operations directly impact more than 10,000 smallholder farmers and their families.

Sabou Capital said the financing was structured as an Impact-Linked Debt facility, a funding model that ties investor returns to measurable social and economic outcomes. Tomato Jos currently employs 204 Nigerians directly and meets all four criteria of the global 2X Challenge benchmark for gender-lens investment.

The investment also reflects Sabou Capital’s broader strategy of directing funding toward growth-stage businesses in underserved African markets, particularly outside major commercial hubs.

Headquartered in Abuja, Sabou Capital provides structured debt and adaptive credit solutions to SMEs across Nigeria, Senegal and Côte d’Ivoire, with investments spanning agribusiness, fintech, healthcare, logistics and essential consumer services.

title: Why Startup Kano’s Climate Innovation Push Matters for Northern Nigeria
excerpt: “Northern communities are facing a dual threat. While rising temperatures contribute to severe droughts, the rainy seasons have become shorter and more intense, often leading to flash floods that destroy...
content:
“Northern communities are facing a dual threat. While rising temperatures contribute to severe droughts, the rainy seasons have become shorter and more intense, often leading to flash floods that destroy infrastructure and displace thousands.”

That warning by African Climate Reporters captures the reality many communities across Northern Nigeria are already living through. In states such as Kano, Jigawa, Kebbi, Sokoto, Yobe and Borno, climate change is no longer a distant environmental debate discussed only in policy rooms in Abuja or at international conferences. It is visible in shrinking farmlands, irregular harvest seasons, destructive flooding, heatwaves, displacement, food inflation and rising youth unemployment.

For years, Northern Nigeria’s climate crisis has largely been framed around vulnerability. Reports often focus on desertification, insecurity linked to resource scarcity, flooding disasters, or humanitarian emergencies. While these conversations are important, they have also created a dangerous gap: the region is constantly discussed as a victim of climate change but rarely as a centre for climate innovation.

That is why the Climate Innovation Ecosystem Development (CIED) initiative by Startup Kano Centre for Innovation Development, its timely and crucial initiative deserves far more attention than it is currently receiving.

In April 2026, Startup Kano convened government officials, development partners, innovators and ecosystem stakeholders to advance the CIED pipeline, an initiative designed to build climate-focused startups and connect them to investment opportunities. At first glance, it may appear like another startup event filled with presentations and policy conversations. But beneath the networking sessions and pitch decks lies something Northern Nigeria has desperately lacked for years: a deliberate system for climate innovation.

The gathering, held during the CIED Green Investment Pitch Event in Kano, marked the close-out phase of the Climate Innovation Ecosystem Development Project, which Startup Kano described as a strategic effort to address climate finance access and investor-readiness gaps across Northern Nigeria.

The significance of the event is not merely in the number of startups trained or the investors invited. The real importance lies in the fact that Kano is beginning to position itself as a climate innovation hub at a time when climate adaptation is becoming an economic necessity.

Across Africa, climate technology is attracting increasing investor attention. According to reports by Partech Africa and Briter Bridges, African climate-tech startups attracted more than $1 billion in venture funding between 2022 and 2025, accounting for a growing share of startup investments on the continent. Yet much of that funding continues to flow into countries like Kenya, South Africa and Egypt, where innovation ecosystems are already more mature and connected to global capital.

Northern Nigeria has largely remained outside that investment map despite facing some of the continent’s harshest climate realities.The irony is impossible to ignore. The region experiencing some of the deepest climate vulnerabilities is also one of the least funded when it comes to climate innovation.

Nigeria itself loses billions annually to climate-related disasters. The World Bank has repeatedly warned that climate change could reduce Nigeria’s GDP by up to 6 to 30 per cent by 2050 if adaptation measures are not strengthened. Meanwhile, the National Emergency Management Agency (NEMA) has consistently recorded devastating floods across northern states during rainy seasons, destroying homes, schools, roads and farmlands.

In 2024 alone, floods displaced thousands across parts of Kano and Jigawa, while food insecurity worsened in conflict-affected communities in the North-East. Rising temperatures are also affecting livestock productivity and agricultural yields, deepening economic pressure on already vulnerable populations.

Against this backdrop, Startup Kano’s intervention represents something bigger than startup incubation. It is about creating local economic systems capable of responding to local climate realities.

The most striking part of the CIED initiative is its attempt to connect innovation with policy and finance simultaneously. What makes the initiative particularly important is the calibre of institutions beginning to align around it. The event convened stakeholders from the Kano State Investment Promotion Agency (KanInvest), the Kano State Information Technology Development Agency (KASITDA), the Kano State Accountant General’s Office, and the Green Legacy Initiative led by the Magajin Garin Kano. Their presence signalled that climate innovation is gradually moving beyond isolated startup conversations into broader governance and economic planning discussions within the state.

For too long, innovation ecosystems in Northern Nigeria have existed in silos. Young innovators build solutions without access to funding. Policymakers develop climate policies without engagement from innovators. Investors remain hesitant because local ventures lack investment readiness structures.

CIED appears to understand that climate innovation cannot scale without solving these gaps together. Through the project, Startup Kano supported participating ventures to build governance systems, align with environmental, social and governance standards, and develop investor-ready business models in sectors including clean energy, waste management, climate-smart agriculture and green services. The initiative also introduced the CIED Climate Readiness Toolkit, a digital resource designed to help startups track climate metrics, align with ESG frameworks and meet investor expectations.

Startup Kano described the initiative as “a structured approach to building a climate innovation pipeline, one that identifies, supports, and positions startups to move from early-stage ideas to scalable, investment-ready solutions.” That framing matters because the region does not merely need ideas; it needs institutions capable of transforming ideas into sustainable enterprises.

This is where the Kano State Government’s involvement becomes particularly important. Beyond policy conversations and stakeholder engagement, the state is beginning to position itself as an active player in the climate innovation ecosystem. Through its backing of the CIED initiative and the announcement of financial support for selected startups, the government is signalling a shift toward innovation-led development and ecosystem financing. That transition matters because it reflects a growing recognition that climate innovation is not merely a technology conversation, but an economic and development strategy capable of attracting investment, creating jobs and strengthening climate resilience across Northern Nigeria.

That move may appear small on paper, but symbolically, it represents a shift in thinking. Northern state governments have historically approached innovation through empowerment schemes or short-term ICT training programmes. Direct engagement with climate-focused startup financing suggests a growing recognition that innovation is now part of economic development strategy.

What ultimately determines the success of climate innovation ecosystems is whether local institutions are willing to sustain them after donor funding cycles end.

That is why Startup Kano’s effort to embed CIED into existing incubation and acceleration systems is perhaps one of the smartest aspects of the initiative. Northern Nigeria has seen too many promising programmes disappear once grants expire. Sustainability matters.

Equally important is the programme’s emphasis on youth and women-led participation. Northern Nigeria has one of the youngest populations in Africa, yet youth unemployment remains alarmingly high. According to Nigeria’s National Bureau of Statistics, youth underemployment and unemployment have continued to disproportionately affect northern states, creating conditions that fuel migration, poverty and social instability.

Climate innovation offers a different pathway. Instead of viewing climate action solely as environmental activism, initiatives like CIED frame it as economic opportunity. Waste recycling startups, solar energy ventures, climate-smart agriculture solutions and green manufacturing businesses are not simply environmental projects; they are job creators.

Recent developments in Kano already show the possibilities. Earlier this year, BURN Manufacturing showcased its clean cookstove facility in Kano, which currently produces about 35,000 stoves monthly with plans to scale production significantly. The company says it has already distributed more than one million clean cookstoves across Nigeria while supporting green jobs and emissions reduction. 

This matters because it demonstrates that climate innovation is no longer theoretical in Northern Nigeria. There is already a growing ecosystem emerging around clean energy, carbon finance, sustainable manufacturing and climate adaptation.

Still, optimism alone will not solve the region’s problems.

Northern Nigeria’s innovation ecosystem continues to face structural obstacles ranging from poor infrastructure and weak research-commercialisation pipelines to limited venture capital presence and policy inconsistency. According to a recent FutureMap Foundation communiqué from innovation stakeholders in Kano observed that many technology and innovation centres in the region remain underutilised despite existing infrastructure because ecosystems are still fragmented and poorly coordinated. 

Climate innovation ecosystems cannot thrive without patient capital, research collaboration, digital infrastructure and long-term policy stability. There is also the danger that climate innovation could become another buzzword dominated by conferences and donor language without translating into actual enterprises capable of scaling solutions across communities.

But even with these challenges, initiatives like CIED deserve recognition because they attempt to build systems rather than headlines.

Northern Nigeria cannot afford to remain absent from the global climate economy. With institutions such as the Nigeria Sovereign Investment Authority increasingly positioning Nigeria to access global climate finance mechanisms, initiatives like CIED could become critical entry points for Northern startups seeking participation in emerging green investment markets. Startup Kano has already stated that its long-term goal is to deepen investor engagement, continue pipeline development and scale climate-smart ventures led by youth and women across the region.

The future of development finance, industrial investment and economic competitiveness will increasingly be tied to sustainability and climate resilience. Regions that fail to build climate innovation capacity risk becoming economically marginalised in the decades ahead.

The conversation, therefore, should no longer be whether Northern Nigeria is vulnerable to climate change. That question has already been answered by rising temperatures, floods and worsening agricultural pressures.

The more important question now is whether the region is prepared to build the institutions, talent pipelines and investment ecosystems capable of responding to that reality.

Startup Kano’s CIED initiative may not solve Northern Nigeria’s climate challenges overnight. But it represents something the region urgently needs: a deliberate attempt to move climate action away from rhetoric and into enterprise, investment and scalable innovation.

And perhaps for the first time in a long while, Kano is beginning to show that Northern Nigeria does not only want to survive climate change; it wants to build through it.

title: Breaking the Language Barrier: Inside Da Hausa Initiative’s Push for Digital and Financial Inclusion
excerpt: For millions of young people across Northern Nigeria, the digital economy is a difficult concept, it is not coming with ease, clarity and largely in a language that is not...
content:
For millions of young people across Northern Nigeria, the digital economy is a difficult concept, it is not coming with ease, clarity and largely in a language that is not their own. Financial tools, data platforms, and economic opportunities are expanding, but the gap between access and comprehension to this knowledge remains wide.

One initiative is working to close it, not by waiting for the system to change, but by meeting people where they are. In this edition of The Zango Spotlighting Series, the focus turns to the Da Hausa Initiative (DHI), a system built to close that gap by delivering practical financial and data skills in Hausa, making complex knowledge usable in everyday life. Its guiding idea is captured in its motto: “Simplifying concepts, strengthening communities — through financial and data literacy for Northern Nigeria.”

At its core, the Da Hausa Initiative operates as a knowledge delivery system built around language accessibility, translating technical concepts in finance and data into formats that can be understood and applied within everyday contexts. Based in Abuja, the system is structured to ensure that individuals who are often excluded from mainstream financial and digital ecosystems are able to engage with information in a way that is both practical and culturally relevant.

The system works by combining research, training, and advocacy into a continuous cycle of engagement. It begins with community-led research, where specific gaps in financial understanding and data usage are identified within Northern communities. These insights then shape the design of training programmes, ensuring that the content reflects real-life needs rather than abstract theory. The training itself is delivered through multiple formats, including in-person sessions, online classes, and hybrid models, allowing for wider reach across different locations.

A defining feature of the system is its use of Hausa as the primary language of instruction, particularly in technical areas that are often dominated by English. Through this approach, participants are taught how to manage personal finances, understand budgeting, and make informed financial decisions. At the same time, the system introduces data literacy by training individuals to interpret information, use digital tools, and apply data in decision-making processes.

Recent activities have focused on building practical digital skills, including a 24-week training programme on data visualisation, where participants learn tools such as Microsoft Power BI and Excel, including the use of pivot tables. By delivering these sessions entirely in Hausa, the system reduces the learning barrier often associated with technical education and allows participants to engage more confidently with digital tools.

Beyond its ongoing programmes, the initiative is preparing to launch the DHI Hausa Tech Scholarship 2026, a new training opportunity aimed at expanding access to digital and data skills. The programme will offer 50 fully funded slots for young people in Northern Nigeria, with courses delivered entirely in Hausa. Applications are scheduled to open on April 30, positioning the scholarship as an entry point for participants seeking practical, language-accessible digital skills at no cost.

The problem this system addresses is both linguistic and structural. Many individuals across Northern Nigeria are excluded from financial systems and digital opportunities not because of a lack of interest, but due to limited access to understandable and relevant information. Traditional training models often fail to bridge this gap, relying heavily on language and formats that do not align with local realities. The Da Hausa Initiative responds to this by redesigning how knowledge is delivered, making it more accessible, relatable, and usable.

The system is led by Lailah Sanusi Gumbi, a Nigerian data enthusiast, finance advocate, and social impact leader with over a decade of experience spanning research, policy, and financial systems. She previously worked within the Central Bank of Nigeria, contributing to research on banking systems and financial behaviour, and has since focused on expanding access to knowledge through localised learning models.

Her decision to establish the Da Hausa Initiative was driven by a clear gap she identified: language as a barrier to opportunity. She has consistently argued that the lack of educational resources in Hausa excludes many potential learners from participating in digital and financial systems, and her work centres on addressing that gap by translating complex concepts into accessible formats.

Through her leadership, the initiative has positioned language not just as a communication tool, but as a gateway to inclusion, using Hausa to deliver data literacy, financial education, and digital skills to underserved communities across Northern Nigeria.

Beyond training, the system extends into advocacy, using research findings to push for policies that support wider access to financial and digital education. This creates a feedback loop where insights from the community inform both learning programmes and broader discussions around inclusion and development.

In the broader context of digital and economic transformation, the Da Hausa Initiative reflects a shift towards language-driven innovation, where access to knowledge is treated as a foundational layer for participation in modern systems. By focusing on how people learn rather than just what they learn, the system highlights the role of local language in unlocking both financial inclusion and digital capability.

As more communities seek to engage with digital tools and financial systems, models like the Da Hausa Initiative point to a growing recognition that access is not just about availability, but about understanding, delivered in a language people can use and act on in their daily lives.

title: Afraah Tech Hub to Host Innovation Challenge Targeting Grassroots Solutions in Katsina
excerpt: Afraah Tech Hub has announced it will host the Afraah Innovation Challenge 2026 on April 21, 2026, in the Funtua Senatorial Zone of Katsina State, as part of efforts to...
content:
Afraah Tech Hub has announced it will host the Afraah Innovation Challenge 2026 on April 21, 2026, in the Funtua Senatorial Zone of Katsina State, as part of efforts to identify and scale community-driven solutions to local challenges.

The initiative is designed to bring together young innovators, problem-solvers, and stakeholders from across the region to develop practical ideas addressing issues in education, healthcare, agriculture, and community development. According to the organisers, the programme responds to the limited access to structured innovation platforms in many parts of Northern Nigeria, which has hindered the ability of youths to transform ideas into scalable impact.

Founder of Afraah Tech Hub, Ibrahim Muazzam Ibrahim, said the challenge is part of a broader strategy to build a pipeline of solution-oriented innovators within underserved communities.

“The Afraah Innovation Challenge is not just an event—it is a deliberate effort to build a pipeline of problem-solvers who can develop and implement solutions that directly impact our communities. We are shifting the focus from conversations about problems to the execution of solutions,” he said.

He added that the challenge forms part of a broader vision to establish a lasting innovation ecosystem in the Funtua axis—one that continuously nurtures talent, supports execution, and drives measurable outcomes.

In line with this vision, Afraah Tech Hub is opening its doors to partnerships with educational institutions, media organisations, NGOs, community-based groups, and other innovation stakeholders. Partners are expected to contribute through outreach, participant mobilisation, mentorship, technical support, and logistical backing.

The move signals an increasing recognition of grassroots innovation as a critical driver of regional development. By positioning Funtua as an emerging node for community-based innovation, the initiative aligns with broader efforts to decentralise Nigeria’s tech ecosystem beyond major urban centres.

As preparations continue, Afraah Tech Hub says it is focused on building a scalable model that not only discovers ideas but ensures they are supported through to implementation—turning local insights into solutions with lasting impact.

title: Africa Innovation Foundry Launch Sets Agenda for Decentralised Innovation Ecosystem
excerpt: The Africa Innovation Foundry (AIF) has officially launched in Abuja, signalling a renewed push to build a more inclusive and regionally distributed innovation ecosystem across the continent, with a strong...
content:
The Africa Innovation Foundry (AIF) has officially launched in Abuja, signalling a renewed push to build a more inclusive and regionally distributed innovation ecosystem across the continent, with a strong emphasis on Nigeria’s underserved startup communities.

Held on Tuesday, April 7, in Abuja, the launch event, themed “Building Africa’s Innovation Future,” convened founders, ecosystem builders, policymakers, and development partners in what organisers described as the beginning of a coordinated national innovation movement.

The programme opened with guest arrivals and networking sessions that brought together a cross-section of stakeholders, followed by a welcome address introducing AIF’s core mandate. Early remarks from the advisory board chair, Dr. Zayyad Tsiga, set the tone for the event, highlighting the urgency of building scalable structures that support African innovators beyond traditional tech hubs.

A central highlight of the event was the official unveiling and presentation of Africa Innovation Foundry (AIF), where organisers outlined the initiative’s vision, mission, and programme framework. The presentation detailed plans for a regional rollout across Nigeria’s six geopolitical zones, alongside opportunities for partnerships aimed at strengthening startup development, talent pipelines, and access to funding.

Goodwill messages delivered by ecosystem leaders and partners reinforced the need for collaboration across public and private sectors to unlock innovation at scale. Speakers emphasised the importance of bridging gaps in access to infrastructure, capital, and technical capacity, particularly in regions that have historically received limited attention in Nigeria’s tech landscape.

The event also featured a fireside chat with Deji Garuba, Executive Director of AIF, who provided further insight into the initiative’s strategic direction and operational priorities. During the session, Garuba outlined that AIF is designed as a multi-regional accelerator and innovation platform that integrates talent development, startup incubation, and policy alignment into a single ecosystem framework.

He noted that the initiative aims to establish innovation hubs across Nigeria’s six geopolitical zones, while also targeting the upskilling of more than 150,000 individuals through structured programmes. According to him, AIF will run startup accelerators and talent development initiatives to build a pipeline of scalable ventures, while fostering a connected, nationwide innovation ecosystem.

Garuba further highlighted that key programme components will include keynote engagements with industry and policy leaders, the rollout of regional innovation programmes, and structured discussions around MSME and startup funding pathways. He added that networking and ecosystem matchmaking sessions would play a critical role in linking founders with investors, partners, and enablers.

The AIF Executive Director also pointed to early institutional partnerships, particularly in areas such as MSME support, skills development, and access to funding, including collaborations with financial and development institutions aimed at strengthening the broader innovation landscape.

AIF’s advisory board, unveiled as part of the initiative’s governance structure, includes a diverse mix of ecosystem leaders and professionals such as Toyin Chukwudozie, Beryl Lamptey-Jahara, Adeola Bojuwoye, Opeyami Iredumare, Bayo Adalemo, Ahmad Shuaibu, Lars Ling, Aisha Tofa, and Oma Areh, with Dr. Zayyad Tsiga serving as Board Chair.

The programme concluded with partner recognition and an acknowledgement of the advisory board, followed by closing remarks and a networking session that allowed participants to deepen conversations initiated during the event.

For Northern Nigeria’s innovation ecosystem, the launch of AIF introduces a potential framework for expanding access to resources, mentorship, and funding pathways. By prioritising regional inclusion and ecosystem coordination, the initiative positions itself as a bridge between emerging founders and the broader African innovation economy.

As implementation begins, attention will turn to how effectively AIF translates its vision into measurable outcomes, particularly in regions where innovation potential remains high but support structures are still evolving.

title: Inside DeepSecure 360, a System Built for Intelligent Cyber Defence
excerpt: As digital systems expand across sectors, DeepSecure 360 is positioned as a cybersecurity platform designed to continuously monitor, detect, and neutralise threats across entire digital environments. Built as an integrated...
content:
As digital systems expand across sectors, DeepSecure 360 is positioned as a cybersecurity platform designed to continuously monitor, detect, and neutralise threats across entire digital environments. Built as an integrated system rather than a single-purpose tool, it reflects a shift towards always-on, intelligence-driven security in response to increasingly complex cyber risks.

DeepSecure 360 operates as an AI-powered cybersecurity system that brings multiple layers of protection into a single framework. Instead of focusing on one point of vulnerability, the system adopts a 360-degree approach, scanning across networks, user behaviour, cloud environments, and external threat spaces at the same time. This structure allows organisations to move away from fragmented security setups and operate within a unified environment where monitoring, detection, and response are centralised.

At the heart of the system is a continuous intelligence loop built around real-time data processing and automated response. Once connected to an organisation’s digital infrastructure, the system analyses activity patterns using machine learning models to identify irregular behaviour that may signal a threat. It detects risks such as phishing attempts, suspicious logins, and compromised credentials, while also extending its reach beyond internal systems by scanning dark web environments for leaked data and emerging threats. When a threat is identified, the system triggers alerts and, where necessary, initiates actions to contain or neutralise the risk. These processes are made visible through a secure cloud-based dashboard that provides real-time insights, reports, and analytics, ensuring that organisations remain aware of their security posture at all times.

The system also integrates capabilities that extend beyond traditional cybersecurity tools. It includes deepfake detection and media verification powered by artificial intelligence, as well as digital forensics tools that support incident investigation and evidence analysis. In addition, it incorporates satellite-aided surveillance to support infrastructure monitoring and geospatial threat assessment, pointing to an expanded view of what modern cybersecurity systems are expected to handle.

A key issue the system addresses is the fragmented nature of cybersecurity in many organisations, where different tools manage different threats and detection often comes too late. At the same time, the scope of cyber risk has widened, with threats now existing not only within internal systems but also across external digital environments.

DeepSecure 360 responds to this by combining internal monitoring, external threat intelligence, and automated response into a single, continuous system that prioritises early detection and proactive defence.

The system simplifies cybersecurity by reducing the need for multiple tools, accelerating response time through real-time alerts, and improving accuracy through AI-driven analysis. Its ability to operate across different sectors, from enterprise systems to government infrastructure, reflects a level of scalability that aligns with the growing digital demands of organisations.

DeepSecure 360 was developed by cybersecurity expert Ibrahim Isah Liman, whose work centres on threat intelligence and automated defence systems. His approach to the platform reflects a focus on anticipating threats rather than reacting to them, using artificial intelligence and continuous monitoring to stay ahead of evolving attack patterns. Through this system, the emphasis is placed on building a security environment that is adaptive, data-driven, and capable of responding in real time.

In the broader context of digital transformation, DeepSecure 360 reflects a shift from reactive security models to integrated systems that continuously analyse behaviour, detect threats early, and respond automatically. As organisations become more reliant on digital infrastructure, the demand for systems that operate in this way continues to grow.

As digital adoption deepens across sectors, systems like DeepSecure 360 point to a future where cybersecurity is no longer treated as a separate layer but becomes an embedded, continuous process running across everyday operations.

title: International Women’s Day 2026: Northern Women Driving Tech Forward Through “Give to Gain”
excerpt: Today, 8 March 2026, as the world marks International Women’s Day, the theme “Give to Gain” feels especially personal for Northern Nigeria’s tech ecosystem. It is not just a slogan....
content:
Today, 8 March 2026, as the world marks International Women’s Day, the theme “Give to Gain” feels especially personal for Northern Nigeria’s tech ecosystem. It is not just a slogan. It is a lived reality embodied by Arewa women who are building platforms, opening doors, investing capital and mentoring the next generation of founders across the region.

For years, conversations about technology in Northern Nigeria were dominated by statistics about gaps such as funding gaps, skills gaps, and representation gaps. But behind the headlines, women have quietly and steadily been closing those gaps.

A new generation of women technologists, educators, founders and innovators are opening pathways for others to participate in the digital economy.

Among them is Hafsah Garbati, a software engineer and tech entrepreneur from Kano State. Garbati is also the co-founder and CEO of TaveStack, an artificial intelligence-powered workplace productivity platform designed to improve how teams manage meetings and collaborative discussions. The platform transforms conversations into actionable outcomes by generating smart summaries, identifying tasks and integrating them into team workflows. Built with hybrid and remote teams in mind, the platform represents the growing wave of AI-driven innovation emerging from Northern Nigeria.

Garbati has also showcased her work at major technology gatherings including GITEX Nigeria, highlighting the increasing visibility of innovators from the region on global stages.

Salma Phillips brings yet another layer of ambition to the tech ecosystem. As co-founder of Arewa Tech Fest, she has helped create one of the region’s most visible technology festivals, a gathering that celebrates innovation and bridges the digital divide. In late 2024, she launched the Arewa Tech Fund, which she co-founded with Deji Garba, that was initiated by Mallam Nasiru El-Rufai to provide investment and structured support for tech-driven solutions emerging from the North.

Her entrepreneurial reach extends to fintech as well. As the founder of RewaPay, a digital banking platform designed to serve underserved communities, she is addressing financial inclusion at scale.

Another influential voice shaping inclusive technology spaces is Safiyya Muhammad Ali-Daba, a technology leader and artificial intelligence educator whose work sits at the intersection of technology, language and community storytelling.

Through her social enterprise Her Tech Hub, Ali-Daba promotes digital literacy and AI education using Hausa-language training programmes that make technology accessible to women and young people across Northern Nigeria. By removing language barriers, she ensures that local communities can participate meaningfully in the digital economy.

Ali-Daba is also recognised as the longest-serving female community manager in Northern Nigeria’s tech ecosystem. Over the years, she has led platforms such as Google Developer Group (GDG) Kano and Women Techmakers Kano, and she currently serves as Community Manager for AI in Kano State. Her work connects grassroots innovation communities with global technology networks.

At the policy and institutional level, Dr. Amina Sambo-Magaji is shaping the future of digital talent development. Leading the Digital Literacy and Capacity Development Department at NITDA, she focuses on artificial intelligence, digital literacy and skills development for women and young girls. Her work underscores a simple but urgent truth: if girls are not introduced to technology early, the pipeline will remain narrow.

Through structured programmes and capacity-building initiatives, she is helping to widen that pipeline, ensuring that the next generation of Arewa girls see AI, cybersecurity and software development not as distant possibilities, but as viable career paths.

Hafsah Baba El-Yakubu is an emerging leader contributing to talent development within the Northern ecosystem. She is a product manager and startup founder who co-founded Maha Technologies, a platform designed to connect businesses with Africa’s top tech talent. Through its flagship initiative MahaTech, the company operates as a hub linking organisations seeking technical professionals with developers and technology specialists looking for meaningful employment opportunities. The platform aims to strengthen Africa’s digital job marketplace by improving access to talent and project opportunities.

On International Women’s Day 2026, these stories reflect what “Give to Gain” truly means. It means giving space when there was none. Giving capital when access was limited. Giving mentorship where there was uncertainty. Giving platforms where silence once existed and in doing so, gaining stronger businesses, stronger communities and a stronger Arewa tech ecosystem.

But today must also be a moment of honest reflection. According to the Northern Nigeria Tech Ecosystem Report in 2023 by TechTank Labs (TTL), it is reported that 23.4% represents the percentage of female founders within the Northern Nigeria ecosystem. Despite the years after the report was released, female-led startups still receive a fraction of available venture funding and grants. Cultural expectations can still shape career choices. Rural girls still face barriers to digital access and knowledge, and visibility for startups, innovators remain uneven.

The challenge for Northern Nigeria’s tech ecosystem is clear: scale the support and spotlight the innovators. Innovation hubs must actively support women founders. Investors must expand funding opportunities for female-led ventures with intention, not tokenism. Educational institutions must strengthen pathways for girls in science and technology. Established founders must mentor beyond their immediate circles.

Because representation does more than inspire; it reshapes ambition. When young girls across Kano, Kaduna, Zaria and other parts of Northern Nigeria see women building AI platforms, leading data science projects, teaching digital skills and launching startups, technology begins to feel less distant and more achievable.

International Women’s Day is a celebration, yes but it is also a reminder that ecosystems are not neutral. They are built. And they can be rebuilt.

As we mark 8 March 2026, Northern Nigeria stands at a critical intersection. The region’s youthful population, expanding internet access and growing innovation culture present enormous potential. But that potential will only be fully realised if women are not just participants but leaders, funders, architects and innovators.

“Give to Gain” is a cycle. When women are empowered, the entire ecosystem benefits. When one founder succeeds, she often becomes a mentor. When one investor writes a cheque, she often opens a network. When one girl learns to code, she often teaches another.

Today, The Zango celebrates the women who are not waiting for permission to lead and calls on the entire ecosystem to give more, support more and believe more.

Because the future of Northern Nigeria’s tech revolution will not be built by men alone. It will be built by everyone and it will be stronger because women are at the centre of it.

The National Information Technology Development Agency (NITDA), in collaboration with the Office for Nigerian Digital Innovation (ONDI), has announced the commencement of applications for the iHatch Cohort 5 Hub Upskilling Programme, a nationwide initiative aimed at strengthening innovation hubs and accelerating startup growth across Nigeria.

In a post shared on its official X (formerly Twitter) handle, NITDA called on innovation hubs with the structure, team, and operational experience to nurture emerging founders to apply for the programme.

The agency described iHatch 5.0 as an opportunity for qualified Hub Managers to deliver structured startup training and drive measurable impact within their ecosystems. Applications open on 23 February 2026 and close on 16 March 2026.

The iHatch Cohort 5 upskilling programme is exclusively designed for innovation hubs seeking to deepen their capacity to support startups.

According to the eligibility criteria, interested hubs must have operated for a minimum of one year with a verifiable track record and demonstrate a clear commitment to startup ecosystem development, measured by the number of startups or initiatives supported. Applicants are also required to show experience in startup support or innovation management and possess physical infrastructure suitable for incubation activities.

The programme targets hubs with operational capacity, proven founder engagement experience, and incubation-ready facilities, positioning them to plug into a broader national innovation network.

By onboarding Hub Managers nationwide, NITDA and ONDI aim to standardise startup training delivery, strengthen local innovation ecosystems, and expand access to structured entrepreneurial support across the country.

The initiative underscores ongoing efforts by the federal government, through its digital innovation agencies, to build a more resilient and interconnected startup ecosystem capable of producing the next wave of Nigerian founders.

title: Google Opens Applications For Startup Accelerator Africa Cohort 10, Invites African AI Startups

content:
Google has opened applications for the 10th cohort of the Google for Startups Accelerator Africa, calling on startups across the continent building artificial intelligence solutions to apply.

The company announced in a statement on Thursday that applications will remain open until March 18, 2026.

According to Google, the 12-week AI-first accelerator is a hybrid programme designed for Series A startups based in Africa or building Africa-focused solutions using AI and machine learning.

Selected startups will gain access to Google’s AI expertise and technical resources, receive mentorship from experienced AI professionals, and connect with peers and industry leaders across the global tech ecosystem.

The company said the programme is aimed at helping participating startups strengthen their products, scale responsibly, and translate advanced research into real-world solutions.

Speaking on the new cohort, Head of Startup Ecosystem Africa at Google, Folarin Aiyegbusi, said the continent’s innovation landscape is evolving rapidly.

“Africa’s tech landscape is seeing a vibrant shift toward deep tech innovation,” Aiyegbusi said.

“For Class 10, we are focusing on the potential of AI to drive health and societal benefits, providing the infrastructure and expertise to turn these startups into the research labs of the continent,” he added.

Since launching in 2018, the Google for Startups Accelerator Africa has supported more than 180 startups across 17 African countries.

Collectively, participating startups have raised over $350 million in funding and created more than 3,700 direct jobs, underscoring the programme’s role in strengthening Africa’s startup ecosystem and attracting investors.

Google added that this year’s focus reflects growing interest in applying AI to sectors such as healthcare, climate and agriculture, areas with wide societal impact across the continent.

Last year, six Nigerian startups, E-doc Online, GoNomad, Midddleman, Myltura, Pastel and Scandium were selected among 15 AI-driven ventures from Ghana, Ethiopia, Kenya, Nigeria, Rwanda, Senegal and South Africa tackling challenges across fintech, healthtech, logistics and agritech.

With the programme open to startups building Africa-focused solutions regardless of location within the continent, founders operating outside traditional tech hubs, including those in Northern Nigeria, are also eligible to apply provided they meet the Series A and AI product requirements.

The application window closes on March 18, 2026.

title: Capital has Many Faces, and Every Deal has a Price
excerpt: Musa is a startup founder who, in the beginning of his journey, had little knowledge about funding, and what funding is all about. He believed it worked in a linear...
content:
Musa is a startup founder who, in the beginning of his journey, had little knowledge about funding, and what funding is all about. He believed it worked in a linear format; build a product, pitch it, and someone writes a cheque. It was only after his third rejection from a programme that he realised capital had rules, personalities, and expectations of its own.

Musa’s first funding did not come from a venture capitalist or a bank, but from a donor-backed accelerator that released funds in tranches, each tied to reports, milestones, and weekly check-ins. The money helped him hire two developers, but it also taught him something more important: capital is not just money; it is a relationship.

As the innovation ecosystem continues to expand in Northern Nigeria, it is crucial for founders to understand that funding does not wear a single face. It arrives as grants, loans, equity, revenue-sharing agreements, or blended models shaped by risk appetite. Understanding which capital fits a business stage often matters as much as the idea itself.

Funding

At its core, funding is simply external money used to build or grow a business. But in practice, funding comes in distinct forms, each with its own expectations, trade-offs, and consequences.

Some capital demands ownership, some require repayment, and others demand accountability. For founders in Northern Nigeria, the challenge goes beyond access to capital, alignment also matters. This is choosing a capital that matches where the business truly is. Understanding these forms is often the first strategic decision a founder makes.

Grants: Money that Helps, Not Scale 

For early-stage founders in the North, grants are often the first formal encounter with capital. A grant is a sum of money given by a government body, organization, or foundation to fund specific projects or programs. Unlike loans, grants do not need to be repaid, making them highly sought after; however, they are often earmarked for a specific purpose and come with conditions regarding their use. This structure explains why grants often come with heavy reporting requirements. Every naira must be tracked, justified, and tied to impact metrics.

Grants are best suited for early-stage ideas, pilot projects, community-focused solutions, and salary support. They allow founders to experiment without the pressure of immediate returns.

They are typically awarded based on merit, project viability, and alignment with the grantor’s objectives. 

For example, Aisha, a startup founder in Kaduna, joined a donor-backed accelerator focused on digital skills and inclusion. Her startup, a learning platform for public-school teachers, received a small grant spread over three months. The money paid stipends, internet subscriptions, and basic operations.

For Aisha, the grant lets her run payroll for three months, but she has to track every naira. Every receipt mattered in relation to grants.

The limitation of grants is scale. Few grant programmes are designed to support rapid growth or long-term expansion. Once the programme ends, founders must either generate revenue or find another form of capital.

Still, for many Northern Nigeria startups, grants are the first door into the funding ecosystem.

Angel Investors and Equity: Capital that Wants a Share 

If grants are the first lifeline, angel investors are often the first real vote of confidence. An angel investor is an entity that provides capital to startups, usually in exchange for equity in the company. The financial backing they provide may only be a one-time investment, or it could be ongoing financial support to help the company in its early stages. Angel funding involves individuals or small groups investing their own money in exchange for equity. Angels usually come in at the early revenue or post-MVP stage, which is when a product exists, and customers are paying. Unlike grants, angel capital expects growth and often influence

For Sadiq, a fintech founder in Zaria, angel funding only became possible after several referrals, meetings, and introductions.

“Finding the right angel required several months and multiple referrals through the hub,” he says. “No one just sends cold money.”

The typical flow looks like this: Angel investor → Syndicate or informal network → Founder

Angel capital brings more than cash. It introduces governance expectations such as shareholder agreements, reporting structures, and strategic oversight. For founders used to operating informally, this shift can be uncomfortable.

The risk, however, lies in misalignment. Not all angels understand the Tech ecosystem, especially in emerging markets like Northern Nigeria, and not all founders are prepared to give up equity early.

Debt Capital: Loans with an Attachment

Debt capital simply means borrowed money that a business takes with an agreement to pay it back over time. Unlike equity capital, where investors become partial owners, debt financing involves a loan agreement. The company receives a specific amount of money upfront, which it must repay with interest over a predetermined period. This type of funding is commonly provided by commercial banks, development finance products, SME-focused interventions, microfinance institutions, and government-backed loan schemes. 

Debt capital is often used to support operations, purchase assets, or expand an existing business. However, lenders usually require evidence that the business can repay, such as steady revenue, financial records, or collateral. While debt allows founders to grow without giving up shares, it also comes with risk, as missed repayments can place serious pressure on the business. This is why it works best for businesses with steady revenue, predictable cash flow, and basic financial systems; it is rarely suitable for idea-stage startups. 

In Katsina, a manufacturing startup seeking a Bank of Industry loan discovered that innovation alone was not enough. The founders had to adopt proper accounting, payroll, and inventory management software to demonstrate financial discipline. “Our accounting software convinced the bank we could handle repayment,” the founder explained.

Collateral requirements and strict repayment schedules remain major barriers, especially for young entrepreneurs without assets. For founders who can manage it, loans can fund expansion without diluting ownership, a rare advantage in a capital-scarce environment.

Revenue-Based Financing: “Easy” Capital for Cash-based Businesses

As traditional funding models struggle to fit local realities, alternative approaches are gaining ground. Such as the fixed and high-risk debts from commercial banks, equity-hungry VCs, unrealistic demands from angel investors and so on. Revenue-based financing (RBF) allows businesses to raise capital by giving investors a share of their ongoing gross revenues. It differs from debt and equity financing because investors don’t hold ownership, and there’s no interest on outstanding balances. 

It allows a business to raise money by agreeing to repay investors with a small percentage of its sales over time, instead of fixed loan repayments or giving up ownership. Payments rise and fall with revenue, making it a flexible option for businesses with steady but changing cash flow.

Payments to investors depend on the company’s performance. This is because payments vary based on the level of the business’s income. If sales fall off in one month, an investor will see his or her royalty payment reduced. Likewise, if the sales in the following month increase, payments to the investor for that month will also increase. 

Revenue-based financing sits between debt and equity. Instead of fixed repayments, founders repay capital as a percentage of revenue until an agreed amount is reached.

This model suits e-commerce, agri-tech, SaaS (Software as a Service), and other businesses with consistent sales but limited collateral.

For example, in Jos, a SaaS founder named Aliko used RBF to deploy software across several cooperatives. Repayments adjusted as revenue fluctuated.

“The first tranche came with flexible repayment as revenue trickled in,” he says.

In Northern Nigeria, blended finance models also include Islamic finance instruments such as Qard ḥasan (benevolent loans) and murābaḥah (cost-plus financing). These structures align with faith-based principles while offering practical alternatives to interest-bearing loans.

The challenge with RBF is discipline. Founders must track sales meticulously and resist overextending during strong months.

Venture Capital: The Hardest Door to Open

Venture capital (VC) remains the most aspirational and elusive form of funding for Northern founders. VC is a form of private equity and a type of financing for startup companies and small businesses with long-term growth potential. Venture capitals invest equity in high-growth start-ups, typically seeking scale. 

Investors do not expect loan repayments but aim to profit if the company grows and becomes more valuable, which means founders must share ownership and some control.

Venture capital generally comes from investors, investment banks, and financial institutions. It can also be provided as technical or managerial expertise. 

In Northern Nigeria, the problem is not talent, but access. Many Northern startups struggle to attract early VC attention due to geographic bias and limited visibility. 

“VCs want numbers you often can’t generate without first getting local support,” one founder notes.

Without accelerators, angel backing, debt-finance or early traction, most Northern startups never reach VC radar. This creates a funding gap that local ecosystems are only beginning to address. Not all money is good money. For first-time founders, the choice of capital can define the future of the business. Early ideas benefit from grants and donor programmes. Growing products need angel investors or RBF. Stable SMEs can explore loans. Venture capital, while attractive, should come only after traction is proven. The wrong capital, taken too early, can stall a business faster than no capital at all.

Barriers, Bridges, and the Road Ahead

Despite progress, barriers remain. Geographic bias, visibility gaps, and informal networks continue to shape investors’ decisions. Although hubs and accelerators continue to play an important role in bridging the gap by helping to refine pitch decks, translating local innovation into investor language, and connecting founders to funders.

Many first-time founders tend not to be well-versed in financial literacy, making capital management more challenging than accessing capital. Therefore, it is important for hubs to not just connect founders to funders but to teach founders how to manage funds.

As blended finance models expand and regional hubs mature, the Northern funding ecosystem continues to diversify. More founders will now understand that funding is not a prize; it is a tool. In Northern Nigeria, capital may have many faces, but each one tells a story of persistence, adaptation, and belief in possibility.

title: Sokoto Government, NITDA Open Applications for Digital Skilling Programme for MSMEs
excerpt: The Sokoto State Ministry of Innovation and Digital Economy has opened applications for a new Digital Skilling Mentorship Programme (DSMP-MSME) targeted at Micro, Small and Medium Enterprises (MSMEs) across the...
content:
The Sokoto State Ministry of Innovation and Digital Economy has opened applications for a new Digital Skilling Mentorship Programme (DSMP-MSME) targeted at Micro, Small and Medium Enterprises (MSMEs) across the state.

The programme, organised in collaboration with the National Information Technology Development Agency (NITDA), is designed to equip registered business owners with practical digital skills to improve sales, visibility, and customer engagement in an increasingly digital economy. Applications close on 15 January 2026.

According to the ministry, the initiative is part of ongoing efforts to strengthen the digital capacity of local businesses and support economic growth through technology-driven entrepreneurship. The programme specifically targets eligible MSMEs operating in Sokoto State who are seeking to expand their reach and competitiveness using digital tools.

The DSMP-MSME will offer a free three-day intensive practical training, with a strong emphasis on hands-on learning. Participants will be trained in digital marketing strategies, the use of online platforms to promote products and services, and practical approaches to growing sales through digital channels.

To encourage excellence and active participation, the organisers disclosed that laptop prizes will be awarded to the top three performers at the end of the mentorship programme. The incentive is intended to support continued digital learning and application beyond the training period.

The Ministry of Innovation and Digital Economy noted that the programme aligns with Sokoto State’s broader digital transformation agenda, which seeks to empower business owners, enhance productivity, and create new economic opportunities through innovation and technology adoption.

NITDA’s partnership in the initiative reflects the agency’s mandate to drive nationwide digital skills development and support MSMEs as key contributors to Nigeria’s digital economy. The agency has consistently emphasised the importance of building digital capacity at both federal and subnational levels to promote inclusive growth.

Eligible applicants are required to be registered business owners, and interested MSMEs are encouraged to apply before the deadline, as participation slots may be limited. Applications can be submitted via the official portal: mide.sokotostate.gov.ng/nitdatraining.

Industry observers note that programmes such as the DSMP-MSME are increasingly critical, as small businesses face growing pressure to adapt to digital commerce amid changing consumer behaviour and market dynamics. For many MSMEs in northern Nigeria, limited access to digital skills has remained a major barrier to scaling operations and accessing wider markets.

By offering free, practical training and mentorship, the programme is expected to lower these barriers and provide participants with tools they can immediately apply to their businesses. Stakeholders believe the initiative could contribute to improved sales performance, resilience, and long-term sustainability for MSMEs across Sokoto State.

The ministry has urged business owners to take advantage of the opportunity, describing the programme as a timely intervention aimed at empowering MSMEs to “sell more digitally” and remain competitive in today’s economy.
