title: FutureMap Foundation Hosts North-West Innovation Stakeholders at Roundtable 1.0
excerpt: The FutureMap Foundation organized its first FutureMap Roundtable 1.0 (North-West Edition), a closed-door, solution-focused dialogue aimed at strengthening the innovation ecosystem across Northern Nigeria. Held under the theme “Building What...
content:
The FutureMap Foundation organized its first FutureMap Roundtable 1.0 (North-West Edition), a closed-door, solution-focused dialogue aimed at strengthening the innovation ecosystem across Northern Nigeria.

Held under the theme “Building What Works for Northern Nigeria’s Innovation Ecosystem (North-West Edition),” the roundtable brought together founders, government officials, ecosystem builders and partners committed to translating innovation theory into practical, region-specific outcomes.

As part of ongoing efforts to deepen Nigeria’s digital economy, the Director General of the National Information Technology Development Agency (NITDA), Kashifu Inuwa Abdullahi, engaged participants on the need for people-driven, locally relevant and globally competitive innovation. He underscored NITDA’s commitment to enabling inclusive growth through supportive policies, strategic partnerships and platforms that allow homegrown solutions to scale beyond their immediate communities, in line with the Federal Government’s digital transformation agenda.

The engagement provided an open forum for candid conversations on strengthening regional innovation policies, fostering effective public-private partnerships and addressing structural barriers limiting the growth of startups in the North-West.

Also speaking at the roundtable, the DG/CEO of the Katsina State Investment Development Authority (KATSIDA), Bashir Abdu Muzakkari, stressed the urgency of a harmonised North-West Regional Digital Transformation Policy. He noted that coordinated action among states would reduce fragmentation, improve investor confidence and accelerate technology-driven development across the region.

A key outcome of the meeting was a collective commitment to fast-track startup collaborations with ICT agencies in Kano, Katsina and Zamfara States, with a roadmap to scale successful models nationwide.

Participants at the roundtable included founders, policymakers and ecosystem builders such as Aisha Tofa, Muhammad Dahiru Lawal, Samir Balarabe, Kabiru Mahmud Yabo and Usman Maaruf Yakubu, alongside other delegates and industry stakeholders.

By convening diverse actors around a shared vision, the FutureMap Roundtable 1.0 reinforced the importance of collaboration, trust and strategic coordination in unlocking the North-West’s innovation potential and positioning Northern Nigeria as a critical driver of Nigeria’s evolving digital economy.

title: Kano Startup Weekend 2025 to Bring Tech Leaders Together on December 13–14
excerpt: Kano’s innovation community is preparing for one of the most anticipated tech gatherings of the year as the Kano State Information Technology Development Agency (KASITDA) hosts the maiden Kano Startup...
content:
Kano’s innovation community is preparing for one of the most anticipated tech gatherings of the year as the Kano State Information Technology Development Agency (KASITDA) hosts the maiden Kano Startup Weekend (KSW) 2025 from December 13 to 14 at Coronation Hall, Government House.

The event, which aligns with the state’s Digital Transformation Agenda (2025–2030), aims to ignite the local startup ecosystem, empower early-stage entrepreneurs and foster collaboration among innovators, investors, policymakers and tech professionals.

Participants will engage in a dynamic mix of pitch competitions, masterclasses, expert panels, exhibitions and networking designed to spotlight innovation and unlock opportunities for growth. Twenty pre-selected startups focused on priority sectors such as health, education, agriculture and transportation will battle for seed funding and investment opportunities during the pitch sessions, while the broader audience will benefit from insight-driven conversations with industry leaders.

A diverse roster of speakers and panelists has been confirmed by KASITDA. Among them is Engr. Jamil Galadanci of eHealth Africa; Barrister Ahmed Ismail of PCNGi; Kazeem Oladepo, Senior Vice President at IHS Towers; cloud services pioneer Ahmad Mukoshy of GigaLayer; Halima Rabi’u of Pan-Atlantic University; Usman Ibrahim, Head of Growth at FlexiSAF; and Khalifa U. Mustapha of KDC Foundation. Others include Alh. Kabir Sufi of IFING Media; Barr. Mohammed Nakudu of Nakudu Group; Ahmad Turajo of MTN MoMo; Ahmad Shuaibu of Qorebox; and Dr. Sanah Muaz, a software engineer at Bayero University Kano.

Newly added to the lineup is Al Amin Mohammed Idris, Founder and CEO of Interface Africa, who will feature as a panelist on “Innovation For Impact: Tech Solutions for HEAT Sectors.” His session is expected to explore how innovation can address Health, Education, Agriculture, and Transportation challenges—four sectors central to Kano’s development agenda. Also joining the discussions is Fahad Garba Aliyu, Managing Partner at Ignite Capital and Co-Founder of the Abuja Economic Dialogue (AED), who will serve as a panelist on “Beyond Commerce: Positioning Kano as a Hub for 21st-Century Systems.”

That same session will also feature Ahmed Sani Inuwa, CEO of Locally Led Development, whose expertise in community-driven innovation and systems design is expected to broaden the conversation on positioning Kano as a modern regional economic hub. Another notable figure joining the panels is Atef Fawaz, Executive Director at eHealth Africa (eHA), who will bring perspectives from public health systems, technology deployment, and nonprofit leadership.

Organizers and participants alike have been actively sharing updates across social media, underscoring the potential of the Startup Weekend to connect Kano’s innovators with mentors and investors, while further supporting youth engagement, skills development and economic growth. Beyond the pitch sessions, participants will also benefit from masterclasses on investment readiness, product building, branding, and scaling strategies, while the exhibition area will showcase digital tools, products and prototypes from both startups and partner organizations.

In recent weeks, KASITDA’s promotional efforts have highlighted the accessibility of the event with free registration and its value as a launchpad for innovators. The agency also emphasized that the event is open to students, volunteers and enthusiasts, making it one of the most inclusive ecosystem gatherings ever held in the state.

With expectations already running high, the Kano Startup Weekend 2025 is shaping up to be a transformative moment for Kano’s technology landscape offering visibility, mentorship and potential funding opportunities for founders looking to build solutions for real-world challenges across Arewa and beyond.

title: HackJos 2025 Champions Homegrown Innovation to Tackle MSME Challenges in Northern Nigeria
excerpt: Agrivault, Haraji, and Lalita have emerged as the top winners of HackJos 2025, showcasing how innovation can transform the future of Micro, Small, and Medium Enterprises (MSMEs) in Nigeria. Their...
content:
Agrivault, Haraji, and Lalita have emerged as the top winners of HackJos 2025, showcasing how innovation can transform the future of Micro, Small, and Medium Enterprises (MSMEs) in Nigeria.

Their groundbreaking solutions ranging from cold room storage for farm produce to digital tax and savings platforms for small businesses which captured the spotlight as the three-day hackathon and innovation summit concluded on November 12, 2025, in Jos, Plateau State, marking the climax of nHub Nigeria’s 10th anniversary celebration and a decade of driving digital transformation across Northern Nigeria.

HackJos 2025 brought together developers, entrepreneurs, investors, and policy leaders to co-create solutions aimed at accelerating the growth of Micro, Small, and Medium Enterprises (MSMEs) through technology and innovation. The event’s theme, “Igniting MSME Growth Through Innovation,” underscored the central role of innovation in driving inclusive economic growth across Nigeria.

In his welcome address, Mr. Theodore Longji, Convener of HackJos and CEO of nHub, described the event as both a celebration of nHub’s ten-year journey and a continuation of its mission to empower youth through technology.

“Today is not just the beginning of another hackathon; it is the continuation of a bold story that started right here in Jos ten years ago — a story of possibility, resilience, and innovation. This year, as we gather for the 6th edition of HackJos, we are also celebrating a very special milestone — nHub at 10 years. The seed planted a decade ago has taken root and is flourishing.” Longji said. 

He encouraged participants to see beyond competition, emphasizing that their work represented a movement to spark real change for Nigeria’s MSMEs, which remain the lifeblood of the economy.

Delivering the Founder’s Keynote Address, Mr. David Daser, President of the Digital Bridge Institute (DBI) and Founder of HackJos, spoke about the vision that birthed the event a decade ago.

“When we started HackJos, it was not just an event, it was a statement that innovation and creativity could thrive right here in Jos,” Daser said. “Over the years, HackJos became more than a hackathon; it grew into a movement nurturing startups, building skills, and birthing a community of thinkers and doers.”

Reflecting on the hiatus before its 2025 revival, Daser expressed pride in HackJos’ enduring legacy and reaffirmed its mission: “HackJos is back. Let’s ignite growth. Let’s continue to build not just apps or startups, but ecosystems that power the next wave of digital transformation across Africa.”

Delivering a goodwill message on behalf of GIZ-SEDIN, Mr. Akinropo Omoware, Esq., Head of Component, Business Enabling Environment & Investment and Sustainable Infrastructure, highlighted the need for collaboration in addressing the structural challenges facing MSMEs.

He emphasized that HackJos serves as a practical platform to co-create solutions that address barriers such as limited access to finance, poor market linkages, and low digital adoption. “We expect that the outcomes and MVPs from this hackathon will not just end as creative prototypes but will transition into real, adoptable solutions that MSMEs can integrate into their daily operations,” he said.

Omoware reaffirmed GIZ’s commitment to supporting the piloting and scaling of viable solutions emerging from HackJos, praising the creativity and energy of the participants.

The Innovation Summit featured four panel sessions, each exploring critical dimensions of MSME development in the digital economy.

The first panel, titled “Building Sustainable MSMEs: The Roles of Innovation, Skills, Policy, and Business Education,” featured Founder, David Daser (DBI), Parker Benson Majei (PICTDA), Jennifer Turai (PLASMIDA), Hauwa Anita Mankilik (GIZ-SEDIN), and Bashir Sheidu (nHub), moderated by Theresa Nana of ThinkHub.

Subsequent panels examined topics including “From Idea to Impact: Building MSMEs that Solve Real Problems,” “Tech-Driven Growth: How Digital Tools Are Transforming Small Businesses in Nigeria,” and “Bridging the Gap: Access to Finance, Markets, and Talent for the Next Generation of MSMEs.”

Each session offered practical insights into how innovation, policy, and collaboration can strengthen Nigeria’s entrepreneurship ecosystem.

The highlight of the event was the HackJos 2025 Hackathon Demo and Pitch Presentation, where teams showcased solutions designed to empower small businesses. The judges— Manbyen Daki (GIZ), Nnamdi Ibe (Axia Innovation Hub), Olumide Akinsoyinu (nHub), Eric Nanle (ED Nhub), and Longji Pemun Gotar (Blockfuse), evaluated the pitches based on creativity, impact, and scalability.

Agrivault, the first-place winner of the hackathon, is a solution providing cold room storage for agricultural products. While Haraji, a tax solution platform for MSMEs, and Lalita, a digital savings tool for small businesses.

As the curtains fell on HackJos 2025, it was clear that nHub’s decade-long journey had evolved from a small tech hub in Jos into a national force driving innovation, digital inclusion, and youth empowerment.

Over the last ten years, nHub has trained thousands of young Nigerians, supported hundreds of startups, and become a central pillar in Northern Nigeria’s growing innovation ecosystem.

The event concluded with a resounding sense of optimism, as stakeholders, innovators, and partners celebrated the progress made and reaffirmed their commitment to building a more inclusive and technology-driven economy for the next decade and beyond.

HackJos 2025 proved once again that innovation thrives where vision meets opportunity  and from Jos, that vision continues to shape Nigeria’s digital future.

title: Northern Innovators Drive Solutions to MSME Challenges at HackJos 2025

content:
Young innovators from across Northern Nigeria gathered on Monday, November 10, 2025, at the Fox Hotel in Jos for HackJos 2025, a 48-hour hackathon organized by nHub Nigeria to mark its 10th anniversary, where participants are developing technology-driven solutions to address key challenges faced by Micro, Small, and Medium Enterprises (MSMEs) across the country.

The event, organized by nHub Nigeria as part of its decade-long milestone, nHub’s CEO, Mr. Theodore Longji, delivered a welcome address to the hackathon participants and attendees. He also delivered a speech on the theme “Igniting MSME Growth Through Innovation.” 

This year’s HackJos features eight dynamic teams competing across four critical innovation tracks, which are E-commerce Solutions, Financial Inclusion, Productivity Tools, and Logistics & Last-Mile Delivery. Over the next 48 hours, these teams will brainstorm, design, and prototype solutions aimed at improving the MSME landscape in Nigeria.

Day one also featured insightful sessions from distinguished speakers including Mr. Adamu Fun Bala from the German Cooperation (GIZ) and Mr. Steven Sunday, who shared practical insights on innovation, partnership, and sustainability within the tech ecosystem.

The atmosphere at HackJos was charged with creativity and purpose as participants collaborated, brainstormed, and tested their ideas well into the night, all in a bid to present innovative prototypes that could redefine the future of MSMEs in Nigeria.

HackJos 2025, now in its sixth edition, continues to serve as a hub for innovation in Northern Nigeria, bridging the gap between startups, policymakers, and investors. The event will climax with the HackJos Innovation Summit on November 12, where the most promising ideas will be showcased, and conversations will focus on policies and partnerships needed to scale innovation for sustainable growth.

As nHub marks a decade of powering digital transformation in the North, HackJos 2025 stands as a testament to how far the region’s ecosystem has come, transforming local passion into global potential, and positioning Northern innovators at the heart of Nigeria’s tech-driven economic future.

Theodore Longji, Chief Executive Officer (CEO) of nHub, explained that the change will not affect the event’s structure or theme.

Themed “Igniting MSME Growth Through Innovation,” HackJos 2025 will still feature a 48-hour hackathon, innovation summit, mentorship sessions, and investor networking aimed at strengthening MSME development through technology.

With the growing momentum in Northern Nigeria’s tech ecosystem, the event is expected to spotlight the region’s progress in digital entrepreneurship and innovation. The adjustment, organisers say, is part of their commitment to delivering a landmark edition that not only celebrates nHub’s 10-year journey but also reinforces Jos as a rising innovation hub in Africa.

title: HackJos 2025 Set for November as nHub Marks 10 Years of Powering Northern Nigeria’s Innovation Ecosystem
excerpt: HackJos 2025 brought to you by nHub, Northern Nigeria’s pioneering tech hub, will hold from November 11 to 13, 2025, as part of activities marking nHub’s 10th anniversary, celebrating a...
content:
HackJos 2025 brought to you by nHub, Northern Nigeria’s pioneering tech hub, will hold from November 11 to 13, 2025, as part of activities marking nHub’s 10th anniversary, celebrating a decade of pioneering digital transformation and tech entrepreneurship across Arewa.

The event, now in its seventh edition, is set to showcase how far the region’s ecosystem has evolved, while charting a new course for innovators and Micro, Small, and Medium Enterprises (MSMEs) to thrive through technology-driven solutions.

According to Theodore Longji, Chief Executive Officer (CEO) of nHub, HackJos 2025 is more than just a hackathon, it represents the culmination of ten years of innovation, collaboration, and community-building. “HackJos 2025 is not just another hackathon; it is a decade of innovation coming full circle. This shift gives us the time to ensure every detail reflects the transformative impact nHub has had on Nigeria’s tech ecosystem,” Longji said.

Themed “Igniting MSME Growth Through Innovation,” the three-day event will feature a 48-hour hackathon and an innovation summit designed to empower MSMEs, a sector that contributes over 50 percent to Nigeria’s Gross Domestic Product (GDP) and remains a cornerstone of national development.

Participants will be tasked with developing creative technology solutions across critical areas such as digitalization and e-commerce, financial inclusion for underserved populations, productivity and operational efficiency, and logistics and last-mile delivery, all aimed at tackling the real-world challenges that hinder MSME growth in Nigeria.

The event will also include mentorship sessions, investor networking, and policy discussions through the HackJos Innovation Summit, where founders, developers, and innovators will connect with stakeholders shaping the future of the digital economy.

The Rise of Northern Nigeria’s Innovation Ecosystem

Over the past decade, Northern Nigeria has witnessed remarkable progress in its innovation landscape, evolving from a largely untapped region into one of the country’s most promising tech frontiers. The transformation has been driven by consistent investment in human capital, the rise of youth-led startups, and the establishment of community-driven innovation hubs such as nHub, Startup Arewa, Colab, and Blue Sapphire Hub. These institutions have nurtured a new generation of coders, product designers, and digital entrepreneurs who are building solutions tailored to local needs while competing on a national and global scale.

nHub, in particular, has played a central role in this transformation by creating a sustainable ecosystem where collaboration and mentorship thrive. From its early days as the first technology hub in Northern Nigeria, nHub has expanded its reach through accelerator programs, coding bootcamps, and startup incubation platforms that have empowered thousands of young Nigerians with digital skills. Its alumni network now includes several startup founders who have gone on to attract investment, scale operations, and contribute to the region’s growing innovation economy.

Jos City has become a beacon of tech innovation in Arewa, a place where startups are emerging in fields like agriculture technology, fintech, logistics, and e-commerce. Events like HackJos have been crucial to this progress, acting as a springboard for collaboration between developers, founders, investors, and government agencies, while fostering a sense of community among emerging tech talents.

HackJos 2025 has attracted notable partners, including the German Cooperation (GIZ), GOPA Worldwide Consultants, the Digital Bridge Institute, and the Plateau State Microfinance Development Agency (PLASMIDA). Their collective support underscores the increasing recognition of nHub’s leadership role in fostering digital entrepreneurship and youth innovation across Northern Nigeria.

Reaffirming the event’s purpose, Longji described the upcoming edition as a moment of progress and reflection. “The postponement is an upgrade. The wait is worth it for a bigger, better, and more impactful event that will redefine how MSMEs leverage technology to thrive,” he emphasized.

As a proud media partner, The Zango will be covering the HackJos 2025 journey and the landmark nHub@10 celebration, highlighting how innovation continues to redefine opportunities for Nigeria’s next generation of entrepreneurs.

title: Startup Abuja Conference 2025 Crowns One Click Med as Overall Winner of Innovation Challenge
excerpt: One Click Med, a digital healthcare startup founded by Reagan Rowland, has clinched the top prize at the Startup Abuja Innovation/Hackathon Challenge 2025 during the Startup Abuja Conference held on...
content:
One Click Med, a digital healthcare startup founded by Reagan Rowland, has clinched the top prize at the Startup Abuja Innovation/Hackathon Challenge 2025 during the Startup Abuja Conference held on Saturday, October 25, 2025 at the Main Auditorium of the National Merit House, Maitama. 

The event, organised by Startup Abuja, focused on the theme “Accelerating Africa’s Digital Economy with Infrastructure, Innovation, and Investment,” bringing together investors, founders, and policymakers for a day of speeches, panel sessions, and pitches from the 30 startup finalists.

According to Chigozie Ezugwu, Executive Director and Convener of Startup Abuja, the hackathon initiative aims to strengthen Africa’s digital transformation by empowering its most promising innovators.

“We had more than 5,000 startups apply, and only 30 emerged as finalists,” Ezugwu noted in his opening remarks.

The competition’s total prize value stood at ₦102 million, including cash rewards, AWS credits, and tailored business mentorship.

One Click Med claimed the top spot with ₦10 million worth of prize value, including ₦5 million in cash. CDail AI secured second place with ₦8 million worth of rewards, while NafoloPay finished third, taking home a ₦7 million package. Ten runner-up teams each received ₦200,000 cash and ₦1.5 million worth of AWS credits, while every finalist was awarded ₦500,000 worth of AWS credits.

The conference featured several thought-provoking talks from technology and investment leaders. Dr. Kabir Umar Dasuki, CEO of Duke Logistics & Consult Ltd., delivered the first keynote address on “From Traditional Sectors to Tech-Enabled Ventures: Unlocking Innovation in Agriculture, Transport & Trade.” 

This was followed by a presentation by Dr. Steve O. Ogidan, CEO of Global Knowledge Consulting Group, who spoke on “Smart Investment: Financing Africa’s Digital Transformation.” A panel discussion themed “The Startup Journey: Technical, Legal, and Team Requirements” set the stage for the first pitch session involving 10 finalists. Afterward, Arc. Dr. Barka Umaru Mshelia, Group Managing Director and Founder of Mshel Groups, delivered a session on “Unlocking Investment Opportunities in Africa’s Infrastructure and Digital Transformation Agenda,” leading into the second panel discussion titled “Scaling a Startup: Products, Market Fit, Investment, and Revenue,” and another round of pitches.

Later presentations came from Mubashir Shahzad, PhD, R&D Coordinator at Nigeria Tulip International College, and Mr. Nelson Olanipekun, CEO/Founder of Podus AI and Citizens’ Gavel, as well as Mr. Sean Makulowich, CEO of IdeaFire USA, before the final pitch session took place. The event also recognised winners in the Team Manager category, where Deep Secure 360 (DS 360), headed by Ibrahim Isah Liman, received a ₦300,000 cash award.

In his winning pitch, Reagan Rowland recounted a personal emergency that inspired the creation of One Click Med, a digital health passport that places patient records directly in their hands and ensures instant accessibility across hospitals nationwide. He explained that over 80 percent of Nigerian hospitals still rely on paper-based records, leading to delays in treatment. 

“Our unique value proposition is the fact that you, as a patient, becomes the owner of your health record, and you decide where it goes to and at what time,” he said.

The startup has already piloted across 13 hospitals and generated its first revenue in just one month. Rowland revealed that the company has already recorded its first revenue during the pilot phase and aims to tap into at least 10 percent of Nigeria’s over $500 million digital healthcare market.

With recognition given to all 13 winning startups, including runner-ups Solve, Niteon, Venille AI, Home Match, Ledga Finance, Runteller, Intellyjent, Reap Vest, Ace Core, and Aboki Na, the conference concluded with optimism from organisers and participants alike. 

The Startup Abuja Conference 2025 reinforced the capital city’s role as a growing innovation hub and committed to advancing investment avenues that will accelerate Africa’s digital economy through local talent and sustainable technological solutions.

title: KASITDA Secures $50,000 Cloud Grant to Boost Startup Innovation in Kano
excerpt: Kano State’s digital future received a major boost as the Kano State Information Technology Development Agency (KASITDA) secured $50,000 worth of cloud credits to empower top-performing startups that participated in...
content:
Kano State’s digital future received a major boost as the Kano State Information Technology Development Agency (KASITDA) secured $50,000 worth of cloud credits to empower top-performing startups that participated in the just-concluded HEAT Hackathon 2025.

The event, which took place on Saturday, 11th of October, 2025 at the E-Health Africa Auditorium, forms part of Governor Abba Kabir Yusuf’s Digital Transformation Agenda, designed to build a thriving innovation ecosystem that empowers youth and drives inclusive economic growth through technology.

According to a statement released on Tuesday, 14th of October, 2025 by the governor’s spokesperson, Sunusi Bature Dawakin Tofa, the hackathon brought together 36 teams of innovators and over 150 participants to design practical, tech-driven solutions within the HEAT sectors — Health, Education, Agriculture, and Transportation.

Representing the governor at the event, the Director-General of KASITDA, Dr. Bashir Abdu Muzakkari, said the initiative reflects the administration’s long-term vision to make Kano a regional leader in innovation, entrepreneurship, and digital inclusion.

“This hackathon is not a conclusion, but a commencement,” Dr. Muzakkari said.

“His Excellency, Governor Abba Kabir Yusuf, is determined to make Kano a centre of technological excellence where our youth can transform ideas into impact. KASITDA will continue to support innovators to scale their solutions and create opportunities for all,” the statement assured.

According to reports the $50,000 cloud credit package was facilitated through a strategic partnership with CloudPlexo, an Amazon AWS partner, to help the ten top-performing startups access world-class cloud infrastructure for developing, testing, and scaling their solutions.

Additional support for the winners came from All for Tech, which provided premium VPN access for secure and unrestricted development, and Enovate Lab, which offered post-hackathon mentorship — including business model development, pitch refinement, and investment readiness training.

Governor Yusuf, who commended the success of the HEAT Hackathon, described it as a testament to his administration’s commitment to investing in innovation and youth empowerment.

“Our goal is to unlock the potential of technology as a driver of jobs, education, and inclusive development,” the governor said.

“This milestone achieved by KASITDA reflects our shared belief that innovation is the engine of Kano’s future.”

The initiative underscores Kano’s growing recognition as Northern Nigeria’s emerging technology and innovation hub.

In recent months, the state government has rolled out new broadband expansion projects, launched digital skills training programmes, and introduced startup-friendly policies to attract investors and empower young innovators.

Governor Yusuf reaffirmed his administration’s resolve to keep strengthening ICT infrastructure and accelerating the state’s digital economy to “create a new generation of job creators and innovators who will shape the state’s economic future.”

title: From Classrooms to Startups: The Scath Companies is Nurturing Arewa’s Next Gen of Innovators
excerpt: Since opening operations in 2022, The Scath Companies (TSC) Limited has steadily positioned itself as one of Northern Nigeria’s boldest venture capital firms, a hybrid platform investing across four verticals...
content:
Since opening operations in 2022, The Scath Companies (TSC) Limited has steadily positioned itself as one of Northern Nigeria’s boldest venture capital firms, a hybrid platform investing across four verticals which are Technology, Arts, Creatives, and Sports. The firm has provided early-stage funding of up to $50,000 per startup through its Accelerator and Incubation Programmes, while also supporting youth innovation through initiatives like the Innovative Pitch Contest (IPC) for secondary school students.

At its core, TSC’s mission is simple yet ambitious: to mentor, seed-fund, and build some of Africa’s most promising startups and creative ventures, particularly those that transform local challenges into global opportunities.

“What we do is simple at TSC, we provide early-stage funding for startups within underserved regions in Nigeria. Our major focus is within the tech ecosystem. We identify the space where we can apply the venture model, which is identification, incubation and scale,” said Oladipo Lawson, Portfolio Developer Officer. 

Through this model, TSC identifies potential-driven founders, incubates them through mentorship and training, and helps them scale through structured accelerator funding and investor access.

Laying the Foundation for Innovation

From its base in Kaduna, The Scath Companies has focused on regions often overlooked by mainstream venture capital.

According to Ahmed Adebisi, Executive Manager of TSC, the region remains underserved.

“We have seen a lot of entries from this part of the country, but the talk of consideration of funding towards this region is kind of low. Hence, that is why we said, why don’t we have a similar structure that is in the Southern part of Nigeria, here in the North, and push some of these innovative solutions to their best peak,” he added.

For Lawson, ideas are not confined by geography. “The best ideas usually come from places that don’t have a lot of visibility,” he said. “These regions here in Northern Nigeria bring great ideas because people are constantly thinking of what’s next. They see places like Southern Nigeria getting all the attention and say there’s nothing different between them and us. We see high growth potential here in population, in young people, in energy.”

Aisha Yetunde, Head of Programs and Partnerships, echoed that inclusivity is key to TSC’s strategy.

“We are sector agnostic so there are no limitations. We won’t say we are only focused on tech startups or anything like that; we go across the board,” she said.

Innovative Pitch Contest (IPC): Catching Them Young

Among TSC’s most exciting initiatives is the Innovative Pitch Contest (IPC), a competition for secondary school students (SS2 and SS3) launched in 2024.

“It is our ‘catch them young’ project,” Lawson said. “We launched this contest last year as a way to shape and reshape the Nigerian innovation tech sector. We see it as a way to identify ideas at their lowest and most purest forms and provide young Nigerians with the opportunity to see that their ideas are valued.”

He explained that the IPC aims to inspire young Nigerians to see entrepreneurship as attainable from an early age.

Lawson said, “People with the boldest ideas are the ones that reshape the world. What we are doing with IPC is giving the youths, not just those coming out of universities, but those in secondary schools, the opportunity to see their ideas as valuable.”

Adebisi confirmed the programme’s focus group are students in secondary school across Kaduna, who have ideas that can be the next unicorn.

“It is just a contest between secondary school students, (Senior Secondary School) SS2 and SS3 to be precise, just to shape their thoughts regarding pitching business ideas,” he said.

Last year’s pool prize was $1,000, while the 2025 edition increased to $1,250. Winners receive not only prize money but also incubation support and scholarships for tech skills training.

“We have plans to expand, first we would like to make sure Kaduna State, where we are based, has as many schools participate in the contest, maybe not this year but next year. We are already having discussions with creatives in Katsina State to expand the programme into other Northern states, with hopes to have it become a national competition.” Lawson revealed. 

The contest is one of TSC’s deliberate steps to build an innovation pipeline from an early stage giving secondary school students a chance to develop business ideas, learn presentation skills, and gain exposure to the world of startups and entrepreneurship. 

The Accelerator Programme

At the heart of TSC’s operation is its Accelerator Programme, where tech-enabled startups receive funding, mentorship, and business development support. Each selected startup can receive up to $50,000 in seed or pre-seed capital for an average equity of 7.5%, according to Adebisi.

“The Accelerator is mostly for tech-enabled solutions and businesses that are ready to strike the market,” he said.

The programme aims to nurture founders with scalable solutions ready to enter the market. It provides structured guidance on product development, market strategy, and investor relations.

“Our Accelerator Programme is very much driven towards tech-enabled startups,” Lawson explained. “We identify them, help them grow, and provide technology-based solutions that can also help them scale.”

Balancing Tech and Traditional Sectors: The Incubation Programme

While the Accelerator targets tech-driven businesses, TSC’s Incubation Programme focuses on small and medium enterprises with strong local potential but limited access to modern tools and market exposure.

“The Incubator is mostly for businesses that are not fully tech-enabled but have potential as well,” said Adebisi. “That’s the two aspects which are the Accelerator and the Incubator.”

Lawson explained that, “This balance is where we already kind of identify with our funding programme. Our Incubation Programme is for other sectors closer to home that still have a strong market base. We also identify them, help them grow, and provide technology-based solutions that can also help them scale.”

He further said that through this programme, TSC offers workshops, knowledge-sharing sessions, and access to partners who can provide complementary funding and support.

“Even if they don’t necessarily get funding directly from us, there has been an impact, knowledge shared and information passed along to them,” he said.

Beyond Funding: Mentorship and Advisory Support

Beyond funding, The Scath Companies continues to strengthen the ecosystem through mentorship, business advisory, and creative incubation.

“We have a side of our company that does business advisory through that, we can provide support to different businesses that might not necessarily require funding. Every Wednesday, we have an open call and people send in their ideas, where we have a quick five-minute discussion with them.” Lawson said. 

He added that mentorship is a recurring theme across all of TSC’s verticals, designed to empower both founders and creatives to sustain long-term growth.

“We take unknown but young artists and pair them with mentors that have experience in the art space,” he explained. “That process is what we replicate across all our verticals. Mentorship and development are done at the grassroots level from our end.”

Yetunde elaborated on the company’s arts engagement. “We have four verticals which are Creatives, Tech, Arts and Sports. For all of them, we apply the identify, incubate and scale model. The artists work on a project after the incubation programme, it is exhibited in a gallery where there is more exposure and hopefully they can go global as talented artists.” 

The Scath Companies is shaping a new narrative of venture capital from Northern Nigeria, one that is rooted in access, mentorship, and long-term development. By combining seed funding with grassroots incubation, the firm is proving that innovation is not limited to geography.

title: Interface Africa Wins £1.5m at NextGen Innovation Challenge in London

Interface Africa, a Kaduna-based clean energy startup, has emerged winner of the NextGen Innovation Challenge, taking home a cash prize of £1.5 million at the grand finale held on Thursday at the Hilton London Paddington.

The company, led by its Chief Executive Officer, Al’amin Muhammed Idris, was recognized for its pioneering work in affordable solar financing for small businesses across Africa, a model that has expanded access to clean energy in underserved communities.

The NextGen Innovation Challenge, a national initiative spearheaded by the National Board for Technology Incubation (NBTI) in partnership with UKALD London, was created to unlock and promote the innovative potential of Nigerian youths under the framework of President Bola Ahmed Tinubu’s Renewed Hope Agenda.

According to the President, the cash award would further support Interface Africa’s mission to expand clean energy access across the continent.

President Tinubu also reaffirmed his administration’s confidence in Nigerian innovators, noting that “the innovative potential of Nigerian youths is boundless; hence, his administration’s deliberate policies and programmes to harness and catalyse this vital resource.”

While congratulating Interface Africa, the President extended his appreciation to the other 104 participants in the competition, urging them to continue “innovating, improving lives, and shaping humanity’s future.”

The NextGen Innovation Challenge continues to serve as a key platform for spotlighting Nigerian innovators driving technological and social change both at home and abroad.

title: Breni Finds Global Classroom, with Strong Growth in Asia
excerpt: Breni, an educational technology tool, is experiencing rapid international growth, with the majority of its users located outside Africa, particularly in Asia. The Arewa-based company has seen unexpected global traction...
content:
Breni, an educational technology tool, is experiencing rapid international growth, with the majority of its users located outside Africa, particularly in Asia. The Arewa-based company has seen unexpected global traction just months after its official launch.

Founded by Abubakar Sadiq Umar and Bilal Abdullahi in August 2025, it was developed to improve learning access through an AI-powered app that adapts to each user’s pace, language, and preferred subject areas. Originally targeted at Nigerian students struggling with traditional learning systems, currently, about 90 percent of its users are based overseas, led by Nepal, Russia, Uzbekistan, and Azerbaijan. The startup also records active users from the UAE, South Africa, Canada, the United States, and the United Kingdom.

The app allows users to learn in several languages, including Hausa, English, French, and Spanish, and covers a wide range of subjects beyond formal academics. Breni’s personalised features, such as micro-learning lessons, gamified quizzes, and progress tracking, have helped it gain popularity among students seeking flexible and low-cost learning options abroad.

Umar, the co-founder, said the team was surprised by the speed of foreign adoption, noting that most of the growth came from organic referrals rather than paid marketing. “We built Breni to help Nigerian learners adapt to modern study tools, but it’s encouraging to see students from Asia and Europe using it daily,” he said in an interview with Techpoint Africa.

The company currently operates a freemium model, offering free access supported by ads and a paid subscription plan that varies by region. In its first 37 days of operation, Breni generated about ₦200,000 (US$137), an early indicator of potential commercial success despite limited funding and competition from global platforms such as Duolingo and Coursera.

Breni’s expansion marks one of the few instances of an Arewa-based tech company achieving global recognition within its first few months. Its growth underscores the increasing international competitiveness of Northern Nigerian startups, particularly those outside Lagos, where most of the country’s tech ecosystem is concentrated.

The founders plan to scale up Breni’s presence in Asian markets through partnerships and content localisation, while also expanding access for students in Northern Nigeria. “Our long-term goal is to connect learners everywhere through technology that understands them,” said co-founder Abdullahi.

With its growing international footprint, Breni is emerging as one of Northern Nigeria’s most promising digital exports, proving that local innovation can find a global audience.

title: Why We Need More VCs in Arewa
excerpt: Venture capital (VC) is smart money for young companies, because investors buy a small slice of a startup and, in return, provide cash and hands-on help such as strategy, mentorship,...
content:
Venture capital (VC) is smart money for young companies, because investors buy a small slice of a startup and, in return, provide cash and hands-on help such as strategy, mentorship, hiring support, customer introductions, and credibility. VC matters to innovation ecosystems because it accelerates ideas that already show promise, helping founders move faster from prototype to product-market fit and scale. In Nigeria, bank debt is often expensive and collateral-heavy, but in Arewa the challenge bites harder because alternatives are scarce, leaving high-potential founders without affordable pathways to capital. VC fills a critical gap by funding high-potential teams based on traction and insight, not on assets.

The Northern Nigeria innovation ecosystem is surging, fueled by dynamic entrepreneurs developing solutions tailored to the region’s unique problems from agritech and edtech to healthtech and logistics. Ecosystem frameworks such as incubators, accelerators, and business networks are gradually forming, yet one critical element remains scarce, which is structured venture capital support specifically designed to nurture this growth in Arewa.

Although venture capital remains scarce in Northern Nigeria, a few firms have begun stepping forward to support the region’s innovators. Each brings a distinct strategy for funding and growth, and collectively, their emergence underscores an important turning point for investors rooted in the North who are now beginning to shape the future of its entrepreneurial ecosystem.

Aduna Capital Nigeria, for instance, is focused on funding early-stage startups across Africa with a strong emphasis on female founders and underserved regions, particularly Northern Nigeria. The firm unveiled a $20 million fund targeted at empowering startups in the region and beyond, reflecting a long-term commitment to equity and growth.

PennPromise Venture also reflects this vision as an ethically driven alternative investment firm that is reshaping Africa’s private capital markets. With its focus on transformative growth across underserved middle-market economies, PennPromise leverages venture capital, growth funding, alternative credits, and infrastructure investments to build long-term value. It offers pre-seed checks up to $20,000 and seed funding up to $100,000, coupled with a venture studio model that provides structured support through their PMVIF framework for idea-to-MVP incubation.

The Scath Companies (TSC) Limited, founded in 2019, operates as a hybrid venture capital firm providing early-stage funding and business development services to startups in Africa. Headquartered in Kaduna, the firm is particularly committed to emerging, underrepresented, and underserved regions with a primary emphasis on Northern Nigeria. TSC closed its most recent funding round on February 2, 2022, through an undisclosed round, signaling its continued activity in nurturing the North’s innovation ecosystem.

Likewise, Babban Gona, meaning “Great Farm” in Hausa, has since 2012 functioned as a financially sustainable and scalable agricultural social enterprise, making farming more profitable for smallholder farmers and addressing poverty and unemployment, especially among young people in rural areas. 

Recently, Babban Gona raised a $7.5 million debt round from the British International Investment (BII), the UK’s development finance institution, to offer capital to smallholder farmers in Northern Nigeria. The company uses AI to provide end-to-end services, including credit, training, support with harvesting, storage, and access to markets, helping farmers overcome barriers such as climate change. Over the years, Babban Gona has raised more than $41.7 million across multiple funding rounds and is widely regarded as one of the most successful social enterprises in Africa.

Though less public on investment volume, all signal that Aduna, Babban Gona, PennPromise, and TSC are injecting tens of millions into the region, across agriculture, fintech, logistics, and grassroots enterprise sectors.

Recent years have shown that venture capital and growth funding are already altering outcomes in Northern Nigeria. Aduna Capital’s portfolio is a testament to this shift, with startups like Yaada Technologies, a Kaduna-based fintech founded in 2023, which is simplifying financial inclusion by offering USSD-powered seamless payments from P2P to utility bills.  Other startups backed include Agriarche, an agritech startup established in 2020, which uses its Kasuwa platform to digitize the agricultural supply chain, enabling farmers and aggregators to access markets, build credit histories, and reduce waste. Sudo Africa, a fintech enabling businesses to issue physical and virtual cards via modern APIs. 

Today, the landscape is evolving with multiple players stepping up in Northern Nigeria. These players collectively signal that Arewa’s VC ecosystem is slowly assembling a backbone but Arewa needs many more such players. Northern Nigeria is “hot cake”: a rapidly expanding region rich in opportunities across sectors like agriculture, education, healthtech, logistics, and fintech yet the region is under-capitalized. If the region fails to attract more capital and institutional support, it risks letting this potential slip away.

Why Northern Nigeria Cannot Be Ignored

Northern Nigeria boasts one of the country’s youngest populations and some of its most promising untapped markets. Startups emerging from schools, universities, and innovation hubs are tackling critical issues such as rural healthcare delivery, access to quality education, agricultural extension services, and logistical access across dispersed communities.

Arewa is no longer waiting in the shadows; its startups are gaining international recognition. At GITEX Africa 2025 in Morocco, a number of Arewa-based ventures were selected to represent Nigeria. Northino is leveraging digital innovation to build scalable tech solutions from the North; Flowdiary is redefining how students manage academic records and collaboration; Schoola, an EdTech startup from Northern Nigeria, is bridging gaps in learning access through digital platforms; while Interface Africa is connecting African businesses through a robust networking platform. These startups represent the diversity and ambition of the ecosystem, showing that Arewa is not just capable of competing but of leading in key sectors.

However, despite this promise, many of these ventures remain underfunded and under-mentored. Without VC support, ideas risk stalling before they scale. Financial capital alone isn’t enough. What Northern startups critically need are mentorship, strategic guidance, networks, credibility, and market exposure, the “value-added” infrastructure that transforms early ideas into national or international success stories.

What VCs Are Saying at GITEX Nigeria 2025

An important message echoed by VCs at GITEX Nigeria 2025 was that they’re not chasing hype, but strong, lasting fundamentals.

Oluwakemi Olajide, Investment Principal at Africa Climate Ventures, warned founders: “As you build, you’ll get all sorts of advice from investors. Be open-minded, but also remember your why. Don’t get derailed. Stay grounded in your unit economics, don’t overpromise and under-deliver.”

Brian Waswani Odhiambo, Partner at Novastar Ventures, added an even sharper edge:

“If you’re a founder in Africa, you’re probably one of the best entrepreneurs in the world. But venture capital isn’t for everyone, maybe just 1% of entrepreneurs. It comes with big obligations and expectations. It’s not free money, so think deeply before you take it.”

The collective message from all the VCs present at the event was clear: discipline, resilience, and clarity of purpose matter far more than flashy growth charts or hot valuations.

More Than Just Money: The Mentorship Gap

In a recent interview with Muhammad Auwal Ahmad, the founder of Flowdiary, who was selected among Nigeria’s top 12 startups to represent the country earlier this year at GITEX Africa 2025 in Morocco.

One of his remarks stuck with me: “Mentorship is more important than funding sometimes. If you get funding but don’t know how to manage it, you just run around in circles. We focused on solving real problems first, and the opportunities followed.”

This mindset shows why Arewa startups need more than just cheques; they need VCs who can walk the journey with them. Mentorship matters because capital without direction can become a burden. A founder might raise funds, but without seasoned guidance on market strategy, operations, or product positioning, the enterprise can falter. Mentorship bridges the experience gap, by helping founders prioritize, pivot intelligently, build resilient business models, and access broader networks. This kind of close partnership often defines outcomes where high-risk ventures either flounder or flourish.

A Call to Action for VCs

Northern Nigeria is brimming with innovators ready to scale, yet the capital and mentorship pipelines remain thin. The few VCs already planting roots such as Aduna Capital, PennPromise, TSC Limited, and Babban Gona are leading the way, but the North needs more.

Venture capitalists must start looking at Arewa through the same excited lens they apply to Lagos, Nairobi, or global tech hubs like Silicon Valley. Investing in Northern Nigeria is not charity, it’s strategic, forward-thinking business. Startups from the North are crafting innovative, region-rooted solutions with the potential to scale and redefine markets. For Nigeria’s broader digital economy to thrive in a truly inclusive way, VC infrastructure must stretch beyond Lagos and Arewa cannot, and must not, be sidelined.

title: Babban Gona Secures $7.5m Boost to Scale Farmer-Led Model and Strengthen Climate Resilience in Northern Nigeria
excerpt: Babban Gona, Nigeria’s pioneering agri-tech platform, has secured a $7.5 million debt investment from British International Investment (BII) to expand its farmer-led franchise model and deepen support for smallholder farmers...
content:
Babban Gona, Nigeria’s pioneering agri-tech platform, has secured a $7.5 million debt investment from British International Investment (BII) to expand its farmer-led franchise model and deepen support for smallholder farmers across Northern Nigeria.

Babban Gona, which already works with thousands of smallholders in the region, is tackling the entrenched barriers that limit their productivity — from lack of access to finance and quality inputs to gaps in agronomic training and reliable markets. These challenges are magnified by rising climate risks such as floods and droughts, which threaten harvests and worsen food insecurity.

Through its AI-powered platform, Babban Gona delivers comprehensive end-to-end services including working capital, high-quality seeds, climate-smart training, harvest and storage support, and direct market access. A hallmark of its approach is the franchise system, where top-performing farmers establish micro-enterprises that provide services and credit to peers, before scaling up to attract local bank funding.

With BII’s latest investment, Babban Gona aims to improve yields, increase incomes, and strengthen climate resilience for about 140,000 farmers in Northern Nigeria by 2029. Its services also include drought-resilient seeds and area yield insurance, giving farmers tools to withstand shocks and recover faster.

Babban Gona’s Managing Director Kola Masha described the new funding as both validation and acceleration. He said: “The British government played an instrumental role in our story, becoming the first institutional investor in our 2013 public debt raise. Now, a little more than a decade later, to have British International Investment commit an amount 10x larger is a powerful testament to our shared vision for bettering the lives of smallholder farmers. We are thrilled to have them partner with us in this next phase of our journey as we accelerate the impact of our work, with the ambition to become the Earth’s highest-impact business.”

UK Trade Envoy to Nigeria, Florence Eshalomi MP, also highlighted the scale of Babban Gona’s work. She said: “Today, I’m proud to stand alongside British International Investment (BII) as we announce a $7.5 million investment into Babban Gona, a pioneering social enterprise transforming smallholder agriculture in Nigeria. 

“This investment will help scale an innovative, tech-enabled model that empowers farmers with access to finance, training, and services, boosting yields and incomes while building climate resilience. From early-stage UK support through Propcom Maikarfi to this milestone investment, Babban Gona’s journey is a powerful example of what’s possible when we invest in Nigeria’s agricultural future. This partnership reflects the UK-Nigeria commitment to sustainable, inclusive growth, and I’m excited to see the impact it will generate.”

For BII, the deal is a clear example of backing innovative African models with global potential. Benson Adenuga, BII’s West Africa Regional Director and Head of Office for Nigeria, said: “Our partnership with Babban Gona is a great example of how BII is using catalytic capital to support innovative, high-impact business models that transform lives and economies. 

He further stated that, “By backing this pioneering franchise model, we are not only addressing a critical financing gap but also helping to build a more resilient and productive agricultural sector and support smallholder farmers in a region that is often overlooked by investors. This investment will deliver tangible impact at scale, strengthening food security and climate resilience.”

This partnership positions Babban Gona not just as a service provider for farmers, but as a blueprint for how local enterprises can drive food security, economic inclusion, and climate adaptation across Northern Nigeria and beyond.

title: GITEX Nigeria Opens with Unified Call for Africa to Shape Its Own AI Future
excerpt: The GITEX Nigeria Summit 2025 opened on Monday in Abuja, bringing together leaders, policymakers, and innovators from across Africa and beyond. The four-day summit, which runs from September 1 to...
content:
The GITEX Nigeria Summit 2025 opened on Monday in Abuja, bringing together leaders, policymakers, and innovators from across Africa and beyond. The four-day summit, which runs from September 1 to 4, is designed to accelerate digital transformation and innovation.

At the opening, speakers made it clear why Africa must build its own inclusive path in artificial intelligence (AI) and digital growth: without doing so, the continent risks being left behind. The event featured keynote addresses, policy discussions, and commitments on how to strengthen the skills, infrastructure, and partnerships needed for Africa’s digital future.

The Minister of Communications, Innovation and Digital Economy, Dr. Bosun Tijani, led the charge, warning that Africa cannot afford to rely solely on foreign models and infrastructure. He stressed that productivity — from agriculture to education and healthcare — will increasingly hinge on AI, and urged African governments to pool resources and expertise.

“The risk for Africa is clear; if we are not deliberate, AI will widen the global productivity gap,” Tijani said. “Countries already ahead will move even faster, and those of us still catching up will find ourselves even further behind.”

Drawing on examples from agriculture, Tijani compared Nigeria’s maize yield of 2.5 tonnes per hectare to South Africa’s 6 tonnes and Brazil’s 12 tonnes, attributing the gap not to natural resources but to technological advantage and AI-driven precision farming.

He pushed for models that reflect Africa’s realities. “There is a world where Africa will bring diversity into AI. For ChatGPT or any other model to be strong, it must understand the reality of everyone,” he said. “We should not see ourselves as disadvantaged because we lack infrastructure. Even in the geopolitics of GPUs, Africa must demand inclusivity so our realities and data are taken into account.”

Alongside his keynote, Tijani outlined four priorities for the continent’s AI future: shared governance that balances sovereignty, massive investment in youth skills, digitisation of local realities to create relevant datasets, and collective investment in connectivity, compute, and clean energy.

The message was reinforced by Kashifu Abdullahi, Director-General of the National Information Technology Development Agency (NITDA), who described AI as “the engine of the Fourth Industrial Revolution.” He highlighted Nigeria’s push to expand digital literacy, build data centers, and roll out initiatives like Project Reach to connect underserved communities.

“We need shared infrastructure and local algorithms that reflect our culture,” Abdullahi said. “Nigeria is already making progress through initiatives in digital literacy, data centers, and projects like Project Reach to connect the unconnected.”

Subnational leadership also took the spotlight, with Lagos State Governor Babajide Sanwo-Olu affirming Lagos’ role as Nigeria’s innovation capital. He said the state is investing heavily in broadband, startup ecosystems, and tech-friendly policies.

“Lagos is home to Nigeria’s most vibrant startup ecosystem, and we are committed to creating an enabling environment where ideas can thrive. GITEX Nigeria is a platform to demonstrate how subnational governments can drive innovation in line with the federal government’s vision,” Sanwo-Olu stated.

Beyond Nigeria, global voices also weighed in. Trixie LohMirmand, Executive Vice President of Dubai World Trade Centre and CEO of KAOUN International, stressed that Africa’s journey will require global partnerships to attract investment and embed the continent in the global technology economy.

As the first day wrapped up, speakers agreed that Africa’s AI journey must be inclusive, contextual, and future-focused. The shared understanding was that the continent’s global competitiveness will hinge on how quickly it develops the skills, policies, and infrastructure needed to harness AI responsibly.

The 2025 Continuum Spark Awards have officially opened applications, offering a $250,000 funding pool to spotlight Muslim-led startups and nonprofits driving bold, values-driven innovation across the globe. 

The Spark Awards are hosted by Collective Continuum, a values-first venture philanthropy platform committed to change through faith-driven innovation and meaningful impact. Launched in 2022 and run out of both the UK and the United States, Collective Continuum brings together a global collective of multi-exit founders, design leaders, Islamic philanthropy experts, social entrepreneurs, and family offices, Collective Continuum operates on the principle that “when values lead, innovation follows.” 

The awards, designed to elevate changemakers from the Muslim world, promise not just financial support but also global visibility, mentorship, and a chance to pitch live in Qatar before international leaders and investors.

Organizers announced that applications have been opened since June 21 and will close on August 31, 2025, with finalists set to take the stage at the GEM Summit in Doha this December. The program is open to Muslim entrepreneurs worldwide, welcoming both early-stage for-profit startups and nonprofits with measurable social impact. 

For-profit ventures at the pre-seed, seed, or bridge stage stand a chance to secure up to $100,000 in capital investment under a SAFE agreement, alongside $25,000 worth of strategic support, brand and tech guidance, and access to global mentors. 

Nonprofits, on the other hand, will compete for $25,000 in grants complemented by capacity-building support worth up to $100,000, with added benefits of ecosystem connections and tailored growth support.

The selection process will see 20 startups and 15 nonprofits shortlisted in the elimination round, with just four from each category advancing to the finals in Qatar. Finalists will have their travel and accommodation fully covered, giving them a platform to present their mission, vision, and values to a high-profile audience of funders and partners.

The Collective Continuum provides capital, community, and capacity-building support to values-driven ventures, with a mandate to fund and elevate 1,000 aligned projects over the next five years.

With its mix of capital support, mentorship, and international exposure, the Continuum Spark Awards 2025 is positioning itself as a global stage for Muslim innovators seeking to scale their impact.

title: Dr. Wudil’s US Patent AI-Powered Laser Technology Set to Transform Soil Analysis
excerpt: Dr. Yakubu Sani Wudil, a physicist, researcher, and technology innovator from Northern Nigeria, and his team have secured a United States patent for a cutting-edge invention that merges laser-induced breakdown...
content:
Dr. Yakubu Sani Wudil, a physicist, researcher, and technology innovator from Northern Nigeria, and his team have secured a United States patent for a cutting-edge invention that merges laser-induced breakdown spectroscopy (LIBS) with machine learning to accurately predict essential soil properties.

The newly patented method combines laser-induced breakdown spectroscopy (LIBS) which uses laser pulses to analyze the chemical makeup of soil samples with machine learning models that can estimate key soil characteristics such as unconfined compressive strength, moisture content, and bulk density. This technology makes soil testing quicker, more accurate, and portable, reducing the need for traditional lab-based procedures. Similar methods are being explored globally, with researchers using LIBS and artificial intelligence to measure things like soil carbon, nutrients, and heavy metals in real time. These developments suggest a growing trend toward mobile tools that can deliver fast and reliable soil data directly on-site.

According to Dr. Wudil, the invention is a fast, non-destructive, and cost-effective method capable of determining critical soil parameters such as unconfined compressive strength, moisture content, and bulk density.

Dr. Wudil hails from Kano State and currently serves as a Research Fellow at the Research and Innovation Center of King Fahd University of Petroleum & Minerals (KFUPM) in Saudi Arabia. A product of rigorous academic training, he holds a Ph.D. in Physics and has built a strong reputation for multidisciplinary research, particularly at the intersection of laser spectroscopy, artificial intelligence, and material science. His work spans renewable energy, thermoelectric materials, machine learning, and density functional theory, with over 900 citations across 41 scholarly publications.

The breakthrough of this new invention represents a significant stride in how soil analysis is approached, particularly for applications in civil engineering, environmental science, construction, and geology. Traditionally, soil testing has relied on time-consuming and often destructive laboratory techniques, but Dr. Wudil’s patented method offers a faster and more portable alternative, with the potential to improve on-site decision-making and reduce project delays in the field.

For civil engineers, this breakthrough means engineers can assess soil stability on-site, in real time, which could significantly reduce delays and enhance project safety. For environmental science and geology, the innovation enables quick and accurate soil profiling useful in land remediation and hazard assessments. In agriculture and land management, the technology has the potential to optimize crop planning, irrigation systems, and soil health monitoring.

Dr. Wudil’s patented method adds to a trajectory of technological progress in rapid soil diagnostics that started with conventional spectrometers and is now embracing AI‑driven, LIBS‑based portable devices. Similar efforts such as portable infrared spectrometer platforms that rival lab accuracy using calibration‑transfer techniques highlight how the convergence of spectroscopy and machine learning is enabling a new generation of real‑time soil assessment tools.

title: GITEX Nigeria 2025: Kano Hosts Northwest Roadshow, Spotlights Startup Innovation and Global Opportunities

content:
Kano took centre stage as the GITEX Nigeria 2025 Startup Roadshow rolled into the Northwest, offering a platform for emerging startups in the region to access mentorship, funding, and global exposure. Organised by the Office for Nigerian Digital Innovation (ONDI), a special purpose vehicle of the National Information Technology Development Agency (NITDA), the Kano edition marks the penultimate stop of the nationwide tour, which has already traversed Enugu, Gombe, Abuja, and Uyo.

Held under the theme “Bridging Nigeria’s Innovation with Global Opportunities,” the Roadshow in Kano reaffirmed the federal government’s commitment to supporting a vibrant innovation ecosystem across all geopolitical zones. It also sets the tone for the final leg in Lagos, representing the Southwest, to ensure full national representation at GITEX Nigeria 2025.

Speaking at the event, the Director General of NITDA, Kashifu Inuwa Abdullahi, who was represented by the Northwest Zonal Coordinator, Engr. Muhammad Kabir Salihu, called attention to the roadshow’s transformative goal of connecting local innovators with international opportunities.

He noted that startups from the Northwest now enjoy increased access to resources through initiatives such as NITDA’s iHatch incubation programme and strategic collaborations with institutions like the Northwest Development Commission (NWDC). These partnerships, he said, are equipping entrepreneurs with tools to scale and thrive in the global innovation space.

“With continued support from government and private stakeholders, we can unlock the untapped digital potential of Northern Nigeria,” he stated. “We’re not just witnessing innovation here, we’re building a future that connects Kano to global tech corridors.”

He also urged stakeholders across sectors such as innovators, investors, and policymakers to actively collaborate in co-creating a thriving digital economy for Africa, stressing that inclusive innovation is central to Nigeria’s digital transformation agenda.

The Kano pitch session featured a diverse mix of tech founders working on digital solutions in agriculture, logistics, finance, and education. Winners from the Northwest will now join finalists from the other regions to compete at GITEX Nigeria 2025, taking place in Abuja and Lagos from September 1–4. Ultimately, the most outstanding startups will go on to represent Nigeria at GITEX Global 2026 in Dubai.

As the GITEX Nigeria Roadshow nears its conclusion, the energy from Kano underscores a growing tech movement in the North, one that is ready to take its place on the global innovation map.

title: The Good, The Bad and The Ugly: Buhari's Legacy In The Tech Ecosystem (2015–2023)
excerpt: On Sunday, 13 July 2025, Muhammadu Buhari, two-time President of Nigeria, passed away. However, what was the outcome of technology under his regime? When Buhari assumed office in 2015, he...
content:
On Sunday, 13 July 2025, Muhammadu Buhari, two-time President of Nigeria, passed away. However, what was the outcome of technology under his regime? When Buhari assumed office in 2015, he was not widely perceived as a champion of technology or digital transformation.

Yet, by the time he left office in 2023, Nigeria’s tech ecosystem had undergone notable changes under his administration both through deliberate reforms and through unintended consequences of other policies. The period between 2015 and 2023 delivered substantial progress in digital infrastructure, identity systems, and the startup ecosystem, but was also marked by inconsistent policy decisions, regulatory overreach, and a few setbacks that hindered trust and long-term stability.

The Good: Growth, Infrastructure, and Policy Foundations

Under Buhari, Nigeria made tangible gains in digital infrastructure. Broadband penetration increased from around 6–10% in 2015 to approximately 46% by 2023. The country launched nationwide 4G and, in December 2021, proceeded to become one of the first African countries to roll out 5G, auctioning spectrum that significantly expanded high-speed internet access. The addition of two new subsea cables during his tenure tripled Nigeria’s available bandwidth capacity. Despite persistent power challenges Nigeria’s national grid was still producing less than 5GW in 2023 which helped the digital sector grew rapidly.

Prior to Buhari, the ICT sector played a relatively quiet role in the national economy, often overshadowed by oil and agriculture. But under his administration, the sector outpaced others in GDP growth, especially during the pandemic, helping to cushion the economic shock. In 2022, Buhari acknowledged this during the launch of Microsoft’s $200 million hub in Abuja, stating, “Our emphasis on the development of our digital economy has positioned the sector as a prominent factor in our economy.” Indeed, the tech sector played a critical role in helping Nigeria exit recession after the COVID-19 lockdowns.

A key structural move was the renaming and reorganization of the Ministry of Communications to the Ministry of Communications and Digital Economy, led by Dr. Isa Ali Pantami. Along with Oswald Osaretin Guobadia, Buhari’s Senior Special Assistant on Digital Transformation, the administration launched the National Digital Economy Policy and Strategy (2020–2030) and a new National Broadband Plan targeting 70% broadband coverage by 2025. These were not just symbolic policies, they laid the foundation for Nigeria’s expanding digital footprint.

Additionally, Executive Order 5, signed in 2018, mandated the prioritization of local tech vendors in public procurement contracts. This measure boosted indigenous technology providers and aligned with the broader goal of strengthening Nigeria’s digital sovereignty.

Perhaps the most consequential legislative action was the signing of the Nigeria Startup Act in 2022. Co-drafted with input from the tech ecosystem, the law defined the regulatory framework for startups, created access to tax incentives, and set up a national council to guide innovation-friendly policy. It formalized a relationship between the tech ecosystem and the government for the first time.

In terms of digital identification, Buhari’s government expanded National Identity Number (NIN) registration from about 7 million people in 2015 to nearly 100 million by 2023, with SIM card registration linked to the NIN database. This large-scale enrollment enabled faster Know Your Customer (KYC) processes across banks and fintech platforms and improved access to digital services.Nigeria also became the first country in Africa to launch a Central Bank Digital Currency (CBDC), the eNaira, in 2021. While uptake was limited, the launch positioned Nigeria among early movers in government-issued digital currencies.Institutions such as the National Data Protection Bureau, an AI and Robotics Centre, and a national blockchain policy were introduced to create regulatory frameworks around emerging technologies and improve Nigeria’s data protection regime.

The financial technology (fintech) sector saw exponential growth. Companies like Flutterwave, Paystack, OPay, Moniepoint, and PalmPay gained scale and investment. Nigeria attracted over $5 billion in startup funding, making it the leading destination for venture capital in Africa during Buhari’s tenure.

Toward the end of his administration, one of Buhari’s most controversial actions was the currency redesign policy ahead of the 2023 general elections that created serious disruptions. The rushed rollout of redesigned naira notes and the subsequent cash crunch left millions without access to physical currency for weeks. While the policy was roundly criticized for hurting small businesses and informal sector workers, it unintentionally accelerated the adoption of digital payments.

With cash unavailable and traditional banks overwhelmed, fintechs filled the gap. Operators like OPay, PalmPay, and Moniepoint became primary payment platforms. According to the Nigeria Inter-Bank Settlement System (NIBSS), mobile money operators processed ₦46.6 trillion in transactions in 2023, a 140% increase over the previous year. Moniepoint alone processed over 5.2 billion transactions that year. A KPMG report revealed that 58% of Nigerians switched from traditional banks to fintechs during the crisis. In effect, the unintended consequence of a flawed monetary policy was a historic leap in digital financial inclusion.

The Bad: Regulatory Inconsistencies and Poor Execution

Despite the clear progress, several actions by the administration either stalled innovation or created uncertainty. The ban on cryptocurrency transactions in February 2021 by the Central Bank of Nigeria disrupted one of Nigeria’s fastest-growing digital sectors. Crypto trading had become a major outlet for young Nigerians to access global finance, yet the CBN’s directive forced platforms to operate through peer-to-peer methods, reducing transparency and pushing innovation underground. Although the ban was lifted in December 2023, the loss in momentum and investor confidence was already felt.

The Twitter suspension from June 2021 to January 2022 followed the platform’s removal of one of Buhari’s tweets. This move caused significant financial losses, especially for small businesses and creators who depended on the platform for marketing and communication. According to estimates, the seven-month suspension cost the Nigerian economy about ₦26 billion.

Another well-intentioned but poorly executed project was the NIN-SIM linkage policy, aimed at integrating national identification with mobile phone records. While the idea was sound, the rollout was inefficient. Nigerians faced repeated deadlines, long queues at enrollment centers, and occasional disconnections of SIM cards due to delays. In rural areas, connectivity remained weak, with 2G networks still prevalent in many communities. Fibre-optic rollout lagged, largely due to state-level Right-of-Way (RoW) charges and bureaucratic delays. This undermined the goal of achieving uniform national access and widened the digital divide.

Another significant challenge was the ongoing “Japa” trend, the mass migration of skilled tech talent to countries offering better opportunities. Although the administration launched several digital skills training initiatives, they were not matched by job creation or industry-scale employment opportunities in the local market. This limited Nigeria’s ability to retain its best-trained talent.

The #NextLevel campaign, which was supposed to drive forward Nigeria’s digital and innovation economy during Buhari’s second term, often lacked clear metrics or publicly tracked roadmaps. Many initiatives were announced but did not translate into measurable results or completed projects.

The Ugly: Policy Backfires and Institutional Control

Despite its early promise, the eNaira failed to gain widespread acceptance. Technical problems with the app, limited public education, and weak merchant participation led to low adoption rates. The project did not achieve its goals in driving financial inclusion or digital payments.

Also, the government’s attempts to expand control over the internet such as social media monitoring proposals and online platform licensing which created suspicion and eroded trust. Instead of building collaborative frameworks, some policies came across as punitive or reactionary.

President Buhari’s legacy in Nigeria’s tech ecosystem is a mixture of clear progress and costly missteps. On one hand, broadband infrastructure expanded, digital identification scaled massively, and Nigeria passed its first real startup-focused legislation. The tech ecosystem became a key part of the national economy.

On the other hand, policy inconsistency, abrupt regulations, and a centralist approach often undermined that progress. From banning crypto to suspending Twitter, the government sent mixed messages to both investors and local innovators.

Still, it is accurate to say that Buhari’s administration laid a structural foundation that Nigeria’s next wave of digital growth can build upon, if future administrations prioritize clarity, consistency, and openness over control.

title: NITDA Launches Tech Talent Hunt in Enugu as GITEX Nigeria 2025 Roadshow Begins
