content:
The National Information Technology Development Agency (NITDA) has officially flagged off the GITEX Nigeria 2025 Regional Roadshow in Enugu, kicking off a nationwide search for the country’s most promising tech startups ahead of the prestigious GITEX Nigeria Startup Festival.

Held on Tuesday, July 15, the Enugu edition marked the first stop of the regional tour and drew young tech innovators from across the Southeast states which are Abia, Anambra, Ebonyi, Enugu, and Imo. These entrepreneurs gathered to pitch scalable solutions in key sectors such as HealthTech, AgriTech, FinTech, Artificial Intelligence, EdTech, ClimateTech, and CreativeTech.

The roadshow is a strategic prelude to the main GITEX Nigeria 2025 Startup Festival, scheduled to take place in Abuja from September 1 to 4. Modeled after the globally renowned Gulf Information Technology Exhibition (GITEX), which has showcased frontier technologies in Dubai since 1981, GITEX Nigeria aims to spotlight homegrown innovation and integrate Nigerian startups into the global digital economy.

Speaking at the Enugu launch event, Enugu State Commissioner for Innovation, Science, and Technology, Dr. Lawrence Ezeh, praised NITDA’s commitment to empowering regional talent. “This is more than a startup competition, it’s a gateway to national visibility and global competitiveness,” Ezeh said. “Our youth must seize this moment to become part of Nigeria’s innovation narrative and potentially represent us at GITEX Global in Dubai.”

Dr. Nkem Momah, Head of NITDA’s Southeast Zonal Office, emphasized the agency’s mission to support startups building real-world, scalable solutions. “We’re looking for bold, problem-solving innovators whose work can transform industries and strengthen Nigeria’s digital economy,” Momah stated.

The Enugu roadshow featured pitch sessions, mentorship opportunities, and networking with ecosystem stakeholders. Finalists selected from the Southeast zone will receive an all-expense-paid trip to exhibit their solutions at the Abuja Startup Festival. There, they will pitch before panels of top-tier investors, government officials, tech media, and global innovation experts. Successful startups will also be considered for international exposure at GITEX Global in Dubai, one of the world’s largest and longest-running tech trade shows.

As NITDA’s regional tour continues through the other five geopolitical zones, the agency is reaffirming its drive to build an inclusive innovation pipeline, one that connects local talent to global opportunities, starting from Enugu and culminating on the world stage in Dubai.

title: Founding in the margins: Rethinking the pathways to Innovation in Northen Nigeria.
excerpt: global conversations about tech and innovation in Africa, cities like Lagos, Nairobi, and Cape Town dominate the spotlight, and rightly so. These are bustling hubs of...
content:
By Fateemah Sanusi

In global conversations about tech and innovation in Africa, cities like Lagos, Nairobi, and Cape Town dominate the spotlight, and rightly so. These are bustling hubs of innovation, capital, and connectivity. They benefit from dense networks of accelerators, high-speed internet, and access to global markets. But they do not tell the full story. Across the margins of this narrative, another story is unfolding. It is one of resilient, creative founders building in less celebrated places like Kano, Gombe, Katsina, and Adamawa.

These cities may not host unicorns or pitch competitions every weekend, but they are birthing startups that solve pressing, local problems with resourcefulness and grit. For example, in Adamawa, GetMedford offers an online pharmaceutical marketplace that links pharmacies and healthcare providers to a broad selection of medical products, simplifying the procurement process and enabling enhance access to reliable, high-quality medicines for healthcare institutions across the country.

Talent in the North often emerges through different paths. Many of the region’s most promising developers, designers, and founders are self-taught or have come through community-led bootcamps, informal mentorship, and peer-to-peer learning. Without access to elite universities or formal accelerators, they rely on grit, open-source tools, and collaborative networks. And it works.

From cyber cafés to youth centers, the journey into tech may be unstructured, but it is no less legitimate. In many cases, it leads to innovative solutions that are more closely tied to the lived realities on the ground. This underscores why ‘Founding in the margins’ demands a different kind of innovation born not out of abundance, but necessity and true commitment to solving real, everyday problems. In the face of constraints where infrastructure is unreliable, broadband is expensive or entirely unavailable, and access to venture capital is virtually non-existent.

Yet despite these barriers, founding in the North continues to grow. Rather than stifling its progress, these limitations have enabled a kind of creativity that’s practical, deeply local, and built out of real need. What we see is a thriving informal economy that is being transformed in communities where access is limited. For instance, Agrivest247 builds for traders, artisans, and farmers as early adopters of their agritech platform. By seeking to connect macro-entrepreneurs and farmers with investors, as well as coordinating logistics, they represent a growing ecosystem of builders who are rethinking what innovation looks like when it’s rooted in place and shaped by necessity.

More crucially, new pathways into northern Nigerian tech ecosystem are emerging beyond fintech and supply chain digital solutions. Hence, broadening access for those often excluded from traditional career routes. In a region where youth unemployment is high and many women are out of formal work, technology offers flexible, accessible alternatives. For instance, women, including stay-at-home mothers, could learn digital skills or offer online tutorials and self-paced trainings.

Gaining the expertise to turn basic digital literacy into scaled businesses and income generating ventures. These entry points may seem small, but they are powerful especially when they enable autonomy, income, and amplify sidelined voices. Similarly, there is fertile ground in the Healthtech sector to tackle problems that are prominent in this region. In areas where access to quality medical care is limited, digital health solutions such as telemedicine platforms, diagnostic tools, and AI-assisted triage systems can bridge critical gaps, especially in rural and conflict-affected regions. For example, solutions that address maternal health, nutrition, and disease awareness in local languages are already showing promise and could be scaled for greater impact.

In education, the stakes are even higher. With higher rates of illiteracy and low school attendance, especially for girls, Northern Nigeria risks a deep learning crisis. But Edtech is stepping in. Offline learning platforms, voice-based teaching apps, and localized content are helping bridge the gap. These aren’t just digital replicas of classrooms, they’re reimagined solutions built for low-literacy, low-bandwidth environments.

Aspiring founders and technologists need more than just capital, they need access. Access to information, mentors who understand their challenges, visibility in national and global discourse, policies that support grassroots innovation, and infrastructure that enables digital inclusion. They need validation that innovation doesn’t have to wear a suit or speak a foreign language. It can be built in Hausa, Fulfulde, or Kanuri, and still solve a billion-dollar problem. Innovation is not a preserve of megacities.

The next great African startup may not emerge from a glass tower. It might rise from a workshop in Jos or a tech hub in Minna. And if properly supported, it could scale solutions to problems no one else has bothered to solve. To unlock this potential, we must expand our lens to tell the full story of African innovation in its diversity and complexity. Not just where it glitters, but where it grows slowly, steadily, and powerfully from the ground up.

The initiative aims to discover and support innovative ventures through regional showcases, offering them visibility, mentorship, and a pathway to compete at GITEX Africa in Dubai.

The GITEX Nigeria Roadshow 2025 is designed to discover and elevate Nigeria’s most promising early-stage startups. It invites applications from ventures that already have a Minimum Viable Product (MVP), are registered with the Corporate Affairs Commission (CAC), and operate in scalable sectors such as FinTech, HealthTech, AgriTech, EdTech, Artificial Intelligence, the Internet of Things, and Cybersecurity.

The official kicks off of the roadshow in the South East on July 15, with Enugu as the host city. This leg of the tour will welcome startup founders and participants from Imo, Abia, Ebonyi, and Anambra States. From there, the roadshow will move to the North East on July 17, where Gombe will host innovators from Bauchi, Yobe, Adamawa, Taraba, and Borno. On July 22, the North Central zone will take the spotlight, with Abuja as the host city, welcoming founders from Kogi, Niger, Benue, Kwara, Plateau, and Nasarawa.

The South South region follows on July 24, with Akwa Ibom as the host state. Startups from Delta, Bayelsa, Edo, Cross River, and Port Harcourt are expected to participate. On July 29, the roadshow will make its stop in the North West, where Kano will host tech founders from Kaduna, Kebbi, Katsina, Jigawa, Zamfara, and Sokoto. Finally, the tour wraps up in the South West on July 31, with Lagos playing host to founders and ecosystem players from Ogun, Oyo, Osun, Ondo, and Ekiti.

Startups selected from each region will receive national visibility, storytelling support, and access to global investors and business leaders. They also stand a chance to represent their region at GITEX Africa in Dubai, where fully sponsored exhibition slots will be awarded to the most outstanding ventures.

According to NITDA’s official announcements, this six-city tour reflects a strategic push to democratize access to innovation platforms across Nigeria. At each regional stop, local founders and tech hubs will convene for sessions designed to pitch, learn, and connect, with final evaluations culminating in Lagos ahead of the global showcase in Dubai.

Applications are now open through July. Interested startups can register via the official GITEX Nigeria Roadshow portal. Real-time updates, spotlight features, and post-event recaps are available on NITDA’s social media platforms including Instagram and Facebook via @nitda_nigeria.

This tour marks the first time GITEX is activating such a grassroots innovation campaign nationwide, offering emerging founders a unique platform to scale, inspire, and compete on a global stage.

title: Tech Hubs Remain the Backbone of Arewa’s Tech Ecosystem
excerpt: Earlier this month, StartupKano, a leading tech hub in Northern Nigeria, celebrated its ninth anniversary. Nearly a decade of shaping the tech ecosystem in Kano by nurturing local startups and...
content:
Earlier this month, StartupKano, a leading tech hub in Northern Nigeria, celebrated its ninth anniversary. Nearly a decade of shaping the tech ecosystem in Kano by nurturing local startups and up-skilling the youth. Startup Kano, founded by Aisha Umar Tofa, is one of many tech hubs shaping the tech ecosystem in Northern Nigeria.

Since inception, tech hubs have served as the backbone of the tech ecosystem. A creative lab where startups are born, talents are groomed, and problems are solved through technology. These hubs train developers, incubate ideas, connect founders to investors, and most importantly, localize solutions. 

In 2015, Alumni of the University of Jos, Daser David and Hyginus Horson, founded nHub, the first tech hub in Northern Nigeria. Its mission was simple: grow technical skills and spark local innovation in Jos. Since its founding, nHub has made so many impacts, including organizing Nigeria’s first regional hackathons and launching educational programs like Sevocoder, positioning itself as a pillar of the northern tech capacity.

From this early initiative, dozens of hubs have sprouted across the region, each with its focus, but sharing a core purpose: to develop talent, incubate startups, and translate ideas into solutions.

Kaduna has always been the pulse of the North, Therefore, it wasn’t surprising that less than a year after nHub launched in Jos, Sanusi Ismaila founded Co-Lab in Kaduna. Co-Lab offers mentorship programmes, skills training and networking opportunities. As a pioneering innovation Hub in Kaduna State, In 2022, the Kaduna State government commissioned the CoLab Innovation Campus as part of the Kaduna Technology City project.

StartupArewa was also launched in 2016 by Muhammad Ibrahim Jega, StartupArewa is one hub in Northern Nigeria that has hubs in 19 different states. To nurture young talents in tech skills, the hub has trained a lot of youth with its incubation programme, supported by  Nigeria’s Bank of Industry (BOi) and Coders for Africa at some point.

In Abuja, Aiivon Innovation Hub, founded by Attah Samson Igoche launched in 2017. Initially launched as a co-working space, it gradually evolved into a full-fledged innovation center, supporting over 60 startups and training more than 500 entrepreneurs across different sectors. One of its distinct programmes is the Children Tech Summer Camp, amongst others. Some of its programmes have been backed by organizations like the British Council, AfriLabs, JICA (Japan International Cooperation Agency), and the British High Commission.

Kano State, renowned for its bustling trade and craft, has become a solid force in Northern Nigeria’s tech hub ecosystem. StartupKano and Blue Sapphire Hub founded by Maryam Lawan Gwadabe, have been at the forefront for almost 10 years. The latter has incubated over a dozen startups while directly and indirectly creating over 3,000 jobs. These hubs are blending digital skills with entrepreneurial acumen, offering a new path for Kano’s youth.

 With strong focus in EdTech, JD LAB’s Labspace Innovation hub is leading the tech movement in Minna, Niger State. It partners with universities and public agencies to provide coworking space, mentorship, interest-free seed funding, and capacity building in the educational sector. It’s one of the few tech hubs with a strong EdTech focus in a semi-urban environment. Its collaboration with TEDx and community-based training models shows how innovation can thrive outside megacities. 

As these tech hubs continue to expand their reach and deepen their impact, their long-term success increasingly depends on the policies and institutional frameworks that support them. While hubs are the engines driving innovation on the ground, the policy environment remains the road they must travel. It is within this context that state-level legislation and government interventions are becoming crucial to sustaining and scaling the tech ecosystem in Northern Nigeria.

Recently, Katsina State signed a Startup Bill into law. The legislation establishes a solid foundation for a knowledge-driven economy, offering incentives, support structures, and streamlined processes for tech entrepreneurs. The law enacts ecosystem coordination via Katsina Directorate of Information and Communications Technology (KATDICT), embeds policy support for startups, and creates frameworks for public-private partnership, all of which could significantly enhance the work of local tech hubs, attract investment, and keep skilled innovators in-state. Interestingly, KATDICT is currently headed by one of the co-founders of the first tech hub in Katsina, Kirakira Hub. This indicates that tech hub founders are not just stopping at building capacity; they are also ensuring the implementation of relevant policies.

Across the 19 northern states, the goal remains the same for tech hubs: nurturing young talent in the region. They nurture startups and early-stage ventures, provide skill acquisition programs in coding, UI/UX design, AI, and more, host pitch events and connect founders to funding, run public-good initiatives like voter education, financial literacy, or telemedicine, and serve as co-working and innovation spaces for youth. These hubs are not charity projects; they’re economic stimulants. 

In Kaduna State, the Kaduna Investment Promotion Agency is partnering with the government to create supportive policies for the tech ecosystem. This policy has translated into significant achievements with tech-enabled SMEs supported by hubs contributing significantly to the state’s Internally Generated Revenue (IGR) in 2023. 

Tech hubs are drawing investment, enabling productivity, and inching the digital economy closer to GDP relevance. According to a report by Tech Cabal, fintech and edtech startups across Northern Nigeria collectively reported revenues in the range of ₦500 million to over ₦1 billion per company, with notable concentrations of these hubs in Abuja, Kano and Kaduna. However, despite all the efforts and the accelerated progress since the first hub in 2015, Arewa tech hubs face serious constraints. Infrastructure gaps, such as electricity and stable internet are constant. Funding droughts persist, and policy inconsistency holds many states back. Hubs operating on donor funds often struggle to develop long-term business models.

For these regional tech hubs to scale their impact, stakeholders must act. Governments should follow Katsina and Kaduna’s footsteps by implementing startup policies and laws, providing consistent incentives, and improving infrastructure. Hubs themselves must innovate not just in tech, but in business sustainability. With the right policies, funding, and infrastructure, Arewa’s tech hubs could do even more. Their current impact shows what is possible. Imagine the scale if they had full support; we might see northern startups not just contributing to internal revenues but driving national tech exports and pioneering solutions for Africa’s challenges. The question is no longer whether they can build the future, but how far they can go with the right backing.

title: Is Zamfara Ready to Host the Next Arewa Tech Fest?
excerpt: Over the last few years, Zamfara has undergone a significant digital revolution aimed at upgrading the state and putting it on par with others across the country. But the big question remains: Is Zamfara ready to host one of the region’s biggest tech events?
content:
At the end of the second edition of Arewa Tech Fest, #SpotlightonKatsina, the baton was passed to Zamfara State. This means the state is expected to host the next edition of the fest. But the big question remains: Is Zamfara ready to host one of the region’s biggest tech event?

Over the last few years, Zamfara has undergone a significant digital revolution aimed at upgrading the state and putting it on par with others across the country. That has been achieved through Zamfara Information Technology Development Agency (ZITDA), the state’s governing body for digital transformation. ZITDA is focused on developing and regulating innovation and the digital economy. Its work includes promoting digital literacy among youth, enhancing e-governance, and laying a foundation for sustainable development.

The agency has led the implementation of technology-friendly policies and strategic partnerships with stakeholders like Oracle and NITDA, It has also launched various digital literacy initiatives that align with the global Incubation 2030 goals.

 Policies and Partnerships

Over the next five years, the administration of Zamfara state aims to position the state as a viable tech hub in Northern Nigeria. To attract private investment and accelerate connectivity, Zamfara State introduced a zero-charge Right of Way (RoW) policy for telecommunication companies. This policy allows telecommunication companies to lay fibre-optic cables in the state without paying the usual per-meter fees charged by the government.

One of the first major partnerships under this initiative is with the Nigerian Communications Commission (NCC) through the Universal Services Provision Fund (USPF) to lay fibre-optic cables across eight public institutions, spanning 10 kilometres.

Additionally, the state is setting up the Institute of Information Technology aimed at training professionals in AI, blockchain, cybersecurity, data analytics, and more. Earlier in the year, Zamfara State also partnered with Oracle to strengthen digital skills development and stimulate the digital economy.

Insecurity: The Elephant in the Room

But no conversation about Zamfara is complete without addressing the security challenges that have long plagued the state.

According to the government, its digital transformation projects now offer real-time visibility of security hotspots, aiding better mobilisation of security resources.Still, one must ask: What does this mean for Arewa Tech Fest? This is an event that brings together tech enthusiasts, innovators, and investors from across the country and beyond. Is Zamfara safe enough to host an event of such magnitude?

Will participants feel confident travelling to the state? Will the third edition of Arewa Tech Fest attract the same level of participation as its predecessors?

In a recent interview with ChannelsTV, the governor claimed security in the state has improved. The administration has introduced initiatives like the Community Protection Guards, vetted by the DSS and trained as a first line of defence against attacks. It has also increased funding and support to security agencies across the state. Still, skepticism remains. Members of the opposition recently called for the governor’s resignation, citing his unfulfilled campaign promise to end insecurity within three months.

The reality is: the security situation in Zamfara remains fragile, and this could have a major impact on the success of the fest. Security is non-negotiable. Every visitor to the event will weigh the risk.

The Tech Ecosystem

Zamfara currently ranks 36th in Nigeria’s digital cluster, a low ranking that indicates the early-stage nature of its tech ecosystem. But there are signs of growth. Startups like ZamTracka, a platform that helps citizens monitor government activities using tech tools, are gaining attention. In 2024, ZamTracka was part of the Zamfara state delegation at GITEX, a global tech exhibition.

Startup Zamfara is another notable initiative, serving as a local innovation hub for digital skills training. Then there’s AGILE (Adolescent Girls for Learning and Empowerment), which addresses the gender gap in tech by partnering with Zamfara College of Arts and Sciences (ZACS) to develop digital skills curricula for girls in secondary schools.

These are some notable startups that indicate something is happening in Zamfara, slow but meaningful. A tech ecosystem is rising, although still in its infancy.

Arewa Tech Fest

Although the budding tech ecosystem in Zamfara is inspiring and the administration is putting in efforts to attract investment, Arewa Tech Fest is an important conference that represents the pinnacle of Northern Nigeria’s tech ecosystem.

The question stands: Should a state without a mature tech ecosystem and with persistent security concerns host one of the region’s biggest tech conferences? Or should such events be reserved for more established players?

Hosting a conference of this scale requires more than enthusiasm. It demands strategic planning, substantial funding, and guaranteed safety. Yes, the fest could create jobs and attract investors, but it will also require resources—resources that might be better spent curbing insecurity.

Without confidence in safety, the best intentions, partnerships, and innovations might not be enough to draw the crowd.

title: GITEX Nigeria Roadshow 2025 Kicks Off Nationwide Search for Next Wave of Innovators
excerpt: The National Information Technology Development Agency (NITDA), through its Office for Nigerian Digital Innovation (ONDI), has officially flagged off the GITEX Nigeria Roadshow 2025. A three-month innovation tour running from...
content:
The National Information Technology Development Agency (NITDA), through its Office for Nigerian Digital Innovation (ONDI), has officially flagged off the GITEX Nigeria Roadshow 2025. A three-month innovation tour running from June to August, aimed at discovering promising tech startups across Nigeria.

The roadshow will visit Lagos, Enugu, Akwa Ibom, Abuja, Gombe, and Kano, spotlighting early and growth-stage startups with scale able solutions across key sectors of the economy.

The campaign, which was announced on NITDA’s official Instagram page, calls on founders with game-changing ideas to step forward and apply.

According to NITDA, the roadshow is designed to ensure nationwide inclusivity, enabling founders from every region of the country to pitch their products directly to an expert jury made up of investors, innovation hubs, policymakers, and members of the media.

The best-performing startups from each zone will earn fully sponsored spots at the main GITEX Nigeria 2025 event scheduled to hold in Abuja and Lagos from September 1 to 4, with the potential to also represent Nigeria at the global GITEX event in Dubai later in the year.

To be eligible, startups must either be registered with the Corporate Affairs Commission or have an active profile on the Nigeria Startup Portal. They are also expected to have a minimum viable product or a market-ready solution, with strong potential for impact, scalability, and sustainability. Startups working in fintech, agritech, healthtech, edtech, artificial intelligence, climate and green tech, creatives and content, blockchain, and other digital verticals are particularly encouraged to apply.

The roadshow is part of NITDA’s broader strategy to expand Nigeria’s digital innovation footprint, bridge regional disparities in startup funding and exposure, and build a national pipeline of investable ventures. It also aligns with the implementation of the Nigeria Startup Act, which mandates the government to promote digital entrepreneurship and strengthen the local tech ecosystem.

Applications for the GITEX Nigeria Roadshow 2025 are currently open via the official nomination portal, and interested founders are urged to submit their entries ahead of the zonal events. Updates, dates, and outcomes from each state visit will be published via NITDA’s official platforms and the GITEX Nigeria website. 

As the roadshow begins its journey from the South West to the North East, expectations are high that Nigeria’s next unicorn or regional disruptor may emerge from this grassroots innovation tour.

title: Flexisaf, Tespire Among 12 Startups Selected for Mastercard Foundation EdTech Fellowship

content:
EdTech giants Flexisaf and Tespire have been selected as part of Cohort III of the Mastercard Foundation Education Fellowship, in partnership with Co-Creation Hub (CcHub).

The Mastercard Foundation EdTech Fellowship aims to support education technology companies across Africa that are overcoming learning obstacles in K–12, tertiary education, and vocational training.

The third cohort includes 12 startups from across Nigeria that are using technology to make learning more inclusive and accessible.

Tespire is a platform that provides data-driven insights to help primary and secondary school owners increase revenue and improve educational outcomes.

Flexisaf (Distinction) is an AI-powered learning platform that enables schools and tertiary institutions to track student performance, uncover learning gaps, and make data-driven decisions.

The Fellowship offers participants access to a network of investors, coaching and mentoring from experienced founders and industry experts, and up to USD 100,000 in non-equity grant.

“This fellowship isn’t just recognition. It’s just the needed  fuel for our mission,” said Tespire in a social media post, lauding the opportunity.

The Mastercard Foundation believes these startups are developing innovative solutions to address key challenges in enrolment, educational quality, and access to effective learning tools in Africa.

Both Flexisaf and Tespire have strong roots in Northern Nigeria.

title: Katsina State Signs Startup Bill Into Law, Sets Stage for Tech Revolution
excerpt: The Katsina State Startup Bill has officially been passed into law, positioning the state as a formidable player in Nigeria’s growing tech and digital economy, with a move poised to...
content:
The Katsina State Startup Bill has officially been passed into law, positioning the state as a formidable player in Nigeria’s growing tech and digital economy, with a move poised to transform Northern Nigeria’s innovation landscape.

Naufal Ahmad, the Director-General of the Katsina State Directorate of Information and Communication Technology (KATDICT), described it as a “ bold step towards building a knowledge-based economy and making Katsina the next big tech hub in Nigeria.”

This is the first time startups in Katsina have legal recognition. The law offers a structured ecosystem for entrepreneurs providing them with protection, funding opportunities, and the regulatory backing to grow ideas into scale able businesses.

A major highlight of the legislation is the creation of a Startup Fund to finance early-stage businesses, stimulate youth entrepreneurship, and attract matching investments from the private sector. This strategic move aims to dismantle the longstanding “no capital” barrier.

The law empowers the state to partner with or establish innovation hubs, tech incubators, and co-working spaces across all 34 Local Government Areas. Existing innovation drivers like KirkiraHub and Lumilab are expected to be part of this grassroots expansion.

To reduce friction for startups, the bill includes tax incentives, simplified registration processes, and protections for intellectual property. These measures are designed to foster a business-friendly environment and attract both local and international investors.

By creating a predictable and enabling environment, the law sets the stage for the emergence of vehicles like the Katsina Angel Investors Network. The state hopes to position itself on the radar of venture capitalists and impact funds looking for untapped potential in Northern Nigeria.

The Startup Bill mandates the expansion of broadband internet access and tech infrastructure, especially in underserved areas. This includes building data centers, digital service hubs, and ensuring that all 34 LGAs are digitally connected.

Katsina’s education and training systems will also evolve to align with the demands of a tech-driven economy. Coding, robotics, artificial intelligence, and entrepreneurship will become central pillars in schools and skill programs.

The law establishes a Startup Secretariat under KATDICT to serve as the central point for all startup-related government interaction—cutting red tape and enabling ease of doing business.

“This Startup Bill is not just a document—it’s a declaration: The North can build. And we will,” Ahmad added.

title: Arewa Tech Fest 2.0 Closes with Big Ideas, Bold Pitches, and a Rallying Call for Innovation
excerpt: The second edition of the Arewa Tech Fest wrapped up today, May 22, 2025 in Katsina, delivering three days of groundbreaking discourse, startup showcases, and powerful calls to action aimed...
content:
The second edition of the Arewa Tech Fest wrapped up today, May 22, 2025 in Katsina, delivering three days of groundbreaking discourse, startup showcases, and powerful calls to action aimed at transforming Northern Nigeria through technology and innovation.

The final day of the tech convergence saw the presence of the Governor of Katsina State, Malam Dikko Umar Radda, who delivered a keynote address reaffirming the central role of technology in the region’s development. 

Addressing a hall filled with innovators, entrepreneurs, policymakers, and youth leaders, Governor Radda described digital transformation as the engine of Katsina’s economic diversification strategy. 

He noted that the state’s vision was not to replicate the development models of others but to chart its own course using innovation as a lever to break the cycle of underdevelopment.

In a cross-session discussion with the event host, Governor Radda highlighted the importance of public-private partnerships and inclusive innovation in building a better future. He cited Katsina’s recent efforts to integrate technology into governance through initiatives like the Community Development platform, which empowers local citizens to monitor and manage services in their own communities. 

The governor also spoke extensively on the state’s investment in a high-tech surveillance system aimed at enhancing security across frontline local governments, saying over five billion naira was committed to the project. According to him, the use of technology is the only viable way to secure lives in a country where large swathes of land remain ungoverned and difficult to patrol manually.

The day was also marked by a startup pitch competition tagged “Pitchathon,” which drew rapt attention as young tech founders presented their solutions to a panel of judges. 

Three startups emerged as winners, receiving cash prizes of one million naira, five hundred thousand naira, and two hundred and fifty thousand naira respectively. The initiative was designed to spotlight promising ventures and give them a financial boost to scale their ideas.

In an effort to keep participants energized and involved, the event included a live Q&A challenge in which attendees answered trivia questions for a chance to win ₦30,000. The interactive segment served to both entertain and test attendees’ understanding of the themes covered throughout the conference.

Earlier in the day, Isah Rafeal, CEO of Greysoft Technologies, delivered a thought-provoking keynote titled “Gamifying the Future Economy.” In his address, he emphasized the need to make economic participation more engaging by rewarding citizens for eco-conscious behaviors such as recycling, using renewable energy, or supporting sustainable brands. He urged developers and businesses to think creatively about how technology can unlock a more inclusive and sustainable economy.

The event also received goodwill messages from government and corporate representatives. Aminah Katafo, speaking on behalf of the Office of the National Digital Innovation (ONDI), commended the organisers for uniting grassroots tech actors with national stakeholders. 

From the business community, Abdullahi Sani of Falgates Rice and Isah Mukhtar of Fidelity Bank took turns presenting their products and services while encouraging deeper collaboration with young innovators.

As the curtains fell on the 2025 edition, it was officially announced that Zamfara State will host the next Arewa Tech Fest. The announcement drew applause from the crowd, signalling the growing regional ownership of the festival and its mission to decentralise innovation and technology across Northern Nigeria.

With its mix of strategic dialogue, talent discovery, and grassroots engagement, Arewa Tech Fest 2.0 has firmly established itself as a leading force in reshaping the digital future of the North.

title: Arewa Tech Fest 2.0 Lights Up Katsina as North’s Innovation Powerhouse
excerpt: From idea showcases to inspiring declarations about Nigeria’s digital future, Arewa Tech Fest 2.0 pulsed with energy and ambition as it brought together tech innovators, government leaders, startup founders, and...
content:
From idea showcases to inspiring declarations about Nigeria’s digital future, Arewa Tech Fest 2.0 pulsed with energy and ambition as it brought together tech innovators, government leaders, startup founders, and digital enthusiasts in Katsina state.

Now in its second edition, the festival served as a rallying point for the growing tech ecosystem in Northern Nigeria, with the theme “Innovating for Impact: Technology as a Catalyst for Economic Transformation.” The event spotlighted how local innovation can drive inclusion, create jobs, and reshape regional economies.

The festival opened with a strong endorsement from the Katsina State Government. Representing Governor Dikko Umar Radda, Secretary to the State Government Alhaji Abdullahi Garba Faskari described technology as essential for survival in today’s world. “Without innovation and technology, we are done. We will perish,” he warned, affirming the government’s ongoing support for youth-led tech initiatives and global training opportunities in AI and robotics.

But the tech fest wasn’t just about government promises. It was about momentum. Director General of KATDICT, Naufal Ahmad, emphasized that Arewa Tech Fest 2.0 represents a turning point. “They couldn’t imagine our system making space for it. Today, we are not just hosting, we are leading,” he said, describing how the state’s ICT backbone and people-focused digital strategy are setting a new standard for regional innovation.

The National Information Technology Development Agency (NITDA) also lent its voice to the fest’s mission. In a goodwill message, Muhammad Kabir described technology as a transformative tool capable of bridging inequality and sparking prosperity. “Innovation must solve real problems. It must close gaps and build a resilient economy,” he said.

Highlighting the national significance of the fest, Minister of Communications and Digital Economy, Dr. Bosun Tijjani, returned to Katsina for the second time in three weeks, a sign of what he called “deep convictions” about the region’s potential. “I don’t just see land, I see promise, Arewa is blessed with young minds that can power industries.” the minister said. 

From engaging panel sessions to startup exhibitions, the Tech Fest created a platform for collaboration across public and private sectors. Participants explored topics such as green energy for tech infrastructure, smart governance, and youth-led innovation, positioning Northern Nigeria as a rising force in the country’s digital narrative.

The Arewa Tech Fest 2.0 thus concluded not just as a celebration of digital advancement but as a clarion call for Northern Nigeria to lead with innovation, invest in young minds, and transition into a knowledge-based economy.

title: From Boredom to Brilliance: How Schoola Is Rewriting the Rules of Learning in Africa
excerpt: In the buzzing corridors of innovation at GITEX Africa 2025, one northern Nigerian startup stood out for the boldness of its mission: to make learning fun again. Schoola, an innovative EdTech...
content:
In the buzzing corridors of innovation at GITEX Africa 2025, one northern Nigerian startup stood out for the boldness of its mission: to make learning fun again. Schoola, an innovative EdTech startup, is revolutionizing K–12 education by transforming classrooms into engaging game zones. This pioneering platform blends the captivating power of game mechanics with cutting-edge AI for content creation and insightful analytics, effectively tackling the perennial challenges of disengaged learners and overwhelmed teachers with a gamified learning platform that’s earning recognition well beyond Nigeria.

The genesis of Schoola is a compelling story of innovation born from necessity. As Abdullahi Bature, the founder of Schoola, recounted in an interview, “Ah, well, we started during the lockdown.” Bature’s primary venture, IT Central, a software development company based in Kaduna, faced an unexpected lull as the pandemic gripped the world. “During the lockdowns, nobody cared about their website or whatever we are building for them, right? Everybody was just trying to survive.” This period of reflection and a keen observation of the challenges faced by the education sector sparked the idea for Schoola.

“What we saw was the gap; there was no way the schools were assessing the students,” Bature explained, highlighting the cumbersome process of manual assignments and submissions during the lockdown. This pivotal insight led to the initial iteration of Schoola: “a gamified mobile app for learners, and it rewards them for doing school work and it gives them points for everything and takes off points if they fail.”

I admit, I raised an eyebrow at the idea of education becoming a video game. But then Bature dropped this: a student who answered an astounding “500,000 questions before he graduated.” That’s not just engagement that’s obsession, the good kind. “Kids loved the duel mode,” he said. “A child from one location could challenge a friend from another and tournaments that transformed school content into exciting competitions. It made learning competitive and fun.”

But Schoola’s real genius, I realized, was not just in engaging learners but also it was listening to teachers.

However, as schools reopened, a new challenge emerged. Teachers struggled with the dual demands of creating both digital and offline lessons, leading to a drop in user engagement. This challenge became another opportunity for innovation. “Microsoft gave us access to OpenAI in 2022 around June,” Bature recalled. Leveraging this technology, Schoola evolved beyond gamification to address the core issues of curriculum development and teacher workload. This led to the development of their flagship AI-powered solution, Curri.

“What we want to do is to improve, you know, learning outcomes, especially from where we are from, which is Northern Nigeria, if you check the news for the past 10 years, you can see that learners are recording some of the poorest grades in the country, and we believe that people from Northern Nigeria are very intelligent but then from our research we realised that it is rooted in poor teaching methods and an outdated curriculum that no longer prepares students for the future.” Bature emphasized.

Curri directly tackles these issues by leveraging the power of generative AI to assist schools and teachers in creating high-quality curriculum, lessons, and lesson plans with unprecedented speed and efficiency. “For the teachers what takes them 90 minutes to do, in 2 to 10 minutes they can do that and you can see we have saved them time,” Bature stated. Similarly, curriculum development that traditionally took schools months can now be accomplished in a matter of hours.

The impact of Curri extends beyond mere time-saving. As Bature explained, “Curri has been able to save them a lot of time, they can now focus on what is very important, which is different concepts, better pedagogy on global learning. Some of them have picked up some social emotional learning methodology to help their learners… happy teachers, bred happy learners.”

Furthermore, the AI ensures higher quality and accuracy of content, eliminating common errors. “One thing schools kept telling us was that teachers often made basic mistakes such as spelling errors, poorly structured content, but with Curri, that’s changed. The AI is smart, it understands multiple curricula, and it produces content that’s accurate and well-written. That level of quality has become essential.” Bature explained

This was particularly impactful in a partnership with the International Rescue Committee and USAID, where Curri empowered learning facilitators working with out-of-school children in Yola and Maiduguri to create engaging and effective learning materials.

Schoola’s groundbreaking approach garnered significant attention at the GITEX Africa 2025 event in Marrakech, Morocco. Amidst over 100 Nigerian startups showcasing their ingenuity to a global audience, Schoola stood out, highlighting the burgeoning tech ecosystem in Nigeria, with a strong emphasis on AI-driven solutions across diverse sectors. Their presence underscored the immense potential of Northern Nigerian startups to develop hyper-local solutions with the capacity for global impact.

The Edtech’s presence at GITEX Africa is a strategic move towards scaling beyond Nigeria. Bature, a recurring participant at the event, sees it as a crucial platform to connect with a diverse range of stakeholders from across the continent. “GITEX has been for me, the launch pad into more African countries because we leverage on, AI we were able to do things faster, but you also need local context.” This understanding drives Schoola’s focus on “contextualization heavily in the way that we build,” recognizing that effective learning is deeply rooted in local relevance.

While Schoola initially gained recognition for its gamified learning platform, Curri has emerged as its flagship product. As Bature clarified, “Curri is our top line product at Schoola, it is our number one product at Schoola, it is what we are selling so Curri just stands for short for curriculum and it is teachers’ best friend. It helps teachers set lessons, lesson plans and assessment questions. It is also a tool that helps the schools create new curriculum and makes them compete and become better than their peers. Yeah, it is also the tool that will help government get compliance and track the standard every school has.”

And now they’re building something even more ambitious: a small language model trained on every curriculum in the world from 1990 to date. It sounds wild, but Bature is already knee-deep in making it real. “We’re currently building, actively refining, finalising our small language model, which is fluent on all the curriculums in the world and it comes to as way back as 1990. We will build the number one, curriculum tool in the world. That knows every curriculum,” he said, not as a pitch, but as a declaration. And he’s not stopping at English.

“The next step is fluency in top African languages such as Swahili, Hausa, Yoruba, Igbo, Afrikaans, and French,” he said. That kind of linguistic inclusion could be a game-changer, especially in underserved rural regions where language remains a hidden barrier to learning. This commitment to multilingual support underscores Schoola’s vision of improving accessibility and inclusion in education across Africa.

Schoola’s story isn’t just about a flashy app or a clever piece of code. It’s about building something that meets learners and educators where they are—emotionally, intellectually, and culturally. And in doing so, they’ve quietly become one of the most exciting education stories coming out of Nigeria today.

From a lockdown pivot to a continent-hopping AI curriculum builder showcased at a global tech event exemplifies the dynamism and potential of Northern Nigeria’s tech ecosystem. Schoola is proving that when tech understands context, learning stops being boring and starts being brilliant, one gamified lesson and AI-generated curriculum at a time

title: Arewa Tech Fest Heads to Katsina, Aiming to Drive Innovation in Northern Nigeria
excerpt: In 2024, Arewa Tech Fest launched, hosting over 3,000 participants in Kano State, Nigeria. it is back for the second edition, set to take place in Katsina State from the...
content:
In 2024, Arewa Tech Fest launched, hosting over  3,000 participants in Kano State, Nigeria. it is back for the  second edition, set to take place in Katsina State from the 21-22 of May, under the theme, “Innovating for Impact: Technology as a Catalyst for Economic Transformation.”

Nigeria remains a leading player in the African tech ecosystem, raising up to  $410 million in investments in 2024 alone. Therefore, it is normal for such key player to continue reinventing itself by shaping the next generation through accelerators, tech conferences and others. However, these conferences do not cut across all regions.

Arewa, the Northern Nigeria region has a rapidly growing tech community. Yet, opportunities for collaboration and exposure, such as tech conferences and networking festivals, remain limited. Arewa Tech Fest aims to bridge that gap by creating a platform where local talent, startups, and investors can connect and thrive.

Over the years, the region has seen upwards momentum in its  tech ecosystem, with huge potential of becoming a key player in Nigeria’s tech ecosystem. The vision behind Arewa Tech Fest is to create opportunity for the various potentials in the region to thrive.

According to Deji Garuba, co-founder of Arewa Tech Fest and a tech entrepreneur, the festival was born out of a vision to bridge the gap between talents and opportunities.

“It’s about spotlighting the region’s innovation, resilience, and creativity, creating a platform where founders, startups, tech enthusiasts, and investors can connect, learn, and build together,” he said.

“Arewa deserves its place in the national and global tech conversation, and this fest is our contribution to making that happen,” added the co-founder.

Why Katsina?

Katsina, the host city for the second edition is currently ranked fourth in Northern Nigeria’s  tech ecosystem, with a government that is ambitious about making it a thriving innovation hub.

Katsina Directorate of Information and Communications Technology is at the forefront of this transformation, driving digital initiatives across the state. Their involvement in hosting Arewa Tech Fest is part of a broader push to position the state as a digital leader.

According to Naufal Ahmad, the Director General of KATDICT,” Hosting Arewa Tech Fest is a natural extension of Katsina’s journey towards becoming a technology-driven, knowledge-based economy.”

The state was selected by festival organizers in part due to its fast-growing digital momentum.

 “Katsina has quietly built momentum in digital economy and youth engagement, with a forward-thinking state leadership that’s actively supporting tech-driven development,” said Mr. Garuba.

For stakeholders in  Katsina, Arewa Tech Fest is an opportunity to showcase the innovative ecosystem in Katsina.

“ It’s an opportunity to showcase local talent and startups we’ve nurtured through our training and incubation programs across all 34 LGAs and signal to Nigeria and the world that Katsina is no longer just catching up, we’re leapfrogging ahead as a model of inclusive digital growth in the North.” said the DG.

Curbing Migration

In Nigeria, Lagos remains the leading city in the tech ecosystem, with over 600 startups,  and an ecosystem valued at $9 Billion, for investors, Lagos is always bankable.

For many Northern founders, the path to growth often means relocating to Lagos, where funding, networks, and investor access are more readily available.

One of Arewa’s Tech fest goal is to curb the need for migration  by building a reliable tech ecosystem.

“Our long-term goal is to create a self-sustaining, collaborative tech ecosystem in Northern Nigeria—one where young people can ideate, build, raise capital, and scale, without having to migrate,”  said Mr Garuba.

“We want to inspire confidence in local talent, drive investments to the region, and establish Arewa as a true innovation corridor,” he added.

As with many initiatives outside Nigeria’s established tech hot spots, Arewa Tech Fest faces challenges, with preconceived narrative leading the pack.

“The biggest challenge has been changing the narrative—showing that Arewa isn’t just catching up; it’s a key player,” the co-founder shared.

However, the fest remains promising with few visionary investors banking on the North.

title: Nigeria Steps onto the Global Tech Stage at VivaTech 2025 in Paris
excerpt: Nigeria is gearing up to make a historic debut at Viva Technology 2025 (VivaTech), Europe’s largest startup and innovation event which is set to take place from June 11 to...
content:
Nigeria is gearing up to make a historic debut at Viva Technology 2025 (VivaTech), Europe’s largest startup and innovation event which is set to take place from June 11 to June 14, 2025, at the Paris Expo Porte de Versailles in France.

This marks the first time Nigeria will host a national pavilion at the prestigious event, offering a global platform for the country’s growing tech ecosystem to showcase its talents, secure investments, and forge international collaborations.

Spearheaded by the Federal Ministry of Communications, Innovation & Digital Economy, Nigeria’s presence at VivaTech 2025 is designed to spotlight the country’s most promising startups across sectors such as Artificial Intelligence (AI), EdTech, AgriTech, HealthTech, and Telecommunications.

At the heart of this initiative is a national call to select 15 startups that will represent Nigeria at the Paris-based event. These startups will not only exhibit at the Nigeria Pavilion but will also gain access to curated pitch sessions, global investors, tech giants, media houses, and potential strategic partners.

Selected startups will receive:

  • A fully-sponsored booth space at the Nigeria Pavilion
  • Global networking and investor access
  • Pre-event media exposure and pitching opportunities
  • A structured pre-conference accelerator program
  • Travel support, including visa facilitation, flights, and accommodation

Applications opened on May 7, 2025, and will close on May 14, 2025. While screening and evaluation will follow from 13 – 15 May, 2025. The final selection process is expected to conclude by May 18, with onboarding and pre-conference activities starting from May 19.

Interested startups can apply through the official portal: https://fmcide.gov.ng/vivatech2025

Since its inception, VivaTech has grown into one of the world’s most influential platforms for innovation. The 2025 edition is expected to attract over 165,000 attendees, 13,500 startups, and 3,200 investors. Major corporations, thought leaders, and governments gather to discuss and shape the future of technology.

This year, the event will focus on cutting-edge topics including AI, blockchain, climate tech, deeptech, and digital inclusion. One of the spotlight initiatives, the AfricaTech Awards, will also recognize top-performing African startups, an area where Nigeria has consistently shown strong representation.

Nigeria’s involvement at VivaTech 2025 is more than a ceremonial attendance; it’s a strategic move that underscores the country’s ambition to position itself as a leading innovation hub in Africa and a significant player on the global tech scene.

The national pavilion will not only elevate Nigerian startups to new audiences but also signal to the world that the country is ready for big-ticket investments, cross-border partnerships, and cutting-edge innovation.

For a country often defined by its entrepreneurial spirit and youthful tech talent, VivaTech 2025 is a timely and powerful stage.

With its debut national pavilion at VivaTech 2025, Nigeria is not just attending the conversation around global innovation it’s leading one. The initiative represents a bold, forward-facing vision of what the future could look like for Nigerian technology and entrepreneurship.

title: Northino: Bridging Africa's Digital Divide Through Indigenous Language Learning
excerpt: In the commercial city of Kano State, Nigeria, a tech startup is redefining what accessible education looks like in Africa. Northino, a rising force in e-learning, is tackling a problem...
content:
In the commercial city of Kano State, Nigeria, a tech startup is redefining what accessible education looks like in Africa. Northino, a rising force in e-learning, is tackling a problem often overlooked by global education platforms: language exclusion. By delivering digital skills training in native African languages like Hausa, Yoruba, and Igbo, Northino is empowering local communities to “learn local, fit global.”

At the helm of this movement is Abubakar Almuhandis, CEO of Northino, a former Google Developer Student Clubs Lead and long-time digital skills facilitator. His firsthand experience teaching communities across Northern Nigeria exposed him to a common challenge language was a persistent barrier preventing learners from fully grasping tech concepts.

The digital economy is surging forward, but millions are left behind not for lack of ambition, but due to linguistic barriers. “We are bridging the digital and non-digital educational gap in Nigeria and Africa at large, we relate it with how developed countries are moving forward in terms of educational backgrounds and all that they learn in these developed countries” says Almuhandis.
Northino’s use of AI-driven translation models allows learners to access technical content in languages they actually speak and understand, turning what was once a barrier into a bridge.

“What we are doing is simply bridging those gaps and trying to localise educational contents to empower millions of Africans to get the appropriate skills in their native languages and allowing them to add to the global workforce,” he further stated.

From basic computer literacy to advanced backend development, Northino’s curriculum is both robust and relevant. Whether you’re learning Microsoft Excel or PHP & MySQL, the courses are tailored not just for accessibility, but also for cultural context. This balance of modern tech training and local relevance is what sets Northino apart in the crowded Edtech landscape.

Founded in March 2024, Northino may be a young startup, but its impact is already rippling through the region. Almuhandis noticed how language barriers hindered learning in digital literacy workshops, the venture is built on a unique cultural and technical synergy. What sets Northino apart in the increasingly crowded EdTech space is its goal not just to teach tech skills, but to make those skills stick through language and create a global workforce

Northino has quickly gained recognition. The platform clinched first place in the iHatch Startup Incubation Program and was showcased at the Youth Connekt Africa Summit 2024 in Kigali, Rwanda.

Its biggest stage happened this year at GITEX Africa 2025 in Marrakech, Morocco, where over 100 Nigerian tech startups were featured in the country’s pavilion. For Almuhandis, this was more than just a business opportunity, it was a moment of regional pride.

“I believe it is more of a responsibility to represent, so when you find yourself going out for such kinds of events, one thing you know is that you are representing your country, you are representing the startups within your community” he said.

GITEX Africa also revealed just how universal Northino’s mission is. “The problem we’re solving isn’t unique to northern Nigeria, it’s shared by communities across Africa,” Almuhandis noted. He used the opportunity to connect with founders, investors, and policymakers from across the continent, sparking plans for regional expansion and cross-border collaboration.

Northino is now exploring strategic partnerships with governments, NGOs, and educational institutions that share its vision of inclusive, culturally aware learning.

Northino’s rise also signals a broader shift in Nigeria’s tech ecosystem. Often overshadowed by Lagos and Abuja, northern Nigeria is beginning to stake its claim as an innovation powerhouse.

“The narrative that northern Nigeria lacks tech capacity is outdated. We do face challenges in funding, awareness, training but we’re growing. The ecosystem is surfacing, and everyone has a role to play.” Almuhandis emphasized.

With its foundation laid and its mission validated, Northino is setting its sights higher. The team is actively developing new features, expanding language support, and building partnerships to scale its platform across more African countries.

“We believe we can’t do it alone. To really make the impact we envision, we need the support of governments, institutions, and communities across Africa.”

Northino is not just an Edtech startup, it’s a cultural revolution powered by code and compassion. As it continues to break digital barriers with local voices, it’s proving that innovation rooted in identity is not only possible but powerful.

title: Flowdiary is Bridging the Digital Gap Through Tech Education in Hausa
excerpt: Flowdiary is rethinking how digital education works by teaching tech skills entirely in Hausa and the results speak for themselves. From Android development to Professional UI/UX Design, the online platform...
content:
Flowdiary is rethinking how digital education works by teaching tech skills entirely in Hausa and the results speak for themselves. From Android development to Professional UI/UX Design, the online platform has trained over 6,000 students, delivering career-ready digital education to young Nigerians in a language they understand.

Founded by Muhammad Auwal Ahmad, Flowdiary began as a bold experiment to remove language barriers and expand access to the digital economy. “We are taking a way forward to make digital skills easy and accessible to brothers, friends, and youngsters,” Ahmad said. “Teaching computer skills in Hausa makes it affordable, easy to understand, and available to everyone.”

The startup is anchored on three core pillars. The first is accessibility through language, delivering lessons in Hausa to simplify complex tech topics. The second is mentorship, every student automatically gets a tutor who also acts as their mentor, helping them navigate not just course content, but their career paths.  The third and final pillar is self-reliance, giving learners the skills to freelance, launch startups, or work remotely.

Since its official launch on March 18, 2022, Flowdiary has grown from under 1,000 users to a rapidly expanding platform that now includes courses in Web Development, Digital Marketing, Cybersecurity, Graphic Design, Video Editing, and Social Media Strategy.

The startup’s progress hasn’t gone unnoticed. It won Best EdTech Startup from Arewa Computer Library in 2022, emerged winner of the National App Challenge organized by the Ministry of Youth and Sports in 2023, and took first place at the Yobe State Innovation Challenge in 2024.

This year, Flowdiary achieved a historic milestone by being selected among Nigeria’s top 12 startups to represent the country at GITEX Africa 2025. Although Ahmad himself did not attend the event, he expressed profound pride in their achievement. 

“Taking Flowdiary to a global stage is something that we are proud of, It shows that we are solving a real problem,” he said.

The three-time founder is also clear-eyed about the realities facing tech startups in Northern Nigeria. Reflecting on his earlier ventures like Sky Villo and Stack Plaza, he said he quickly learned that success in the tech world goes beyond just good ideas; it requires mentorship and strategic growth. 

He believes solving problems should always come before chasing investment, emphasizing that startups and any early-stage venture should first focus on product-market fit and real-world value. The right opportunities will follow.

“Mentorship is more important than funding sometimes. If you get funding but don’t know how to manage it, you just run around in circles. We focused on solving real problems first, and the opportunities followed,” he said.

Following GITEX, Flowdiary is opening up to international partnerships aiming to secure mentorship, internship, and employment pathways for its students. The broader vision is clear: to make digital education not just more accessible, but more effective, and to make sure that young people can use what they learn to build careers.

Flowdiary’s broader vision remains unchanged: a Northern Nigeria where the language barrier no longer limits access to digital education, where mentorship is readily available, and where young people can build successful, self-reliant careers in technology.

“We will continue to impact our fellow youngsters, educating them with computer skills, giving them mentorship, and providing them with courses that build careers. By the grace of God, we will double and double on what we are doing,” Ahmad ended.

title: Powering the Unplugged: How Interface Africa Is Delivering Solar Energy and Financial Access to Nigeria’s Forgotten Communities
excerpt: The Problem Across Nigeria, millions of households are struggling with stable power supply, some communities are completely off grid and electricity is a luxury, Interface Africa, one of the startups...
content:
The Problem

Across Nigeria, millions of households are struggling with stable power supply, some communities are completely off grid and electricity is a luxury, Interface Africa, one of the startups that represented Nigeria in GITEX Africa is trying to solve that problem. 

The problem Interface Africa is solving is simple: accessible solar home systems for all. The company is building a digital bridge between underserved households and essential services. Not offering just clean energy, but also access to microfinance and fast-moving consumer goods (FMCGs).

When most people think of Nigeria’s tech ecosystem, the spotlight usually beams on Lagos. But quietly disrupting the narrative from the Federal Capital Territory (FCT) is Interface Africa, an Abuja-born startup redefining how last-mile services reach marginalized communities.

With over 45,000 homes and businesses already lit up by its affordable solar solutions, the startup is on a mission to bridge the critical infrastructure gap for underserved communities—starting with power, but reaching far beyond. According to founder and CEO Al Amin Idris, Interface Africa focuses on communities that are completely off the grid.

“These are the most excluded in terms of social amenities. So we take energy, financial services, social amenities and other essentials to them: starting with solar, because access to energy is a universal challenge,” he explained.

The Solution

In energy, the startup helps solar providers penetrate hard-to-reach markets. In finance, it delivers flexible loan and savings products to help households build security. And in the FMCG space, Interface Africa ensures that critical goods can get to the communities that need them most.

At the heart of its model is affordability. “People want to go solar,” said Idris, “but they can’t afford the outright cost. We enable them to spread it out and pay over time.”

But Interface Africa’s ambition goes  beyond energy access. For Idris, the real mission is reshaping the way technology reaches people in Nigeria. 

“There’s a huge disconnect between what people are building and the market they’re addressing. Everyone’s focused on Lagos. We saw a gap, and we stepped in to fill it.”

GITEX AND THE FUTURE

That vision was on full display when Idris represented Nigeria at GITEX Africa 2025, a major turning point for the startup. 

“We’ve closed multiple partnership agreements, begun investor conversations, and connected with development agencies that are helping amplify our story,” he said.

More than just growth, Interface Africa is chasing global relevance. “We don’t just want to be out there saying we’re from Northern Nigeria. We want to be out there because we’re building world-class, excellent products that deserve to be on the global stage,” Idris emphasized.

Looking ahead, Interface Africa plans to raise seed funding, expand into new African markets, and deepen its reach within Nigeria. It also aims to become a blueprint for tech-driven impact in underserved regions. With a sharp eye on execution and deep faith in local talent, Idris remains optimistic: “We have the skills, the talent, the network, and the expertise. Now it’s time to build great companies that show the world what the north is made of.”

In Interface Africa, the future of inclusive tech isn’t just a dream—it’s already lighting homes, fueling growth, and turning forgotten communities into hubs of possibility.

title: Wuse Zone 3 Marketplace: Powering through the years
excerpt: Computers are at the core of innovation, everything in the world of technology begins on a computer. So, how do computer sellers in Abuja who have been in the business...
content:
Computers are at the core of innovation, everything in the world of technology begins on a computer. So, how do computer sellers in Abuja who have been in the business for decades maintain a thriving business?

Abuja is home to various marketplaces but tucked within the hustle and bustle of Wuse Zone 3 lies a thriving computer marketplace.

This cluster of shops have been selling everything tech-related for over two decades, serving not just the Abuja community but customers from across Nigeria. From selling to repairing computers and its accessories, the vendors cater to a different niche within the tech ecosystem.

This market plays a vital role in Abuja’s technological advancement. Whether for startups or government parastatals, it offers easy access to cutting-edge tech products and services.

Compovine, one of the oldest businesses in the area, has operated there since 2005. For the General Manager, Mr. Adepitan Abiodun, the journey has been rewarding.

“I think you can only truly see the change through revenue growth over the years, and the numbers have been quite impressive,” he said.

The evolution of technological needs has significantly influenced how sellers market their products.

For wholesalers like Compovine, early strategies were rooted in traditional one-on-one marketing, which was the norm before the digital revolution. 

This approach required businesses to focus on the 4 Ps of marketing: Product, Price, Place, and Promotion, said Mr Abiodun.

But technology has changed the strategy. For instance, the “Place” aspect has become less relevant in today’s digital world. Physical location is no longer a barrier to reaching customers. Therefore, businesses like Compovine are adapting by leveraging technology to expand their reach.

“Wherever you are, people can access your product and have it shipped. With the advent of technology, it’s easier, and you can reach more people. It is very precise.”

However, broader accessibility hasn’t necessarily changed their business model. From its inception, Compovine was built on wholesale, and it still thrives on that foundation.

With technology evolving rapidly and innovations emerging constantly, it can be challenging to keep up. But for gadget sellers, staying up-to-date is non-negotiable.

“If we can talk about the gadget, every gadget has now been improved, everyone has been advanced, and it cuts across every technology. We must keep updating them because we don’t want to be left behind, and every gadget is important now because it has the advanced version. For example, any one of the new laptops that doesn’t have the A. I compatability It is not relevant; we are in the era of artificial intelligence, and everything we are doing now must have that. 

That said, the constant updates can be daunting, especially for wholesalers buying in bulk. But Mr. Abiodun sees it differently.

He believes the rise of new technology has complemented the vision of technological equipment (computer) sellers.

“It only complements whatever we are doing because all of us have the same goal: making technology accessible to people. Everyone is playing their part in making this a reality, and I think we are complementing each other,” he added.

Acorn Memories and Networks is another long-standing player in the Wuse Zone 3 market. The company decided to open a shop in the area during its sixth year in business.

“Zone 3 is the computer hub of the city. We were initially in Zone 4, but as the competition became more serious, we opened a branch in the middle of the market so as to attract more walk-in customers,” said the General Manager of the company.

In a marketplace centered around computers and accessories, competition is intense. But business owners have learned how to stand out.

Acorn’s GM explained that the company built its reputation around providing authentic products, which has helped it remain competitive.

“We built our name around original and reliable IT supply, and that has kept us going,” he said.

For Onyeka Chukwu Lawrence, of Prime Choice Technologies Ltd, owning a computer business in Wuse Zone 3 is especially rewarding because Abuja is the administrative capital of Nigeria.

“Abuja being the administrative headquarters of Nigeria, that alone helps our business because people here cannot do without computers. So, I will say the business sales are relatively good.”

Still, not every business has had a smooth ride. With the nation’s economic struggles, some business owners face challenges.

Echije Elight of Livinson Computers Limited has run his business from the Zone 3 shopping complex for over 12 years.

“I have been here for 12 years now, but things are not as they used to be before because of the state of the economy. Most times, we have customers that patronise our business. But now, before you see one customer, it takes a long time but we thank God.

In addition to the economic downturn, the rent at the shopping complex remains extremely high.

According to Mr Elight, “The biggest challenge of having a shop here is the prices are very high and most people have the money but most times the owners of the shops like to collect more from people that have extra money than others. So renting shops here are Millions of Naira.”

Despite the high cost of rent, there are long queues of people eager to secure a shop in this prime location.

” There are a lot of people waiting to rent shops in this shopping complex, because the shops are not readily available and for that reason, we face a lot of price of shop increments, service charges increments. Because if you are not ready to pay, there are a lot of people ready to pay to take up your shop. So in that case we are just left at the mercy of nobody to come for you,” said Mr Lawrence.

The Wuse Zone 3 shopping complex might not always get an uplift, and the rent might be exorbitant, but the sellers remain at par with technological advancement and continue to serve their customers efficiently.

title: Arewa Tech Fest: A Beacon of Innovation for Nigeria’s Tech Future
excerpt: When the inaugural Arewa Tech Fest launched in Kano State in 2024, many dismissed it as just another regional tech gathering. But the turnout—over 3,000 attendees—sent a powerful message: Northern...
content:
When the inaugural Arewa Tech Fest launched in Kano State in 2024, many dismissed it as just another regional tech gathering. But the turnout—over 3,000 attendees—sent a powerful message: Northern Nigeria is not only ready for technological advancement; it is eager for it.

Now, with the second edition set for May 21–22, 2025, in Katsina State, Arewa Tech Fest is proving it’s more than just a conference. It’s fast becoming a movement—a catalyst poised to transform Northern Nigeria into a vital force in the country’s digital economy.

Under the theme “Innovating for Impact: Technology as a Catalyst for Economic Transformation,” this year’s fest will deepen the conversation on how technology can drive tangible, lasting change in communities historically left out of Nigeria’s tech renaissance.

For years, cities like Lagos and Abuja have dominated the tech narrative. Arewa Tech Fest is rewriting that script, showing that the North has ideas, talent, and ambition—it simply needs the right platforms and partnerships.

The economic implications are significant. In a region grappling with youth unemployment and developmental challenges, technology offers more than hope—it offers solutions.

By nurturing innovation, supporting startups, and attracting investment, Arewa Tech Fest helps incubate local solutions to local problems. From agri-tech tools improving farming practices to fintech platforms expanding financial access in rural communities, the potential for impact is vast.

More than that, the event fosters vital collaboration—between entrepreneurs, policymakers, investors, and development partners. This spirit of partnership is exactly what’s needed to bridge Nigeria’s digital divide.

title: Sabou Capital Launches $1.5 Million Fund, Targeting 25 African SMEs
excerpt: Serial founder Surayyah Ahmad has unveiled Sabou Capital, a new SME fund poised to bridge investment gaps across Anglophone and Francophone Africa. The fund will inject between $350,000 and $1.5...
content:
Serial founder Surayyah Ahmad has unveiled Sabou Capital, a new SME fund poised to bridge investment gaps across Anglophone and Francophone Africa.

The fund will inject between $350,000 and $1.5 million into 25 late pre-seed to Series A SMEs operating in agriculture and agroprocessing, renewable energy and climate, supply chain, logistics, and mobility sectors.

Deriving its name from “Sabo,” a Hausa term signifying rebirth or renaissance, subtly blended with French tonality, Sabou Capital is a private enquiry firm. It adopts a distinct strategy targeting SMEs ready for expansion but lack conventional financial backing. It will invest in businesses leveraging technology to enhance their operations rather than solely focusing on tech-driven models, with a gender-lens investment strategy, proritizing funding for women entrepreneurs.

According to Ahmad, the diverging vision within Aduna Capital, an angel investment group in Northern Nigeria, led to the creation of Sabou Capital, boasting a broader scope encompassing SMEs in secondary cities throughout Nigeria, Senegal, and Côte d’Ivoire.

The fund anticipates a moderate 2-3x return on investment, in close range to the 3-5x return of private equity, contrasting with the high-risk 10x expectations prevalent in venture capital.

“We operate more as a hybrid—identifying SMEs with growth potential, not necessarily at VC-scale, but with unmet demand capable of leveraging funding and technical assistance for expansion. Consider us more as a micro-PE,” said Ahmad.

Sabou’s differentiated approach reinforces the argument that the conventional venture capital model doesn’t universally fit most African startups.

A pivotal element of Sabou’s strategy involves the addition of Christian Amouo, a private equity professional with extensive expertise in Francophone markets, as a general partner. Amouo previously launched a fund in Cameroon, investing in four companies, three of which remain operational.

Sabou Capital will be launching a roadshow in July. With 20 startups in the pipeline, the firm aims to shortlist two to three for its initial round of investments.

content:
Sudo Africa has unveiled the Digital First Card, a contactless payment solution designed to transform the way Africans handle financial transactions.

The leading fintech company is known for its Open API, which enables the issuance of cards for both local and international use.

Sudo Africa’s latest innovation, the Digital First Card, eliminates the need for physical cards. Instead, it allows users to make payments conveniently using their smartphones.

Financial institutions can issue the digital card by integrating their applications with Sudo Africa’s Software Development Kit (SDK).

The card ensures enhanced security as it is stored in the cloud rather than on the user’s device. Transactions are processed using a temporary encryption key, minimizing the risk of fraud.

Users can make payments via tap-to-pay applications or QR codes, while merchants can accept payments through tap-to-pay-enabled POS systems or by scanning the QR code generated by the customer.
